1 Executive Summary This work examines how microgravity conditions on spacecraft change the development of smoke aerosol relative to smoke on Earth. We perform simulations of particle formation and growth with the goal of capturing smoke dynamics similar to those realized in experiments performed aboard the International Space Station. The simulations provide detailed information about ﬂuid/thermal/particle interactions that cannot be acquired experimentally on orbit. A surrogate material, dibutyl pthalate, is expelled from a hot surface in a rectangular chamber while ambient air is blown through the domain, convecting the developing smoke downstream. The study considers two ﬂow rates, two geometric conﬁgurations, and the isolated effects of gravitational particle settling and thermophoresis. In Earth gravity, buoyancy produces asymmetries in all ﬁelds of interest and ampliﬁes vapor-to-particle conversion near room temperature surfaces at the upper boundary of the simulation domain. Gravitational settling removes large particles from the aerosol, limiting the maximum particle size to ∼ 40 µm and the mode particle size to∼ 5µm. Without buoyancy or settling, the microgravity smoke plume is spatially symmetric and contains very large particles (> 40µm). A bimodal particle size distribution results in microgravity when prominent recirculation occurs behind the hot vapor source.

The distribution is comprised of large particles (> 20µm) associated with long residency time, vapor rich, high temperature recirculation, and smaller particles (< 10µm) that originate farther downstream of the hot vapor source. A distinct large particle mode does not appear in microgravity ﬂows that do not have prominent high temperature recirculation, although the aerosol still contains large particles. Without recirculation, the mode particle diameter in microgravity is∼ 10µm, or approximately twice that of terrestrial smoke. Results show that future experiments should carefully consider and quantify surface interactions and the presence of hot, recirculating vapor, in order to control geometry-dominated features of the particle size distribution.
A manuscript based on this work will be submitted to the journal Aerosol Science & Technology. The ﬁnal document, when accepted, will be provided to NASA.

2 Introduction Gravity affects the evolution of aerosols by introducing buoyancy and particle settling. Buoyant convection modiﬁes the time-temperature history of the aerosol, as well as the spatial distribution of particles, condensing vapor, and thermal energy. Gravity also causes the settling of large particles out of the aerosol, provided the chemistry and vapor concentrations allow for the generation of large particles with appreciable settling velocities. These factors combine to increase particle residency times in high temperature, vapor rich regions in microgravity systems relative to terrestrial or Earth gravity systems (Urban et al., 1998, 2005). As a result, smoke particles produced in microgravity tend to be larger than those produced on Earth (Ku et al., 1995, Urban et al., 1998). Measurements suggest microgravity smoke particles to be 2− 8 times larger than terrestrial smoke particles (Urban et al., 2005). Moreover, large particles (not only smoke particles) persist in microgravity, with mass concentrations of particles with diameter > 100 µm measured at ten-times that of a nominal terrestrial environment (Liu et al., 1991). Total particulate mass concentrations are also more than ﬁve times greater in microgravity (Liu et al., 1991).

Understanding gravitational effects is of practical interest because it assists in the design of mission-critical smoke detection systems for use in microgravity environments, including the International Space Station (Mulholland et al., 2015); systems developed and calibrated for terrestrial use may not perform correctly in microgravity because of inappropriate particle size sensitivities (Urban et al., 2005).
The present work uses numerical simulation to explore the inﬂuence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke growth from a fundamental perspective. We simulate the formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) particles in Earth gravity and microgravity environments. We utilize direct numerical simulation via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach. The smoke originates from pyrolysis vapor expelled from a heated sample in a geometry similar to that considered in the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al., 2015). The intention of this effort is to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and to identify the ﬂuid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences. This study considers two crossﬂow velocities of sufﬁciently low speed that buoyancy cannot be neglected in the presence of gravity.
Simulations are presented to assess the dependence of particle size distributions on thermophoresis, particle settling, and ﬂow geometry.

The paper is organized as follows: we introduce the simulation and modeling methodology, followed by a description of the ﬂow geometry and the parameter space under consideration; we then examine differences in the wake geometry attributable to buoyancy for the lower of two ﬂow speeds; next, we present and discuss instantaneous scalar ﬁelds as a means to describe particle accumulation and growth in the buoyant and non-buoyant wakes that form downstream of the hot vapor source; after developing an understanding of how the particle ﬁelds interact with the ﬂuid dynamics for the low speed cases, we consider the effects of thermophoresis, particle settling, ﬂow geometry, and the higher ﬂow speed; we conclude with a discussion of the results, summarize ﬁndings relevant to future experimentation, and outline directions for future work.

4 Results 4.1 FLOW CONFIGURATION We simulate the formation and growth of DBP particles in air ﬂowing over a heated sample that expels DBP vapor. The simulation mimics the smoldering or pre-conﬂagration stage of a ﬁre studied in experiments performed aboard the ISS (Mulholland et al., 2015). A schematic of the computational domain is shown in Fig. 1. Room temperature air enters a long chamber and ﬂows over a heated rectangular sample. Vapor released from the sample nucleates into particles that grow and are subsequently collected downstream for analysis. The ﬂow is laminar and steady, allowing the two-dimensional representation to present physical characteristics largely representative of the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al., 2015). DBP is used as the surrogate material because its properties are known and its use in modeling is well-established (unlike the materials used in the SAME experiments).

The enhancement factor required for the nucleation expression, Eqn. (20), is deﬁned for DBP ascnuc = 3.2× 10−4 (Nguyen et al., 1987, Pyyk¨onen and Jokiniemi, 2000).
The thickness of the heated DBP source serves as the reference length scale,Lo = 0.0044 m (illustrated in Fig.

1), which is representative of the length scale in the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al., 2015). The air enters from the left with velocity Uo and temperature To = 300 K . We consider two inlet velocities: Uo = 0.08 m/s, the velocity considered in the SAME experiments, and a slightly faster ﬂow ofUo = 0.10 m/s. The upper and lower boundaries are impermeable, no-slip, iso-thermal surfaces (Twall =To). The heated rectangle is also no-slip, has a ﬁxed temperature ofTs = 473.2 K, and releases DBP vapor at a constant mass ﬂux ofq′′ = 8.4× 10−5 kg/m2· s. The mass ﬂux has been selected to be representative of the mass loss data presented by Mulholland et al. (2015). Zero-derivative conditions are imposed for all species and particle ﬁelds at the inlet and outlet. The gravitational acceleration is considered at terrestrial (go = 9.81 m/s2) and microgravity (go = 0 m/s2) conditions.
The inlet velocities and the gravitational accelerations considered represent four cases with varying Reynolds and Froude numbers. A summary of the simulations performed at the two ﬂow speeds and gravitational levels is given in Table 3.

The ﬂags “EG” and “MG” identify the “Earth gravity” and “microgravity” conditions, while1 and 2 identify the Uo = 0.08 m/s andUo = 0.1 m/s conditions, respectively.
Case 1MG is therefore deﬁned to have an inlet velocity of Uo = 0.08 m/s and go = 0 m /s2, corresponding to a Reynolds number Re = 22.3 and a Froude numberFr =∞. In addition to the four base cases listed in Table 3, we examine the aerosol development sensitivity to: (1) particle settling, (2) thermophoresis, and (3) the ﬂow geometry. For this purpose, a series of additional cases, deﬁned in Table 3, are constructed by modifying the setup of Case 1MG and/or Case 1EG. Case 1EG-NS (where NS stands for “no settling”) is identical to Case 1EG, but the settling mechanism has been neglected. Case 1MG-NT (where NT stands for “no thermophoresis”) is identical to Case 1MG, but the thermophoresis transport mechanism has been neglected. Cases 1MG-R and 1EG-R (where R stands for “rotated”) are identical to Cases 1MG and 1EG, except the heated vapor source has been rotated 90◦. In all cases, data is collected and presented at a time oft = 7 seconds.
4.3 NUMERICAL SPECIFICATIONS The domain is non-uniformly discretized by 960 grid points in the x direction and 240 grid point in the y direction. The governing equations are solved on this computational mesh with a second-order MacCormack scheme.

The particle size space is discretized by 45 particle nodes, with the volume of each successive node increased by a factor of 2.25, i.e.vk = 2.25×vk−1. The volume of the ﬁrst node is selected to be the volume of a DBP molecule, v1 =vm = 4.44× 10−28 m3. 4.4 PHYSICAL ASSUMPTIONS All assumptions utilized in this work are listed below.
• From the perspective of thermal conductivity and viscosity, the condensing vapor phase is considered sufﬁciently dilute such thatµ andk are computed for air as a function of temperature and density (Kadoya et al., 1985). Both the air and the condensing vapor are considered calorically perfect gases with constant properties deﬁned in Table 1.
• The Mach number M is only important for ﬂows with M & 0.3. Although the physics are insensitive to variation in Mach number when the Mach number is small, the ratio of sound speed to convective speed imposes a large computational burden. The computational challenge is often remedied with a Boussinesq approximation, but this approach is not valid in the presence of large density variations. Additionally, an elliptical solve for pressure is computationally intractable for the number of iterations required to resolve the particle time scales.

We instead use a scaled dynamic pressure as the reference pressurePo =ρo (c1Uo)2, such thatP⋆ = ραRαT Po , wherec1 is speciﬁed to reduce the effective speed of sound to 8 m/s. The ﬂow ﬁeld was found to be independent ofc1 for the values used.
• All particles are assumed to be spherical.
• Condensed phase DBP properties are deﬁned by their continuum values.
• There is no momentum exchange between the particles and the ﬂuid (the air/DBP vapor mixture);
the particle velocity equals the ﬂuid velocity, augmented by the thermophoretic velocity and the stokes settling velocity. The stokes settling velocity is assumed to apply for all particles in the domain (including the large particles).
• The ﬂuid and particles are in thermal equilibrium and have the same temperature.
• Particle diffusion coefﬁcients decrease rapidly with diameter. This poses a numerical challenge due to the lack of a physical mechanism for diffusing numerical errors.

For this reason, the minimum diffusion coefﬁcient considered in the particle mass fraction transport equations corresponds to the ﬁfth particle size node – any node greater than the ﬁfth node is assigned the particle diffusion coefﬁcient of the ﬁfth node.
• The mass ﬂux of DPB from the heated rectangle is spatially uniform and all surfaces have spatially uniform temperature.
• Particles that impact a solid surface “stick” with100% efﬁciency, and are removed from the ﬂow.
• The aerosol does not achieve a rigorous steady-state because particle evolution continues (slowly) in regions of the ﬂow with recirculation, particularly behind the hot vapor source. The recirculation is characterized by high temperatures, long particle residency times, and the continuous introduction of additional vapor. The hydrodynamic and thermal ﬁelds, conversely, become steady after only a few seconds. Although a rigorous steady-state does not exist, all aerosol features develop and effectively stabilize shortly after the hydrodynamic ﬁelds. We therefore present all results at timet = 7 seconds, which is considered to be the effective steady-state. At his time, all ﬁelds are either steady, or changing at a rate that does not affect the conclusions drawn from the simulations.

4.5 FLUID FLOW, TEMPERATURE, AND MASS FRACTION The velocity ﬁeld controls the convection of thermal energy, condensible species vapor, and particles.
Vorticityω, deﬁned as the curl of the velocity vector ω =∇× u, (31) is positive in regions of the ﬂow where ﬂuid rotates counterclockwise, and is negative in regions where the ﬂuid rotates clockwise. The sign and magnitude of vorticity therefore identiﬁes the location, orientation, and intensity of vortices and boundary layers.
Figure 2 shows the steady dimensionless vorticity. Panel (a) shows Case 1MG and panel (b) shows Case 1EG. The grey rectangles represent the heated vapor source. Red ﬂuid rotates counterclockwise (positive vorticity) and blue ﬂuid rotates clockwise (negative vorticity). Immediately upon entering the channel, the ﬂuid at the walls is brought to rest by the no slip condition, signiﬁed by the large vorticity gradients in the upper and lower left corners of panels (a) and (b). As the ﬂuid travels downstream from left to right, boundary layers develop symmetrically on the upper and lower walls due to viscous diffusion. Further downstream, the heated rectangle reduces the cross-sectional ﬂow area, and the pressure ﬁeld accelerates the ﬂuid through ﬂow paths above and below the heated vapor source.

The microgravity case in panel (a) remains symmetric near the heated vapor source, whereas the Earth gravity case in panel (b) develops an asymmetry with the majority of ﬂuid passing below the heated vapor source (indicated by larger vorticity magnitudes below than above). Comparatively low vorticity values on the downstream side of the rectangles indicate the presence of low speed, recirculating wakes. The microgravity wake in panel (a) is symmetric, whereas the Earth gravity wake in panel (b) is asymmetric. As the ﬂuid continues to ﬂow downstream, the boundary layers thicken in both cases and the ﬂuid exits the domain to the right. Variations in density due to heat transfer from the rectangle have inﬂuenced the vorticity ﬁelds via baroclinic torque and buoyancy. Because there is no gravity in Case 1MG in panel (a), density variations due to heating do not disturb the symmetry of the ﬂow ﬁeld. The asymmetry apparent in panel (b) is due to buoyancy effects.
Temperature ﬁelds with overlaid velocity vectors are shown in Fig. 3 at time t = 7 seconds. Panel (a) shows Case 1MG and panel (b) shows Case 1EG. The downstream portion of the domain has been expanded for clarity. Velocity vectors in panel (a) show a symmetric wake proﬁle with two counterrotating vortices surrounded by dividing streamlines.

Panel (b) shows an asymmetric buoyant wake, also with two counter rotating vortices: one near the lower right corner of the heated vapor source, and another near the upper right corner of the heated vapor source. Both panels show hot ﬂuid in white, warm ﬂuid in red, and room temperature ﬂuid in black. Thermal energy diffuses from the heated vapor source to the adjacent ﬂuid. Hot ﬂuid convects energy downstream and cools while diffusing energy to cooler ﬂuid and the isothermal upper and lower walls. The highest temperatures appear near the heated surface and in the wake. In both cases, the gas in the center of the channel exits the domain at greater than 350 Kelvin. The microgravity case maintains a symmetric temperature ﬁeld because there is no gravity, and therefore no asymmetric coupling between the vorticity and temperature via buoyancy. In panel (b), buoyant convection resulting from gravitational forces caries the low density, hot ﬂuid towards the upper surface. As the hot ﬂuid encounters the isothermal upper surface, a thin thermal boundary layer develops. Hot ﬂuid cools rapidly when in close proximity to the upper surface due to the thin thermal boundary layer.
DBP vapor mass fraction is shown in Fig. 4 at time t = 7 seconds. Panel (a) shows Case 1MG and panel (b) shows Case 1EG.

Consistent with the vorticity and temperature, the DBP vapor mass fraction is symmetric in Case 1MG and asymmetric in Case 1EG. The highest mass fractions of DBP (approximately 0.05) appear in white on the immediate downstream side of the heated vapor source in both panels (a) and (b). The recirculating wakes in both cases contain a small concentration of DBP vapor, but are encompassed by streaks of DBP vapor issuing from the upper and lower surfaces of the heated vapor source. In Case 1MG, the DBP vapor streaks interact via diffusion at the downstream side of the wake and eventually merge. In Case 1EG, merging velocity characteristics, indicated by the merging velocity vectors at the downstream side of the wake, rapidly combine the upper and lower vapor streaks.
In both Case 1MG and Case 1EG, the majority of the vapor is consumed before the domain outlet.

4.6 P ARTICLE NUCLEATION, NUMBER DENSITY , AND SIZE The particle nucleation rate is a function of vapor mass fraction and temperature (and pressure). Figure 5 shows the DBP nucleation rate at time t = 7 seconds for Case 1MG in panel (a) and Case 1EG in panel (b). Panel (a) shows that nucleation occurs exclusively downstream of the heated vapor source in Case 1MG, and most rapidly at a rate of∼ 1012 [ m3· s ]−1 near the periphery of the recirculating wake.
Nucleation does not occur at a signiﬁcant rate anywhere in the wake. The nucleation rate decreases quickly after approximately ten dimensionless length units downstream of the heated vapor source.
Panel (b) shows two primary zones of nucleation in Case 1EG: downstream of the upper wake vortex and in the region downstream and above the upper wake vortex, near the upper surface. Nucleation occurs at a higher rate,∼ 1014 [ m3· s ]−1 , in Case 1EG than in Case 1MG.
Particle number densities at timet = 7 seconds are shown in Fig. 6 for Cases 1EG and 1MG in panels (a) and (b), respectively. Panel (a) shows a particle number density of∼ 1010 m−3 at the center of each counter-rotating wake vortex.

Thermophoretic forces prevent particles from contacting the downstream surface of the heated vapor source (this will be demonstrated in Section 4.8), resulting in a void of particles between the heated vapor source and the particle-dense wake vortices. Particles are also less numerous on the downstream side of the recirculating wake: particles do not nucleate in this region, dividing streamlines prevent particles from being convected into this region, and low diffusion rates limit particles from rapidly diffusing into this region. Even further downstream, the particle number density remains symmetric, with the largest particle number densities of∼ 1011 m−3 appearing slightly separated from the symmetry line on top and bottom. No particles appear near the upper and lower surfaces. Panel (b) shows the particle number densities for Case 1EG. More particles accumulate in the upper wake vortex than in the lower wake vortex. The Case 1EG wake contains fewer particles than the Case 1MG wake. In Case 1EG, a high particle concentration of nearly ∼ 1012 m−3 appears over a large area near the upper surface due to the high nucleation rate in the region. Signiﬁcantly more particles appear in this near-wall region than anywhere in the Case 1MG particle ﬁeld.

Unlike Case 1MG, Case 1EG contains particles throughout the entire vertical span of the ﬂow chamber: particles that appear in lower concentrations near the bottom wall have arrived there via the gravitational settling mechanism. Particles that settle are sufﬁciently large to be removed from the aerosol via gravity. This can be demonstrated by considering the spatial distribution of particle size.
The diameter of average massdm is deﬁned by dm = ( 6 π ∑Ns i=2viQi ∑Ns i=2Qi )1/3 . (32) Figure 7 shows the diameter of average mass at timet = 7 seconds for Case 1MG in panel (a) and Case 1EG in panel (b). The diameter of average mass is typically 10− 20µm in both cases. The diameter of average mass is notably smaller in regions where nucleation rates or particle number densities are large (near the upper surface in Case 1EG, for example). The Case 1EG wake contains only isolated regions of large particles, including in the upper and lower vorticies, while the entirety of the Case 1MG wake contains large particles. A signiﬁcation region downstream and below the heated vapor source contains very large particles in Case 1EG: particles sufﬁciently large to rapidly settle out of the ﬂow dominate this region. Downstream of the Case 1MG wake, the diameter of average mass depends signiﬁcantly on cross-stream position, but not on stream-wise position.

The largest particles appear on the symmetry line, corresponding to a region of low particle number density.
The particle size distribution (PSD) provides a quantitative measure of particle number and size. We construct the size distribution by numerically “collecting” a volume of the aerosol and counting the number of particles in each node k contained in the sample. The sample is collected by computing the ﬂux of particles through a vertical plane located at x′, where x′ is the dimensionless distance from the downstream surface of the heated element, indicated in Fig. 1. The collected number density ¯Qk [ m−3] of particles belonging to sizek is therefore ¯Qk = 1 h ∫ h/2 −h/2 u (y)Qk (y)dy, (33) where h = 6.82Lo is the height of the domain and u is the x-component of the velocity vector. The collected number density ¯Qk is therefore the number of particles collected per unit time and per unit volume at the measurement planex′.

Figure 8 shows the particle number densities for Cases 1MG and 1EG at downstream measurement plane x′ = 26 at time t = 7 seconds. Case 1MG is shown in red and Case 1EG is shown in black.
The Case 1MG distribution contains particle diameters ranging from hundreds of nanometers to tens of micrometers, with a small percentage of particles approaching one hundred micrometers. The most frequent size is approximately 5µm. The Case 1MG distribution contains two local maximums: one at 5µm and another at 30µm. The Case 1EG distribution contains only one local maximum at5µm. Case 1EG contains a larger number density than Case 1MG for all particle sizes < 20 µm, and Case 1EG contains no particles> 40µm – these large particle settle out of the system. Case 1EG contains orders of magnitude more particles< 5µm than Case 1MG.
4.7 EFFECT OF P ARTICLE SETTLING In order to isolate the effects of particle settling, we modify Case 1EG by neglecting the settling mechanism (by settinguss⋆ j,k = 0). This case is referred to as Case 1EG–NS, where NS stands for “no settling”.
Figure 9 compares size distributions for Case 1MG, Case 1EG, and Case 1EG–NS at measurement planex′ = 26 at timet = 7 seconds. The Case 1EG–NS distribution is considerably wider than the other cases. It contains particles ranging in size from nanometers to 100 µm.

Case 1EG–NS also contains two local maxima in the particle size distribution, much like Case 1MG and unlike Case 1EG. Eliminating the settling mechanism has expanded the size distribution to include both smaller and larger particles, and has also introduced a new local maximum in the size distribution near 35µm.
4.8 EFFECT OF THERMOPHORESIS Figure 10 shows particle number densities at time t = 7 seconds for Case 1MG in panel (a) and Case 1MG-NT in panel (b) (where NT stands for “no thermophoresis”). When thermophoresis is active, as in panel (a), particles do not appear adjacent to the surface of the heated vapor source; the temperature gradient is large normal to the surface, and thermophoresis forces the particles out of this region.
When thermophoresis is inactive, particles are able to remain near the hot surface. In this region, the temperature is sufﬁciently high to cause evaporation. Small particles are able to diffuse out of the wake, resulting in lower particle number densities inside the Case 1MG-NT wake than the Case 1MG wake.
Downstream of the wake, larger particle number densities are present in Case 1MG-NT relative to Case 1MG, following from the decreased number of particles trapped in the Case 1MG-NT wake vorticies.
Figure 11 shows particle size distributions for Cases 1MG and 1MG-NT at timet = 7 seconds. Consistent with Fig.

10, the peak number density in Case 1MG-NT is greater than Case 1MG by approximately a factor of ﬁve – the most frequent particle size is∼ 5µm for both cases. A local maximum appears in both distributions around dp = 30 µm. This local maximum contains fewer particles in Case 1MG-NT than in Case 1MG, potentially because this local maximum is comprised of particles that have interacted with the wake region. In Case 1MG-NT, some of these particles have undergone evaporation and shifted to smaller particle sizes.
4.9 EFFECT OF HEATED VAPOR SOURCE ORIENTATION Figure 12 shows the particle number densities at time t = 7 seconds for Case 1MG-R in panel (a) and Case 1EG-R in panel (b) (where R stands for “Rotated”). Cases 1MG-R and 1EG-R are identical to Cases 1MG and 1EG, except the heated vapor source has been rotated 90◦. The wake regions of Cases 1MG-R and 1EG-R are considerably smaller than Cases 1MG and 1EG, and neither Case 1MG-R nor Case 1EG-R contain particles in their wakes.

The results from Case 1MG-R differ from Case 1MG in that they do not prominently display two high particle number density streaks around the symmetry line, but instead contain large particle number densities everywhere near the symmetry plane.
Case 1EG-R presents large particle number densities near the cool upper surface, similar to Case 1EG.
Unlike Case 1EG, Case 1EG-R does not contain particles inside its comparatively small downstream wake region, but instead contains particles in a large recirculation region that appears above the heated vapor source. The number density of particles in the recirculation region directly above the heated vapor source is lower than the particle number density downstream of the recirculation region. Figure 13 shows particle size distributions for Cases 1MG-R and 1EG-R at time t = 7 seconds. Both distributions present a single local maximum in particle size – the local maximum prominent at dp = 30µm for Case 1MG is not present in Case 1MG-R. Consistent with Case 1EG, Case 1EG-R contains fewer particles larger than approximately dp = 10 µm, and no particles larger than dp = 40 µm. The most frequent particle size for Case 1EG-R is the same as Case 1EG (dp = 5 µm). The most frequent particle diameter for Case 1MG-R is dp = 10 µm – approximately two times larger than Cases 1MG, 1EG, and 1EG-R.
4.10 EFFECT OF FLOW SPEED The Case 1 simulations were performed with an 8 cm/s inlet ﬂow velocity. Case 2MG and Case 2EG consider a 10 cm/s inlet ﬂow velocity. Particle number densities and velocity vectors for Case 2MG and Case 2EG are shown in Fig. 14 at time t = 7 seconds. Panel (a) shows Case 2MG and panel (b) shows Case 2EG. Case 2MG presents many features similar to Case 1MG, including symmetry about the center line and high particle number densities in the wake vortices. Case 2MG has an elongated wake associated with a higher ﬂow speed.

Case 2EG differs from Case 1EG in that particles are not prominent near the upper surface until much farther downstream – this is attributable to the decrease in Froude number, and corresponding decrease in upward motion due to buoyancy. Although the particle ﬁeld remains asymmetric, the increased ﬂow velocity has decreased the inﬂuence of buoyancy, reducing interaction with the upper surface. The presence of particles in the lower portion of the domain, as in Case 1EG, is attributable to the gravitational settling dynamic.
Particle size distributions for Case 2MG and Case 2EG computed at x′ = 26 and time t = 7 seconds are shown in Fig. 15. The most common particle size is∼ 5µm for both cases. Case 2EG, unlike Case 1EG, contains particles on the nanometer scale – nucleation begins near the upper surface further downstream, and particles resulting from nucleation remain in the ﬂow near the measurement plane x′ = 26.
4.11 SMOKE VISUALIZATION The simulated smoke is visualized by computing the particle surface area densityS(x) according to S(x) = Ns∑ k=2 πd2 kQk(x). (34) The particle surface area density S(x) is shown in Fig. 16 at time t = 7 seconds. Panel (a) shows Case 1MG, panel (b) shows Case 1EG, panel (c) shows Case 2MG, and panel (d) shows Case 2EG.
Darker regions correspond to large smoke concentrations and white areas contain no smoke.

High concentrations of smoke are apparent in the wake vortices of all cases. The microgravity cases in panels (a) and (c) contain larger and darker wake regions than the Earth gravity cases in panels (b) and (d). Panel (b), corresponding to Case 1EG, presents high smoke concentrations near the upper wall.
The visible smoke in Case 1EG also occupies a larger downstream area than the other cases, resulting from the high nucleation rates near the upper surface. When gravitational forces dominate, wall effects can be signiﬁcant, as demonstrated by case Case 1EG in panel (b). In Earth gravity, the smoke is more prominent downstream than in the wake region. Visual inspection also suggests the Earth gravity smoke to be more sensitive to small perturbations in ﬂow speed than the microgravity smoke (in the conﬁguration tested).

5 Summary We have simulated smoke formation and growth in microgravity and Earth gravity to examine how buoyancy and particle settling affect thermal/ﬂuid/particle interactions and the resultant smoke particle size distributions. The simulated geometry emulates the SAME experiments performed aboard the International Space Station (Mulholland et al., 2015). Dibutyl pthalate (DBP) vapor is released from a heated rectangular sample, which serves as a surrogate for the smoldering material used in the SAME experiments.
Large particles (> 30µm) are present in the wake region downstream of the heated vapor source, and large particle number densities (∼ 1010 m−3) occur inside the wake vortices. The wake contains large particle number densities because dividing streamlines prevent the particles from being convected away, and the particles continue to grow as condensation consumes all available DBP vapor. The particles simultaneously grow via coagulation. Downstream of the wake, two parallel particle streams contain high number densities of both large and small particles. No particles are present far downstream with diameter< 400 nm because nucleation only occurs for a short distance downstream of the heated vapor source. The particle size distributions contain local maximums near dp = 5µm and dp = 35µm for both ﬂow speeds.

The faster ﬂow conditions present a slightly larger wake but this does not manifest as a meaningful difference in particle size distribution. Thermophoresis prevents particles from contacting the heated surface, which has been demonstrated by turning off the thermophoresis mechanism.
Without thermophoresis, particles contact the heated vapor source and undergo evaporation. With respect to the particle size distribution, this has the effect of decreasing the number of large particles and increasing the number of small particles – this supports an assertion that the wake is responsible for producing the largest particles in the system.
When gravity is present, all ﬁelds become asymmetric due to buoyant convection. Upward convection in the faster ﬂow brings DBP vapor into close proximity with the cool upper surface, resulting in locally high nucleation rates near the upper wake vortex and the upper surface. Large particle number densities (∼ 1011 m−3) are present along the upper surface, and slightly lower number densities are present in the upper wake vortex. Comparably few particles are present in the lower wake vortex, where the diameter of average mass is maximized. Downstream of the wake vortices, gravitational settling eliminates all particles with diameter> 35µm.

Unlike the microgravity case, the 8 cm/s Earth gravity case is not bimodal, with a single local maximum at dp = 5µm. Without particle settling, a bimodal distribution results with two local maximums at particle diameters comparable to the microgravity case. Rotating the heated vapor source 90◦ dramatically reduces the wake volume, and no particles appear in the small wake. Rotating the heated vapor source does not affect the Earth gravity case as signiﬁcantly as the microgravity case. Increasing the ﬂow speed from decreases the prominence of buoyancy, delays interaction with the upper surface until further downstream, widens the particle size distribution to include particles on the nanometer scale, and introduces a second local maximum to the PSD neardp = 30µm.
Microgravity smoke presented in this study contains larger particles than terrestrial smoke. When the microgravity PSD is bimodal, the larger mode contains particles with dp > 35µm, while the terrestrial PSD contains effectively zero particles in this size range. Alternatively, the microgravity PSD can be unimodal with a mode diameter of dp = 10 µm – roughly twice that of the terrestrial case.

Results exhibit three primary mechanisms that differentiate the microgravity and Earth gravity smoke: (1) different recirculation geometries and volumes modify the time-temperature-concentration history of the aerosol in regions of high temperature and high vapor mass fraction; (2) particle settling eliminates large particles from Earth gravity smoke, which reduces the maximum particle size and modiﬁes aerosol development by changing coagulation and condensation rates of the remaining particles; (3) buoyant convection can transport condensible species toward relatively cool surfaces, increasing vapor-to-particle conversion.
Each of these factors tend to increase the size of particles in microgravity relative to Earth gravity. However, each of these factors is also highly material- and geometry-dependent: (1) the wake dynamic becomes unimportant if nucleation occurs far downstream of the wake, or if there is a time dependent ﬂow without a stable recirculation region; (2) particle settling is irrelevant if the condensing species forms particles that are too small to settle (the DBP considered in this work forms large particles); (3) if smoke is produced in an open environment, there may not be cool surfaces nearby to increase nucleation rates. In these situations, microgravity and Earth gravity smoke are hypothesized to be more similar.

contrast, a quiescent, enclosed system is a relevant case where Earth gravity and microgravity smoke are hypothesized to differ signiﬁcantly, and is a consideration of future work.

Numerous efforts have examined the combustion of butanol from the perspective of low dim ensional gas-phase transport configurations that facilitate modeling and validation of combustion kinetics. text: 100 5.1 ABSTRACT This chapter reports the results of experiments on the isolated droplet burning characteristics of butanol isome rs (n-, iso-, sec-, and tert-) under standard atmosphere conditions in an environment that promotes spherical combustion. The data are compared with predictions from a detailed numerical model (DNM) that inc orporates complex combustion chemistry, radiative heat transfer, temperature depe ndent variable fluid properties, and unsteady gas and liquid transport. Computationa l predictions are generated using the high-temperature kinetic models of Sarathy et al. (2012) and Merchant et al. (2013). The experiments are performed in a free -fall facility to reduce the effects of buoyancy and produce spherical droplet flames. The m otion of single droplets with diameters ranged from 0.52 mm to 0.56 mm was eliminated by tethering them to two small-diameter SiC filaments (d ∼14 μm diameter). In all the experiments, minimal sooting is observed, offering the opportunity for direct compar ison of the experimental measurements with DNM predictio ns that neglect soot kinetics. T he experimental data showed that the burning rates of iso- and sec-butanol are very close to that of n-butanol, differing only in flame structure.

text: 124 5.5 CONCLUDING REMARKS Experimental results of droplet burning under reduced gravity ( O~10-4 g) show that D2 histories of n-, iso-, and sec- butanol are almost identical w hile tert-butanol has noticeably lower burning rates. FSR results suggest that n-buta nol has the smallest FSR with the other three butanol isomers having FSRs close to each other. Numerical simulation using detailed combustion chemistries repo rted by LLNL and MIT. The LLNL model does a good job predicting the D 2 and FSR of n -butanol, but it overshoots the burning rates and FSRs of the other three iso mers. The MIT model best predicts the evolution of droplet diameter for iso-butanol and provides acceptable predictions for the other isomers. The predictions for tert-but anol from either LLNL or MIT model are not as aligned with the data as for the other iso mers which suggest room for improvement in the future. Finally, the influence of chemical kinetics, thermodynamic and transport properties of Sarathy et al model (LLNL) for droplet combustion is individually analyzed. The rigorous computational analysis highlights that t he difference in transport property coefficients of isomer specific species for LLNL model is responsible for the deviations observed for droplet combustion experiments. A reexa mination of updated transport parameters for the LLNL model is thus suggested.

text: 134 6.1 ABSTRACT Cool flame combustion of individual and isolated sub-millimeter sized n-heptane (n-C7H16) and n-decane ( n-C10H22) droplets are computationally investigated for atmospheric and higher operating pressure (25 atm) conditions with varying leve ls of ozone (O 3) mole fractions in the surroundings. A sphero-symmetric, one-dimensio nal, transient, droplet combustion model is utilized, employing reduced versions of det ailed chemical kinetic models for the fuel species and an appended ozone reaction subs et. Comprehensive parametric computations show that the regime of the cool flame burning mode and the transition from cool to hot flames are sensitive to the changes o f O3 loading, pressure, diluent variation, the strength of initiation source, and the influence of fuel vapor pressure at the ambient condition. For both fuels and over a range of O 3 concentrations in the ambient, sustained cool flame burning can be directly produced, even for sub-millimeter sized droplets. Over some range of O 3 concentrations, operating pressure, and drop diameter, a self-sustaining, continuous cool flame burn can be produced without incurring a hot flame transition. For sufficiently high O 3 concentrations, combustion initiation is always followed by a hot flame transition.

For fuels with flashpoints h igher than the ambient temperature (e.g. n-decane), the reaction progress is limited by the local fuel va por concentration and the necessity to heat the droplet surface to sufficiently high temperatures to produce locally flammable conditions. As a result, the initi al transient for establishing either cool flame or hot flame transition is significantly long er for high flash point fuels. The transition of locally partially premixed reaction to diffusive burning conditions is more evident for high flash point conditions. 6.2 INTRODUCTION Observations of long-duration cool flame burning of isolated n-alkane droplets with a large initial diameter (Do) under microgravity conditions [1-5] demonstrate an interesting venue for the study of diffusive cool flame burning. The term, “cool flame” has been historically associated with observations involving homogenously premixed conditions [6, 7]. The cool flame diffusive bur ning mode of an isolated drople t is governed by a strong coupling between the low-temperature chemistry and diffusive tr ansport that is significantly different than for premixed cool flame, static re actor or flow reactor conditions.

text: 173 7.1 ABSTRACT This chapter reports simulation results of oscillatory cool fla me burning of an isolated, sub-millimeter sized n-heptane (n-C 7H16) droplet in a selectively ozone seeded nitrogen-oxygen environments at atmospheric pressure. An evolutionary one-dimensional droplet combustion code, as discussed at length in chapter 2, e ncompassing relevant physics and detailed chemistry was employed to explore the role s of low-temperature chemistry, ozone seeding, and dynamic flame structure on burnin g behaviors. For XO2=21% and a range of selective ozone seeding, near-quasi-steady cool flame burning is achieved directly (without requiring hot flame initiation and r adiative extinction). Under low oxygen index conditions, with 5% ozone seeding (v/v), a nea rly quasi-steady cool flame is initially established that then transitions to a dynam ically oscillating cool flame burning mode until the droplet is completely consumed. It is fo und that the oscillation is initiated by the depletion of fuel vapor-oxidizer layer evolving near the droplet surface and its dynamic re-establishment through liquid vaporization and va por/oxidizer transport.

text: A kinetic analysis indicates that the dynamic competition between the reaction classes- (a) degenerate chain branching and (b) chain termination/propagation - along with continuous fuel and oxygen leakage through the flame location contributes to an oscillatory burning phenomena of ever-increasing amplitude. Analysis based on single full-cycle of oscillatory burning shows that the reaction pr ogression matrices (evolution of heat and species) for QOOHchain propagation/termination r eactions directly scales with th e gas phase temperature field. On the contrary, the QOOHdegenerate branching reactions undergoes

document: Dissertation_Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka.pdf
text: 174 three distinct stages within the same cycle. The coupled flame dynamics and kinetics suggest that in the oscillatory burning mode, kinetic processes dynamically cross through conditions characterizing the negative temperature coefficient (NTC) turnover temperature separating low temperature and NTC kinetic regimes. The Multi-user Droplet Combusti on Apparatus (MDCA) platform on the ISS [3] has been operated in a mode to initiate cool flame droplet burn ing behavior over a wide range of n-alkane fuels and n-alkane/iso-alkane fuel mixtures, operating pressures, oxygen indices, and diluent compositions.

Ambient condition: P = 1 atm, T = 298 K, XO2 = 10% with balance XN2. 7.5 CONCLUDING REMARKS The dynamics of near-limit cool flame burning of isolated sub- millimeter sized nheptane (n-C 7H16) droplet (D o = 0.5 mm) has been numeric ally investigated under atmospheric pressure condition. To provide the necessary near limit constraint, the oxygen in the ambient was set to a value that is lower than the limiting oxygen index (LOI) criteria for n-C7H16 and ozone (O3) was seeded (5% v/v) to the ambient to accomplish cool flame initiation. Based on the detailed analysis, the following featu res can be drawn as highlighting points for this computational study. 1. At an atmospheric O2 concentration (21%) with 5% O3 (both v/v), sub-millimeter sized n-C7H16 droplet attains direct initiation of cool flame upon ignition e nergy initialization. Heat feedback to the droplet surface stemming from the consequence of ‘pre-vaporized fuel + atomic O’ reaction contributes as secondary initiation energy. 2. For the exemplary reduced O 2 case (10%), the resultant ignition energy escalates the local gas phase temperature ~1150 K, consuming the fuel vapor n ear the droplet, and

document: Dissertation_Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka.pdf
text: 190 simultaneously increasing the O 2 mole fraction ~16% (v/v) following the decomposition of O3. Due to the diffusive/thermo-kinetic balance of heat generatio n, the system attains a quasi-steady cool flame burn for a brief period of time which then enters an ever-oscillatory low-temperature cool flame burn. 3. It is found that within each full oscillatory cycle, the maximu m local gas phase temperature (i.e., flame) resides closest to the droplet, and the flame positions itself to the furthest radial location when its value reaches the cycle minima. At each successive pulse, the flame region (including the reaction zone) progressively grows outward as a result of continuous fuel leakage through the flame location. 4. The inception of oscillation is initiated by the local depletio n of O2 below the critical mole fraction of 12%. This reduction of O2 compels the flame to grow outside to meet the O2 requirement for spherical diffusion flame. 5. Further analyses indicate that the dynamic interaction of degen erate chain branching and chain termination/propagation reaction classes of QOOH asso ciated with the low temperature and NTC kinetic regimes, and continuous fuel leakag e across the flame location contribute to the ever-increasing trends of the oscillation magnitude.

text: 198 8.1 PREFACE TO CLOSURE Combustion of sub-millimeter sized (D o < 1.0 mm) isolated sphero-symmetric liquid fuel droplets has been numerically studied in this thesi s work employing onedimensional CFD code for renewable alcohol fuels and higher n-a lkanes. Methanol (CH3OH) and butanol (C4H9OH, including its four isomers) represent the first category of fuels while n-heptane (n-C 7H16) and n-decane (n-C 10H22) consist of the second category. Two major forms of flame configurations, namely high temperatur e and low temperature (including cool) flames, have been extensively studied. In this dissertation, results pertaining to the high-temperature flames are exclusively related to the renewable alcohol fuels, while the low-temperature flames are examined through th e higher n-alkanes. To emulate the practical droplet combustion in reduced or near-abs ence of gravity condition, all the relevant physics are incorporated in the modeling formu lation along with detailed description of kinetics. For selective case studies, experimental comparison and validation have also been performed on ad-hoc basis against international space station (ISS) and terrestrial drop-tower test data. The unified goal of this research work is to demonstrate the droplet combustion’s unique capab ilities in relation to both th e applied and scientific understanding of fuel combustion.

text: 199 8.2 MAJOR CONTRIBUTIONS a. Understanding the fire-suppression mechanism under zero-gravity environment is important in designing next-gene ration spacecraft fire safety p rotocols. Practically speaking, it is also very relevant to the existing space progra ms in relation to inadvertent fire hazards. Therefore, the necessity to assess the effectiveness of different fire-suppressant mediums is critical. However, testing these suppressants under the g~0 condition is logistically challeng ing and expensive. In this th esis, it has been demonstrated that the computational droplet combustion study ca n contribute to predicting the fire-extinguishme nt behavior of any untested gas eous suppressant. An exemplary case has been reported for xenon (Xe) in chapter 3, the-then considered as a potential fire extinguisher for space application by the Nati onal Aeronautics and Astronautics Agency (NASA). Through exhaustive numerical calculations, it has been unambiguously shown that xenon underperforms compared to other existing firesuppressants due to its uniquely low thermal diffusivity. As a direct contribution from our research effort, NASA also realized the possible drawbacks of xenon as a microgravity fire suppressant and postponed testing and investing resources on it. b.

The mechanistic features of such direct establishment of cool flame are thoroug hly explained to encourage the experimental res earchers to conduct tests on grou nd-based drop tower test facilities. In addition, the oscillatory behavior of such smaller droplet cool flame is further investigated to elucidate the kinetic competitions (i.e ., pathways) responsible for such oscillatory flame behavior. 8.3 FUTURE RECOMMENDATIONS The strength of the current version of isolated droplet combus tion CFD code stems from the simplicity of low dimensional flow field that augments the coupling of large kinetics and other associated thermo-fluid sub-models. To further transcend its capability, the following recommendations are provided in light of the experiences harnessed through the course of this dissertation work. The author believes that each of the three proposals reported here could be a Ph.D. a nd/or M.S. level research topic by their own prospect for future exploration. a. Sooting fuel simulation. To model the sooting fuels, currently, the CFD code has two versions of soot model, namely- the BIN method [1] and the moment method [2]. Both of these soot modeling methods are fairly detailed in nature, therefore the simulation complexity increases tremendously when coupled with detailed gas phase kinetics.

text: 202 b. The inclusion of real gas formulation. The ideal gas law is a t ypically the default choice for the equation of states (EOS) for most of the availab le commercial and in-house legacy codes. This simplified formulation of EOS is fo und to work satisfactorily at ambient and above ambient pressures for both the reacting and nonreacting CFD simulations. However, ideal gas law starts to unde rperform significantly as the gas phase system approaches critical press ure regime for the species of interests. Therefore, to address this concern, the real gas effect should be included and the overall code structure has to be updated and v alidated against experimental targets accordingly. c. Multi-dimensional effect. Although the one-dimensional droplet combustion is simple in terms of fluid physics, it is relevant to the complex spray combustion by incorporating moving boundary effects, unsteady heat transfer, mass diffusion to and from the droplet surface, temperature dependent variable pr operties, phase equilibrium at the interface and radiative perturbation. In order to progress towards real spray arrangement without compromising in terms of kinetic aspect, the next step should be to include multi-dimensional effect for isolated droplet combustion.

 Local depletion of O2 (<13.5%) near the droplet initiates the pulsing behavior with initial small fluctuation in flame temperature.
 The oscillation is found to increase in magnitude with time, and at each successive cycle.
 Dynamic interaction of degenerate chain branching and chain propagation / termination reaction classes of QOOH (within NTC region) is responsible for the observed oscillation.
 Continuous fuel leakage through the flame location assists the oscillation to grow in radial direction with time.

Supplementary Slide # Governing Equations  The complete set of coupled partial differential and algebraic equations are discretized first in space and then integrated in an automated fashion as a set of coupled ordinary differential-algebraic equations in time.
 Spatial discretization is performed according to a node-centered finite volume scheme with a second order accuracy.
 The innermost liquid node is centered at the origin, providing the required no-flux condition.
 The discretized mass flux is represented on cell interfaces and not cell centers, in the manner traditionally referred to as a staggered grid to avoid oscillatory solutions.
 Numerical integration of the final set of discretized equations is performed using a backward difference formula with a variable order of up to fifth order and a variable time step utilizing a fully implicit multipoint interpolation.

Introduction The purpose of this report is to provide a description of the experimental hardware and operations of used in the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments ( ACME) project that is sufficient for informed interpretation of the experimental results. In contrast, it is not the intent of this document to review the project management, engineering development, design process, etc. although such aspects may be briefly addressed. The ACME suite of experiments are being carried out on the International Space Station ( ISS) in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). ACME features investigations with gaseous fuels, such as methane and ethylene. In addition to the fuel state , the current ACME experiments use laminar, non -premixed (i.e., diffusion) flames for their studies. To simplify analysis, these flames are furthermore either axisymmetric or spherically symmetric, depending upon the experiment. Currently, ACME includes six independent experiments of which the first five were selected for testing in spaceflight by NASA while the sixth was selected by the Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS) and the National Science Foundation (NSF). The CIR facility was launched in 2008 and with the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) was used for a series of liquid-fueled experiments from 2009 to 2017.

The facility was reconfigured and set up for ACME testing by the ISS crew in September and October 2017, where over 2 5 astronauts from Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan, Russia and the United States have thus far supported the project’s research. As of this writing, over one thousand ACME flames have been ignited on the ISS, where that began in Nov. 2017. It is expected that the planned ACME testing will be completed in 2021, when the CIR operations should subsequently shift to the Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) project. The discussion of the CIR hardware herein is limited, but the research facility is described in various documents, such as those listed below. General Description This section provides a general description of the ACME engineering from the ‘3.0 Experimental’ section of the following 2014 conference paper: Dennis P. IMPORTANT: The 2104 paper from which this section was extracted proceeded completion of the spaceflight hardware which was mostly launched in 2017. As a result , it does not accurately describe the final engineering in some regards . Therefore updates, clarifications, additional details, shortcomings, references, etc. have been included in boxed notes like this following the original description. As a minor note, the sizes of figures were adjusted in this report, but none were cropped. As previously discussed, the ACME experiments will be conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) using a chamber insert, depicted in Figure 2, which was designed to accommodate gas delivery to a variety of exchangeable burners.

Besides the chamber insert, other ACME-unique hardware includes a high -definition color camera and an avionics package, which is for data acquisition and control. Figure 2: Design of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) chamber insert that will be used in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on ISS.

ACME Engineering Implementation 19 May 2022 6 ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter. As depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1 and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm). Most burners will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux transducers. The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring of the pressure differential across the outlet surface. The igniter will have a crew -exchangeable tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper -motor drive will allow for precise positioning. Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner, porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment. Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm, and the fabricated gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm.

However, only the larger gas -jet burner was used during the spaceflight tests. The burners are addressed in detail in section 3.C. Unfortunately, the spherical burners have not always yielded spherically symmetric flames, presumably as a result of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local flame quenching. Two types of igniter tips have been used during ACME testing. Most tests have been conducted using a loop igniter tip like those which had been successfully used in the droplet combustion experiments which preceded ACME research in the CIR. However, some tests were conducted with a coil igniter tip, where that included the second round testing for both the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) and Structure and Respons e of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s -Flame) experiments, with the exception of the latter’s first day testing. The CFI-G investigation will also use the coil igniter tip. For more information about the igniter tips, see section 3.D. The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner.

The maximum fuel flow is 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), wherea s much higher flows, e.g., 10 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), are possible for the oxidizer and nitrogen lines. The crew can exchange the mass flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow accuracy. Spherical Burners The spherical burners have thus far been used for the CFI -G, Flame Design, and s -Flame experiments. In contrast to initial plans, spaceflight burners were only fabricated with a 6.35-mm porous sphere. It was initially expected that flames which were more spherical might be generated with larger diameter porous spheres, but 2.2-s drop testing indicated that 6.35-mm diameter spheres were as good or better than the larger sizes in creating spherical flames. Multiple copies of the spherical burner were launched to the ISS because of concerns that they might be damaged and/or might prove to yield flames which aren’t sufficiently spherically symmetric. The porous spheres were fabricated from sintering 316 stainless steel with 10-micron media grade, for which the porosity is approximately 41% and the density is 4.6 g/cm3. More specifically, each sphere was formed by sintering together sintered disks, where the supply tube should extend to the sphere’s center. Neglecting the interior of the supply tube, there is presumably no cavity within the porous sphere.

Each sphere was furthermore sinter-bonded to its stainless-steel supply tube. As a side effect, the tubing lost its temper and became very pliable because of the high temperature required for the bonding . Therefore, a close -fitting support tube, with an outer diameter of 1.8 mm, was added to the design. It doesn’t quite extend to the porous sphere as can be seen in Figure 46. The gap between the support tube and the burner is often obvious in flame imaging because the supply tube is more reflective than the support tube. Each burner was equipped with an extremely fine, sheathed, type-K thermocouple which was embedded as much as ~1 mm into the porous sphere. The thermocouple hole was 0.76 to 1.0 mm deep (and 0.25-0.30 mm in diameter) where the thermocouple was meant to be inserted fully, i.e., until reaching the hole’s bottom, but that may not be its exact position. The junction is of course not at the extreme end of the sheathed thermocouple, but it is very fine and presumably close. If the porous sphere is imagined as a globe with the supply tube as the south pole, the thermocouple is inserted in the lower hemisphere, between the equator and pole as seen in Figure 46.

The spherical burners were fi rst used for the Flame Design experiment , where the first flame tests were conducted on 25 April 2019. At the high flow rates, the flame ceased to be spherically symmetric and its center didn’t coincide with the burner’s center. The four thermocouple tips on each rake are nominally at the distances below from the center of the burner’s porous sphere Far/short 45, 60, 100, 100 mm Near/long 13, 25, 50, 100 mm In the far/short case, the two thermocouples at 100 mm distance are in orthogonal directions from the spherical burner. ACME-SRD-001.B Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD) 2013-SEPT-30 5 INTRODUCTION Science Summary The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project is now under development with a set of five independent experiments which are each focused on advancing combustion technology through fundamental research. Four of the current ACME experiments are specifically directed at addressing energy and environmental concerns, while the fifth experiment addresses fire prevention, especially for spacecraft. The overall goals are to improve our understanding of materials flammability, combustion at fuel lean conditions where both optimum performance and low emissions can be achieved, flame stability and extinction limits, soot control and reduction, oxygen enriched combustion which could enable practical carbon sequestration, and the use of electric fields for combustion control. While distinct, the ACME experiments share several significant traits. The principal unifying feature of the experiments is their use of gaseous fuels (e.g., methane and ethylene) rather than liquid or solid fuels. With this in common, the experiments will be conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) through the use of a single modular insert.

In addition to the fuel state, the current set of ACME experiments all use laminar, non-premixed (i.e., diffusion) flames for their studies. To simplify analysis, these flames are either one or two dimensional, depending upon the experiment. With the exception of the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment discussed immediately below, the general goal of the current ACME experiments is to gain fundamental understanding that can enable improved efficiency and reduced emissions in practical combustion processes on Earth, for example through the development and verification of models for chemical kinetics and transport processes in computational simulations. In addition to enhanced performance, improved modeling capability can lead to reductions in the time and cost for combustor design. In summary, microgravity investigations of non-premixed flames could lead to eco-friendly combustion systems providing our nation with green power for the future. Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) Unlike the other current ACME experiments, the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is focused on fire prevention, especially in spacecraf t.

Specifically, BRE’s objective is to improve our fundamental understanding of materials flamma bility, such as extinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the relevance of existing flammability test methods for low and partial-gravity envir onments. A flat porous burner fed with gaseous fuel will simulate the burning of solid and liqui d fuels, where measurements are made of the thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon whic h the vaporization of condensed-phase fuels depend. A small number of gaseous fuels (including mixtures with inert gases) will be used to simulate the burning of fuels such as paper, pl astic, and alcohol by matching properties such as the heats of combustion and gasification, the surface temperature, and smoke point.

ACME-SRD-001.B Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD) 2013-SEPT-30 6 Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) Research, especially including that already conducted in microgravity, has revealed that our current predictive ability is significantly lacking for flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, namely for sooty pure-fuel flames and dilute flames that are near extinction. The general goal of the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is to extend the range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and experimentally verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels. The dependence of normal coflow flames on injection velocity and fuel dilution will be carefully examined for flames at both very dilute and highly sooting conditions. Measurements will be made of the structure of diluted methane and ethylene flames in an air coflow. Lifted flames will be used as the basis for the research to avoid flame dependence on heat loss to the burner. The results of this experiment will be directly applicable to practical combustion issues such as turbulent combustion, ignition, flame stability, and more. Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions present as a result of the combustion reactions.

The direct ion transport and the induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the soot or flammability limits, direct heat transfer, and reduce pollutant emission. The purpose of the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and investigate how the ions can be used to control non-premixed flames. Outside reviewers concluded that the experiment “… will contribute to our critical understanding to our knowledge of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields.” The experiment will be conducted with a simple gas-jet flame, where an electric field will be generated by creating a high voltage (up to 10 kV) differential between the burner and a flat circular mesh above (i.e., downstream of) the burner. Measurements, as a function of field strength and fuel dilution, will be made of the ion current through the flame and the flame’s response time to electric forcing. Flame Design The primary goal of the Flame Design experiment is to improve our understanding of soot inception and control in order to enable the optimization of oxygen enriched combustion and the “design” of non-premixed flames that are both robust and soot free.

An outside review panel declared that Flame Design “… could lead to gr eatly improved burner designs that are efficient and less polluting than current designs." Flame Design will investigate the soot inception and extinction limits of spherical microgravity flames, created in the same manner as for the s-Flame experiment. Tests will be conducted with various concentrations of both the fuel (i.e., ethylene or methane) and oxygen in order to determine the role of the flame structure on the soot inception. The effect of the flow direction on soot formation will be assessed by studying both normal flames and inverse flames, where in the latter case an oxygen/inert mixture flows from the spherical burner into a fuel/inert atmosphere. The Flame Design experiment will explore whether the stoichiometric mixture fraction can characterize soot and flammability limits for non-premixed flames like the equivalence ratio serves as an indicator of those limits for premixed flames.

ACME-SRD-001.B Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD) 2013-SEPT-30 7 Structure and Response of Spherical Flames (s-Flame) The purpose of the Structure and Response of Spherical Flames (s-Flame) experiment is to advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both soot-free and sooty flames. The spherical flame, which is only possible in microgravity, will be created through use of a porous spherical burner from which a fuel/inert gas mixture will issue into the CIR chamber. Flames will be ignited at non-steady conditions and allowed to transition naturally toward extinction. Tests will be conducted with various inert diluents, in both the fuel and chamber atmosphere. The fuel gases include hydrogen and methane for soot-free flames, and ethylene for sooty flames. One experiment objective is to identify the extinction limits for both radiative and convective extinction (i.e., at high and low system Damkohler numbers, respectively). Another objective is to determine the existence, onset, and nature of pulsating instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in such flames with fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number.

ACME-SRD-001.B Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD) 2013-SEPT-30 15 1.4.1. The axisymmetric coflow burner shall consist of a small inner tube (normally for fuel or fuel/inert mixtures) within a larger outer “tube” where the coflow gas (e.g., air) flows through the annulus between the tubes. The outer coflow “tube” does not need to have a constant cross-section but can be smoothly converging (toward the outlet). The use of a smoothly converging nozzl e, with no steps or other rapid changes, can minimize the boundary layer on the nozzle’s inner wall. However, testing and analysis at NASA Glenn fo r the E-FIELD Flames experiment has revealed that the ACME velocities are t oo low for the nozzle to significantly reduce the boundary layer.* 1.4.2. The inner and outer tubes shall be concentric within ±0.3 mm along their common length.1,* 1.4.3. The burner annulus shall have a gas permeable outlet surface (e.g., honeycomb, mesh) across the annulus and 3±0.1 mm upstream of (i.e., below) the inner tube’s outlet. The annular outlet surface and inner tube tip (i.e., outlet) shall both be orthogonal to the burner axis and flat to within ±0.1 mm (neglecting the cells or similar openings). Testing at Yale and NASA Glenn suggests that a fine honeycomb can be superior as an outlet surface to both mesh and sintered porous metal in creating an axisymmetric flow and flame. >1,* 1.4.4.

The outlet of the outer tube shall be 0.0 to 0.5 mm downstream of the burner’s outlet surface.1,2,* 1.4.5. The inner tube shall have a 2.1±0.1 mm inside diameter and a 2.4±0.1 mm outer diameter where the thin wall helps minimize th e “dead space” (where gas is not exiting) in the radial flow profile at the burner outlet . The inner tube’s inner diameter shall be constant for a length of at least 40 times the inner diameter to create a parabolic velocity profile . At 10 mm or more upstream of the burner outlet, the wall thickness can increase from the specified value, e.g., to stiffen the tube. The inner tube’s inner diameter and outer diameter (at the tip) shall be measured and known to within ±0.05 mm.<1,* 1.4.6. The inner tube shall be internally a nd externally smooth with an average roughness of no more than 100 μm. The tip shall be free of burs and sharp edges and smoothed to an average roughness of no more than 20 μm to prevent turbulence.2,* 1.4.7. The internal (i.e., fluid) volume of the bur ner’s inner tube from the last upstream solenoid valve(s) to the porous sphere, in cluding any pressure transducer(s), shall be no more than 10 cc and as small as possible. A larger volume between the mass flow controllers and burner outlet increases the time necessary to change between different experimental flow conditions.

Minimizing that volume will help to minimize the changeover time between two flow conditions.1 1.4.8. At the burner outlet, the outer tube shall have an inner diameter of 25±0.5 mm. At the burner outlet, the outer tube’s inner diameter shall be measured and known to within ±0.1 mm.1

ACME-SRD-001.B Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD) 2013-SEPT-30 16 1.4.9. The burner shall have a uniform flow profile that is axisymmetric, i.e., where the velocity is independent of the angular position, especially (at radial positions) near the burner center. For the coflow bur ner, axisymmetric flow means that the variation in axial velocity with angular position (e.g., as measured in 1.4.11) shall be less than 10% of the (mean) velocit y, where this shall hold for all radial positions from 0 to 10 mm. For example, the axial velocities measured on the two sides (i.e., left and right) of a diameter shall match within 10% of the (mean) axial velocity at the same radial distance. The burner gas shall be ejected parallel to the chamber axis and without either swirl (i.e., helically rotating flow) or turbulence (i.e., eddies). To be without turbulence, the axial velocity at any position 0.5 mm downstream of the burner (e .g., as measured in 1.4.11) shall be constant with time within 3% (i.e ., of the time-averaged value). The use of honeycomb for the burner outlet will ensure that there is no swirl and that the flow is ejected parallel to the burner axis. Turbulence can be mitigated by avoiding non-uniformities, wakes, and flow separation.1,* 1.4.10.

The coflow boundary layers outside the inne r tube and inside the outer tube shall be minimized for velocities up to 50 cm/s as verified through measurements (with measurements within 0.5 mm downstream of the inner tube outlet) that are similar to those specified in 1.4.11. 1,* 1.4.10.1. The boundary layer thickness for the inner tube shall be determined as the distance from the inner tube wall (i nto the annulus) to the position where the measured velocity reaches 90% of the plug flow value (i.e., computed from the flow) and that distance shall be less than 0.75 mm and as small as possible.<1,* 1.4.10.2. The boundary layer thickness for the outer tube shall be determined as the distance from the outer tube wall (i nto the annulus) to the position where the measured velocity reaches 90% of the plug flow value (i.e., computed from the flow) and that distance sha ll be less than 3 mm and as small as possible.1,* The boundary layers can be reduced for veloc ities up to 35 cm/s with the use of a minimum of two seamless Haynes 214 honeyco mb disks of cell size 1/64 in. that are at least 1/4 in. thick. Unfortunately, that honeycomb has not been readily available recently, but acceptable results can be obtained with the 1/32 in. cell size. The first honeycomb disk could be placed above the coflow entrance and the second honeycomb disk at the burner exit.

Sp ecial care should be taken to ensure that any penetrations of the inner t ube through honeycomb are symmetric. This might be accomplished through careful cu tting of the honeycomb, either with a tight fit around the central tube or with a symmetric gap comparable in size to the cell size of the honeycomb. The lifted fla mes, as planned for these experiments, are very sensitive to minor inconsistencies that can result (for example) in cutting the honeycomb. While honeycomb (of sufficient thickness as compared to the cell size) prevents swirl, other material such as layer(s) of mesh can be used to reduce the boundary layer.<1,* 1.4.11. The burner’s flow profile, across a plane orthogonal to the burner axis and within 0.5 mm downstream of the inner tube ou tlet, shall be well documented. The

ACME-SRD-001.B Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD) 2013-SEPT-30 17 spatial uniformity shall be verified by 1g measurement of the velocity field using a cold flow (i.e., with no flame) simultaneously through both the annulus and the inner tube. The axial velocity shall be measured across a diameter of 30 mm at increments of no greater than 5 mm, esp ecially within 5 mm of the burner axis where the increments shall be no greater than 1 mm. Unless otherwise specified, measurement across one diameter is sufficient. Smoke wire imaging with air flowing through both the inner tube and annulus is suggested as a way to characterize the burner flow. Another option is hot-wire anemometry.1,* 1.4.11.1. The flow profile shall be measured for a range of flow velocities in 10 cm/s increments from 20 to 50 cm/s where the inner tube and annulus velocities are matched.1,* 1.4.11.2. For the case of matched velocities at 10 cm/s, the flow profile shall be measured for at least four diameters (as just described) at increments of no greater than 45 degrees to ensure the axisymmetry of the flow for at least one flow condition.1,* 1.4.11.3.

The flow profile shall also be measur ed where the inner tube and annulus (i.e., outer tube) velocities are not matched for the following 11 velocity pairs: 0:10, 0:20, 0:30, 0:40, 0: 50, 10:30, 10:50, 30:10, 30:50, 50:10, and 50:30 where each velocity pair is given as inner:outer and the values are in cm/s.1,* 1.4.12. The coflow flame shall be axisymmetric over the full range of flow conditions. To be axisymmetric, (1) the variation in th e radius of the visible flame edge with angular position shall be less than 10% of the (mean) radius for all axial positions from the flame base to tip, and (2) the pl ane of the flame’s visible base shall be orthogonal to the burner axis such that th e variation in axial distance from the visible flame base to the burner outlet (a long the circumference of the base) is no more than 1 mm, especially for lifted flames, where the flame is detached and downstream from the burner outlet . For an example of criteria #1, the flame radii measured on the two sides (i.e., left and right) of a flame image shall match within 10% of the (mean) radius at the same axial position. The axisymmetry of a 50/50 CH4/N2 flame shall be demonstrated in 1g for a range of flow velocities in 10 cm/s increments from 10 to 50 cm /s where the inner tube and annulus velocities are matched.

The coflow burner shall be positioned such that*: 1.4.13.1. burner axis is coincident with the CIR chamber axis within ±2 mm and orthogonal to the CIR chamber window axes,* 1.4.13.2. plane of the CIR chamber window centers is 12±2 mm downstream of (i.e., above) the inner tube outlet.1,* 1.4.14. Operational Requirements The general science requirements are now co mbined in ACME’s Science Operations Requirements Document (SORD), but this does not eliminate the importance of this section of the existing ISRD in describing the ge neral operational sequences.
