The following is a summary of the research activities during the period Oct. 2006 - Sept. 2009. 1) Numerical and Experimental Observations of Spherical Diffusion Flames. Spherical diffusion flames supported on a porous sphere were studied numerically and experimentally. Experiments were performed in 2.2 s and 5.2 s microgravity facilities. Numerical results were obtained from a Chemkin-based program. The program simulates flow from a porous sphere into a quiescent environment, yields both steady state and transient results and accounts for optically thick gas-phase radiation. The low flow velocities and long residence times in these diffusion flames lead to enhanced radiative and diffusive effects.

Despite similar adiabatic flame temperatures, the measured and predicted temperatures varied by as much as 700 K. The temperature reduction correlates with flame size but characteristic flow times and Lewis number also influence temperature. The numerical results show that the ambient gas Lewis number would have a strong effect on flame temperature if the flames were steady and nonradiating. For example, a 10% decrease in Lewis number would increase the steady state flame temperature by 200 K. However, for these transient, radiating flames the effect of Lewis number is small. It was also observed that when hydrocarbon fuel is supplied from the ambient the large diffusion distances associated with these flames can lead to unusual steady state compositions near the outer boundary because decomposition products can diffuse to the outer boundary. This results in a loss of chemical enthalpy from the system but the effect on flame temperature is small. Transient predictions of flame sizes are larger than those observed in microgravity experiments. Close agreement could not be obtained without either increasing the model’s thermal and mass diffusion properties by 30% or reducing mass flowrate by 25%. 2) Radiative Extinction of Gaseous Spherical Diffusion Flames in Microgravity. Radiative extinction of spherical diffusion flames was investigated experimentally and numerically.

The experiments involved microgravity spherical diffusion flames burning ethylene and propane at 0.98 bar. Both normal (fuel flowing into oxidizer) and inverse (oxidizer flowing into fuel) flames were studied, with nitrogen supplied to either the fuel or the oxygen. Flame conditions were chosen to ensure that the flames extinguished within the 2.2 s of available test time; thus extinction occurred during unsteady flame conditions. Diagnostics included color video and thin-filament pyrometry. The computations, which simulated flow from a porous sphere into a quiescent environment, included detailed chemistry, transport, and radiation and yielded transient results. Radiative extinction was observed experimentally and simulated numerically. Extinction time, peak temperature, and radiative loss fraction were found to be independent of flow rate except at very low flow rates. Radiative heat loss was dominated by the combustion products downstream of the flame and was found to scale with flame surface area, not volume. For large transient flames the heat release rate also scaled with surface area and thus the radiative loss fraction was largely independent of flow rate. Peak temperatures at extinction onset were about 1100 K, which is significantly lower than for kinetic extinction.

An important observation of this work is that while radiative heat losses can drive transient extinction, this is not only because radiative losses are increasing with time but also because the heat release rate is falling off as the flame expands away from the burner and the reactant supply to the flame decreases. 3) Soot Inception Limits in Laminar Diffusion Flames with Application to Oxy–Fuel Combustion. For diffusion flames, the combination of oxygen enrichment and fuel dilution results in an increase in the stoichiometric mixture fraction, Zst, and alters the flame structure, i.e., the relationship between the local temperature and the local gas composition.
Increasing Zst has been shown to result in the reduction or even elimination of soot. In the present work, the effects of variable Zst on soot inception are investigated in normal and inverse coflow flames, using ethylene as the fuel. Use of the inverse coflow flame underscores the validity of these concepts, since the convective field in the inverse flame directs particles into the fuel-rich region. Sooting limits based on particle luminosity are measured as a function of Zst. The sooting limit is obtained by varying the amount of inert gas until soot appears above a predefined height. For each limit flame, the adiabatic flame temperature is calculated and the flame temperature at the half-height is measured.

The flame temperature at the sooting limit is found to increase with Zst for both normal and inverse flames. The effects of residence time are also investigated, and the sooting limit inception temperature is found to be dependent on fuel stream velocity for both the normal and inverse configurations. A simple model applicable to oxy–fuel combustion is presented which describes how increasing Zst results in the reduction and ultimately elimination of soot. This model assumes that soot inception can only occur in a region where critical values for species, temperature, and residence time are met. The soot inception region is shown to be bounded by two isotherms: a low-temperature boundary that is a function of residence time, and a high-temperature boundary that corresponds to the location of a critical local carbon-to-oxygen ratio. The effect of increasing Zst is to move the boundaries of the soot inception zone towards each other, until the zone is infinitely thin and thus the sooting limit is reached. By comparing the model to experimental data, a critical local C/O ratio of 0.53 and a sooting limit inception temperature of 1640 K (for a characteristic residence time of 22 ms) were determined for ethylene. 4) Characteristics of Non-Premixed Oxygen-Enhanced Combustion: I. The Presence of Appreciable Oxygen at the Location of Maximum Temperature.

The presence of appreciable molecular oxygen at the location of maximum temperature has been observed in non-premixed oxygen-enhanced combustion (OEC) processes, specifically in flames having a high stoichiometric mixture fraction (Zst) produced with diluted fuel and oxygen-enrichment. For conventional fuel–air flames, key features of the flame are consistent with the flame sheet approximation (FSA). In particular, the depletion of O2 at the location of maximum temperature predicted by the FSA correlates well with the near-zero O2 concentration measured at this location for conventional fuel–air flames. In contradistinction, computational analysis with detailed kinetics demonstrates that for OEC flames at high Zst: (1) there is an appreciable concentration of O2 at the location of maximum temperature and (2) the maximum temperature is not coincident with the location of global stoichiometry, O2 depletion, or maximum heat release. We investigate these phenomena computationally in three non-premixed ethylene flames at low, moderate, and high Zst, but with equivalent adiabatic flame temperatures.

Results demonstrate that the location of O2 depletion occurs in the vicinity of global stoichiometry for flames of any Zst and that the presence of appreciable O2 at the location of maximum temperature for high Zst flames is caused by a shift in the location of maximum temperature relative to the location of O2 depletion. This shifting is attributed to: (1) finite-rate multi-step chemistry resulting in exothermic heat release that is displaced from the location of O2 depletion and (2) the Page 2 of 3 Task Book Report Generated on: 02/28/2024

multi-step chemistry resulting in exothermic heat release that is displaced from the location of O2 depletion and (2) the relative location of the heat release region with respect to the fuel and oxidizer boundaries in mixture fraction space. A method of superposition involving a variation of the flame sheet approximation with two heat sources is shown to be sufficient in explaining this phenomenon. The following is a summary of the research activities during this period. 1) Work has continued on radiative extinction of spherical diffusion flames, which are being investigated experimentally and numerically. The experiments involved microgravity spherical diffusion flames burning ethylene and propane at 0.98 bar. Both normal (fuel flowing into oxidizer) and inverse (oxidizer flowing into fuel) flames are studied, with nitrogen supplied to either the fuel or the oxygen. The computations, which simulated flow from a porous sphere into a quiescent environment, include detailed transport properties, detailed chemistry and an optically thick radiative heat loss model to study the transient radiative extinction of spherical diffusion flames supported by a porous spherical burner. A flow of a reactant (fuel or oxidizer) issued from a porous sphere into a quiescent environment of the other reactant was considered in the simulation. Radiative extinction was observed experimentally and simulated numerically. Extinction time, peak temperature, and radiative loss fraction (ratio of the radiative heat loss rate to the heat generation rate) were found to be independent of flow rate except at very low flow rates. Radiative heat loss was dominated by the combustion products downstream of the flame and was found to scale with flame surface area, not volume. For large transient flames the heat release rate also scaled with surface area and thus the radiative loss fraction was largely independent of flow rate. Peak temperatures at extinction onset were about 1100 K, which is significantly lower than for kinetic extinction. One observation is that while radiative heat losses can drive transient extinction, this is not because radiative losses are increasing with time (flame size) but rather because the heat release rate is falling off as the temperature drops.

2) A new numerical study of limiting conditions for soot particle inception in spherical diffusion flames has been initiated. The flames were modeled using a one-dimensional, time accurate diffusion flame code with detailed chemistry and transport and an optically thick radiation model. Seventeen normal and inverse flames were considered, covering a wide range of stoichiometric mixture fraction, adiabatic flame temperature, and residence time. These flames were previously observed to reach their sooting limits after 2 s of microgravity. Sooting-limit diffusion flames with residence times longer than 200 ms were found to have temperatures near 1190 K where C/O = 0.6, whereas flames with shorter residence times required increased temperatures. Acetylene was found to be a reasonable surrogate for soot precursor species in these flames, having peak mole fractions of about 0.01. 3) Our previous studies have shown a linear relationship between the limit flame temperature and stoichiometric mixture fraction for coflow flames at their sooting limit. The sooting limit in coflow flames is obtained by varying the amount of inert gas until soot appears above a predefined height. In this work sooting limits based on particle luminosity were measured as a function of Zst. For each limit flame, the flame temperature was measured and defined as the limit flame temperature.

The limit flame temperature increases linearly with Zst, for both normal and inverse flames. The effects of residence time have also been investigated, and the soot inception temperature was found to be dependent on fuel stream velocity for both the normal and inverse configuration. Earlier experimental results and modeling indicated that a critical carbon to oxygen (C/O) ratio exists in the fuel rich region of the flame where soot inception is no longer favorable due to the presence of oxygen containing species. We extended this model to include the effects of finite rate chemistry and thus residence time on the sooting limit. This involved considering two boundaries for the soot inception zone, one dictated by the C/O ratio and the other by the finite rate chemistry of fuel pyrolysis and soot inception. By combining these two boundaries, a simple model was developed that describes how a sooting limit is attained. By utilizing measured limit temperature data with the model we found the limit inception temperature for soot formation to be 1640 K and the critical carbon to oxygen ratio to be 0.53. 4) Performed analytical analysis of the kinetic and radiative extinction limits of a steady spherical diffusion flame supported by a porous burner.

A single step, overall and irreversible reaction that follows high activation energy Arrhenius kinetics was adopted to describe the reaction rate. An optically thin radiation model was used to describe the radiative heat loss. The kinetic and radiative extinction limits were observed from the analysis. Results show that the flame is easier to extinguish when the radiation intensity is higher, as expected, and there exists a maximum radiation intensity above which steady burning is not possible. Task Description:
The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons.
These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed 'Flame Design' as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants.
Recognizing the unique benefits of spherical diffusion flames, employ such flames to: 1. Obtain soot-inception limits as functions of stoichiometric mixture fraction, flow direction (direction across the flame front, i.e., towards the fuel or towards the oxidizer), amount of inert (nitrogen) and pressure for ethylene and methane flames. Identify the corresponding soot-inception temperature; 2.

Determine effects of stoichiometric mixture fraction and flow direction on the phenomenon of permanently blue flames and, to this end, determine the effects of stoichiometric mixture fraction and flow direction on flame temperature, size, color and soot volume fraction; 3. Obtain extinction limits as functions of stoichiometric mixture fraction, flow direction, amount of inert and pressure for ethylene and methane flames. Identify the corresponding extinction temperature; 4. Evaluate whether this flame system can be used to obtain a pseudo-flammability limit for non-premixed flames in terms of stoichiometric mixture fraction and amount of inert. If so, determine these limits for ethylene and methane flames. Soot formation and flame extinction are problems of great concern in practical combustors. Recent normal-gravity experiments using counterflow diffusion flames have shown that permanently-blue flames (which are devoid of soot regardless of strain rate) and extinction-resistant flames can be produced for many hydrocarbon fuels by nitrogen exchange (increased stoichiometric mixture fraction). Furthermore, there is a unique stoichiometric mixture fraction wherein the flame temperature at extinction can be up to 200 K lower and the strain rate up to four times greater than that for the standard hydrocarbon/air flame with the same flame temperature.

The present experiments employ microgravity conditions to allow for a unique set of experiments to clarify the underlying mechanisms responsible for flame response to stoichiometric mixture fraction. Rationale for HRP Directed Research: Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
As the goal of this program is to develop an understanding of combustion with the aim of reducing pollutants and increasing combustion efficiency, the results are directly applicable to terrestial power generation. In particular, with the present interest in carbon sequestration via oxygen-enriched combustion the present work is of particular importance as it identifies methods of controlling a number of pollutants through oxygen-enriched combustion. Task Progress:
Below is a summary of the progress on this project for the year ending January 1, 2006: Flame Design benefited from several analytical and computational advances in 2005. These have yielded important insight into many experimental observations by this project. This has laid the groundwork for two journal publications, one which was submitted and one which is nearing submission. Work on the general behavior of spherical diffusion flames has demonstrated that a detailed transient numerical model (with detailed chemistry, transport, and radiation) can predict flame size and flame temperature for microgravity spherical diffusion flames.

A simplified model indicates that Lewis number can have a large effect on flame temperature for microgravity diffusion flames. This work has been submitted to the Combustion Symposium. Work on radiative extinction of spherical diffusion flames has demonstrated that the detailed transient model can predict extinction times for microgravity spherical diffusion flames. The work identified several scaling relationship for extinguishing diffusion flames. This work is being finalized for an upcoming journal submission. A Nikon D100 color digital still camera has been configured for use in the 2.2 second drop tower. This provides four images per drop. The images have 6 megapixels and 12 x 3 bit depth and are among the highest-fidelity images ever recorded in the drop tower. This camera has been used to record images of 15 micron SiC fibers in flames in the 2.2 second drop tower. This has yielded qualitative thin-filament pyrometry results for extinguishing spherical diffusion flames. Eighteen successful drop tests were performed in the 2.2 second drop tower. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed 'Flame Design' as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. Recognizing the unique benefits of spherical diffusion flames, employ such flames to: 1. Obtain soot-inception limits as functions of stoichiometric mixture fraction, flow direction (direction across the flame front, i.e., towards the fuel or towards the oxidizer), amount of inert (nitrogen) and pressure for ethylene and methane flames. Identify the corresponding soot-inception temperature; 2.

Determine effects of stoichiometric mixture fraction and flow direction on the phenomenon of permanently blue flames and, to this end, determine the effects of stoichiometric mixture fraction and flow direction on flame temperature, size, color and soot volume fraction; 3. Obtain extinction limits as functions of stoichiometric mixture fraction, flow direction, amount of inert and pressure for ethylene and methane flames. Identify the corresponding extinction temperature; 4. Evaluate whether this flame system can be used to obtain a pseudo-flammability limit for non-premixed flames in terms of stoichiometric mixture fraction and amount of inert. If so, determine these limits for ethylene and methane flames. Soot formation and flame extinction are problems of great concern in practical combustors. Recent normal-gravity experiments using counterflow diffusion flames have shown that permanently-blue flames (which are devoid of soot regardless of strain rate) and extinction-resistant flames can be produced for many hydrocarbon fuels by nitrogen exchange (increased stoichiometric mixture fraction). Furthermore, there is a unique stoichiometric mixture fraction wherein the flame temperature at extinction can be up to 200 K lower and the strain rate up to four times greater than that for the standard hydrocarbon/air flame with the same flame temperature.

The present experiments employ microgravity conditions to allow for a unique set of experiments to clarify the underlying mechanisms responsible for flame response to stoichiometric mixture fraction. Rationale for HRP Directed Research: Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
As the goal of this program is to develop an understanding of combustion with the aim of reducing pollutants and increasing combustion efficiency, the results are directly applicable to terrestial power generation. THE SPACECRAFT FIRE EXPERIMENT (SAFFIRE) - OBJECTIVES, DEVELOPMENT AND STATUS William Schoren(1), Gary A. Ruff, David L. Urban (1)NASA John H. Glenn Research Center, 21000 Brookpark Road, Cleveland, OH 44135, Email: william.r.schoren@nasa.gov ABSTRACT Since 2012, the Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) has been under development by the Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (SFS Demo) project that is funded by NASA’s Advanced Exploration Systems Division in the Human Exploration and Operations Mission Directorate. The overall objective of this project is to reduce the uncertainty and risk associated with the design of spacecraft fire safety systems for NASA’s exploration missions. This is accomplished by defining, developing, and conducting experiments that address gaps in spacecraft fire safety knowledge and capabilities identified by NASA’s Fire Safety System Maturation Team. This paper describes the three Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire-I, -II, and -III) that were developed at NASA-GRC and that will conduct a series of material flammability tests in low-gravity and at length scales that are realistic for a spacecraft fire. The experiments will be conducted in Orbital ATK’s Cygnus vehicle after it has unberthed from the International Space Station.

The tests will be fully automated with the data downlinked at the conclusion of the test and before the Cygnus vehicle reenters the atmosphere. The objectives of these experiments are to (1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test. The hardware for these experiments has been completed and is awaiting their respective launches, all planned for 2016. This paper will review the objectives of these experiments and how they address several of the knowledge gaps for NASA’s exploration missions. The hardware development will be discussed including several novel approaches that were taken for testing and evaluation of these series payloads. The status of the missions and operational status will also be presented. 1. INTRODUCTION Tests on full-scale transportation vehicles, buildings, homes, and habitats have been common on earth to more fully understand the fire hazards associated with each application and how best to protect the passengers and inhabitants from a potential fire. Fire safety on spacecraft has been a significant concern for NASA during the decades of crewed spaceflight and will remain so as NASA plans future exploration missions.

Many microgravity combustion experiments have been performed on the Space Shuttle and continue to be performed on the International Space States (ISS) and the data from these experiments have contributed to our understanding of how to prevent and protect crewed spacecraft from fire. However, none of these experiments have studied sample and environment sizes typical of those expected in a spacecraft fire [1]. Prior experiments have been limited to samples no larger than 10 cm in length and width whereas a serious spacecraft fire would likely be much larger and consume much more material. Because of the large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, there is a significant lack of data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures. The use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. Despite their obvious importance, full scale spacecraft fire experiments have not been possible because of the inherent hazards involved with conducting a large fire test in a crewed vehicle.

To address this knowledge gap, a project was proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew. In October 2011, the NASA Advanced Exploration Systems (AES) Division of NASA’s Human Exploration and Operations Mission Directorate funded this project to develop and demonstrate spacecraft fire safety technologies in relevant environments. The keystone demonstration to be performed was a largescale fire safety experiment to be conducted on an ISS re-supply vehicle after it has left the ISS and before it enters the earth’s atmosphere. The project team led from NASA’s John H. Glenn Research Center (GRC) was identified and began formulating such an experiment. The NASA team was augmented by an international topical team assembled by the European Space Agency (ESA) [2]. The participation of members from other countries and space agencies not only brings additional skills to the science team but also facilitates international cooperation in the development of an approach to spacecraft fire prevention and response for https://ntrs.nasa.gov/search.jsp?R=20170001636 2018-04-20T15:24:03+00:00Z

future exploration vehicles. The current spaceflight experiment funded and being developed by NASA addresses two objectives. The first objective is to understand the flame spread and growth of a fire over a large piece of flammable material, consistent with clothing or other fabric likely to be in a spacecraft cabin. This sample material is approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide. This will be at least an order of magnitude larger in both dimensions than any prior low-g flame spread experiment. The second objective is to examine the flammability limits of materials in low gravity for comparison with results of NASA’s terrestrial normal gravity evaluation tests. The status of the development of the flight experiment and the individual contributions of the topical team will be discussed in subsequent sections. 2. SAFFIRE EXPERIMENT SAFETY Even though this experiment will be conducted during the un-crewed portion of the flight, the Cygnus vehicle berths with the ISS and, therefore, the experiment is subject to many of the same safety considerations as other ISS payloads. The major safety hazard is inadvertent igniter activation prior to the Cygnus deberthing from the ISS. This would result in the exposure of the flight crew to toxic gases that are produced from the combustion event.

It should be noted that this hazard is a concern prior to Cygnus berthing to the ISS since the toxic gases would be present when the Cygnus hatch is opened to the ISS. The power and communication interfaces between Cygnus and Saffire are utilized to control this hazard. Cygnus provides two power feed circuits to Saffire due to power requirements. One power feed circuit provides power to the Saffire avionics, the other provides power to the igniter circuitry. There are two latching relays in each of these two power feed circuits, one in the power feed side, one in the return. These four latching relays are contained within the Saffire flight unit but are controlled and monitored by Cygnus avionics. A separate ground command to the Cygnus avionics is required to close each of these four latching relays. Igniter activation requires that all four relays be closed. This is because Saffire avionics provides an enable command to a DC/DC converter in the igniter circuitry and also provides commanding to solid state relay switches on the igniter control card within the igniter power feed circuitry. In addition, a ground command to the Saffire avionics via Cygnus avionics is required to initiate an igniter activation for an experiment run.

Cygnus avionics and the associated ground commanding provide the required failure tolerance for control of the Saffire hazard of inadvertent igniter activation. Significant focus was placed on these four latching relays due to their safety criticality. This attention is reflected in the environmental testing performed as shown in Table 3. The relays for all three flight units were vibration tested at the component level. Tailoring of the environmental testing resulted in only Saffire I being vibration tested at a system level. Therefore, vibration testing was performed on the Saffire II and III Power Management Systems that includes the relays to address the criticality of these relays and the associated risk of this tailored system-level vibration testing. Safety engineering input was critical to developing a design solution that was acceptable from an ISS payload safety perspective due to the interface limitations between Saffire and Cygnus. This hazard along with the other typical ISS payloads hazards are documented in the Saffire Unit I Flight Safety Data Package. The ISS Payload Safety Review Panel (PSRP) reviewed and approved this Package at the Phase I/II level in August of 2013 and again at the Phase III level in March 2015.

These Payload Safety Reviews were augmented by a handful of Technical Interchange Meetings (TIMs) with the PSRP including TIMs to address the inadvertent igniter activation hazard. SPACECRAFT FIRE SAFETY KNOWLEDGE GAPS AND FUTURE EXPERIMENTS The experiments being developed for Saffire-I, -II, and –III will be the first of their kind to evaluate low-g material flammability with direct implications for fire safety on future exploration vehicles. One of the drawbacks of these experiments is that a relatively small number of tests will be conducted (two large samples and nine smaller samples). A thorough evaluation of these phenomena would require many more samples and range of materials. Also, if they are typical of most low-g combustion experiments, the findings will raise additional significant questions for material flammability in spacecraft. The Saffire hardware and the Cygnus vehicle provides a unique opportunity to demonstrate other fire safety technologies including fire detection, fire suppression, post-fire cleanup and monitoring. Needs in these areas have been identified by NASA’s Spacecraft Fire Safety Systems Maturation Team and are summarized in Table 5. Because of the importance of addressing these remaining needs to crew safety in exploration missions, AES management authorized the SFS Demo project to plan for three more Saffire experiments, Saffire -IV, V, and VI, that will address objectives not achieved in Saffire-I-III.

Of particular note is that many of these objectives require supporting ground-based experimentation to perform the parametric investigations that are required to fully understand the phenomena in question. The objective of the flight experiment is to anchor the ground-based experiments with flight data. While the planning for the follow-on experiments is underway, the development process is intended to mirror the processes executed with Saffire-I-III. The Mission Concept Review/System Requirements Review is planned for June 2016 with a design review planned for December 2016. 5. CONCLUSIONS The Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration Project has designed, manufactured, assembled and tested three Saffire flight units. The decision to develop flight units of nearly identical design allowed for the tailoring of environmentally testing that resulted in cost and schedule savings without introducing significant risk. This design similarity also allowed for the comparison of test results to verify consistency when testing was performed across all three flight units. Safety engineering input was critical to developing an acceptable design solution to control the inadvertent igniter activation hazard due to the interface limitations between Saffire and Cygnus.

Technical Interchange Meetings (TIMs) with the ISS Payload Safety Review Panel proved to be invaluable to the overall safety approval process by providing a focused review of specific safety issues. Conducting these three experiments will be a milestone for spacecraft fire safety . The data and follow on analysis will provide verification of spacecraft fire safety design and operations for future exploration vehicles and their crews. text: SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 3 2.2 SAME Experiment Background Since the very beginning of the manned space flight program, NASA engineers and scientists have gone to great lengths to prevent fires from occurring on spacecraft. They have done this by adapting fire safety systems and procedures developed on Earth to the unique conditions and operating environment of spacecraft. However, microgravity combustion experiments have shown that fire can behave very differently in space and the best methods to prevent, detect, and extinguish fires on a spacecraft may be very different than those used on Earth. In 2000, NASA's Bioastronautics Initiative began with the objective of ensuring and enhancing the health, safety, and performance of humans in space. As part of this effort, the Life Support and Habitation Branch at NASA Glenn Research Center is responsible for developing and implementing a research plan to significantly improve fire safety on spacecraft and in space habitats. This goal will be achieved by applying a significant amount of fundamental knowledge and the experimental capability of microgravity research to spacecraft fire safety questions. Spacecraft smoke detectors must detect smoke with a variety of particulate types. Hydrocarbon fuels typically produce soot, while overheated plastics produce droplets of recondensed polymer fragments.

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: Paper and silicone rubber produce a smoke that is composed of liquid droplets of recondensed pyrolysis products. Differences in the nucleation and growth processes for these different types of smokes create particles that have different sizes and properties. The Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) experiment that flew in the Glovebox on STS-75 demonstrated that the smokes with solid particulates created in microgravity formed longer chains, and aggregated into larger particles than those created in normal Earth gravity. This is surmised to have occurred because of the increased residence time in the high concentration smoke regions and to have affected the responses of the two spacecraft smoke detectors (ISS and STS) utilized in that experiment. To develop smoke detectors that are sensitive to the type and size of smoke particles that will be encountered in microgravity and to allow them to distinguish between dust and smoke, better knowledge of the size distribution and morphology of the particulates is required. 2.3 SAME Experiment Objectives The major goal of this experiment is to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulates achieve in microgravity and to relate the droplet size and distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment.

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: This will be accomplished by extending the Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) concept to provide a particulate count and mass density determination to the diagnostic array used to analyze these liquid smokes. The experimental design and practical application of this data will be enhanced by the development of a numerical code that will predict the smoke droplet growth as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment. The SAME experiment has the following (listed) objectives: 1. Make measurements of three moments of the particle size distribution for the μg smoke from several materials found in spacecraft considering the effects of sample temperature, air flow, smoke residence time (near the source) and smoke aging. The primary targets are materials that produce liquid smoke particulate but solid smoke producers will also be considered. 2. Make measurements of the effect of µg and 1-g on the size distribution of liquid aerosol smokes (using an idealized smoke e.g. DBT) to provide data for numerical model comparison. 3. Evaluate the performance in µg of the two existing U.S. spacecraft smoke detector designs for the test conditions. 4.

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: Evaluate other smoke detection/sensing devices at NASA’s request for the test materials 2.4 SAME “Firsts” for NASA • Measurements of microgravity smoke: Diagnostics such as the P-Trak and the DustTrak will be used to measure particle count and particle mass concentration, respectively. Both devices are manufactured by TSI. With the aid of these instruments (and others), microgravity smoke will be characterized. • The use of rapid prototype materials for manned flight experiment hardware. • Use of an automatic, remotely adjustable, ‘particulate friendly’ dilution system.

text: SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 4 2.5 The SAME Risk mitigation experiment – DAFT The objective for the risk mitigation experiment, DAFT (Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test), is to provide a microgravity technology demonstration of the P-Trak Ultrafine Particle Counter manufactured by TSI. The P-Trak is a hand held air quality monitor which is capable of counting particles whose mean diameter is in the range of 1.0 to 0.05 microns. After extensive market research performed by both the Engineering and Science teams, it has been determined that the PTrak is the only commercially available hardware that can perform this particle count while maintaining the weight, resource, and space limitations for an MSG experiment. P-Trak measures particle number concentrations in real-time while storing that data in a memory maintained by an onboard battery. These measurements are made in units of particles per cubic centimeter (pt/cm3) versus traditional aerosol measurements of milligrams per cubic meter (mg/m3) made by photometers. P-Trak operates by using the particles in the aerosol as seeds to condense droplets of alcohol (a condensate nuclei counter). These droplets have many times the average diameter of the original particles, and may, therefore, be easily counted with standard optical techniques.

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: The potential problem is that these droplets are directed through a nozzle to facilitate the counting, and some of these droplets (a predictable percentage) collide with the walls and form a film. In a gravity environment, this film is recycled by ‘falling’ down hill. In microgravity, the distinct possibility exists that these droplets will form a film that will bridge and block the nozzle, effectively plugging the flow of droplets and preventing the device from functioning, or obscuring the optics. Furthermore, there is some concern that the droplets inside the optics chamber may get trapped in an internal circular motion and be counted more than once, producing an erroneously high count. The modification that was implemented in order to counteract these potential problems was: 60. 0.006” grooves were machined down the length of the inside of the condenser. These grooves were designed to provide a mechanism in which the smoke particle/ alcohol mixture can wick its way back to reservoir end to simulate the effects of gravity, hence, inhibiting the possibility of the fluid to inhibit the functioning of the unit.

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: The modifications to account for and eliminate this problem have been devised and implemented, however, it is not possible to test the effectiveness of these modifications in any of the available ground based facilities and/or the KC-135 due to the duration of the nominal operation time required (minutes per instance). This testing, and the verification of the accuracy of the instrument functions on orbit, are the core of the DAFT experiment. Two P-Trak units are included in DAFT flight hardware, one being only flight hardened, and the other with the modified condenser and flight hardened. To successfully accomplish P-Trak functional demonstration, additional hardware (which will not be explained in detail here) has to be delivered to the ISS. This hardware includes a dust concentration monitor (DustTrak), data cables, fill assembly, sample bag assemblies, sample holders, virtual impactor, alcohol reservoir, battery packs, a HEPA filter assembly, and appropriate tubing. The P-Trak utilizes isopropyl alcohol as a condensate, and its use must therefore, be carefully monitored and requires a specific agreement for that use on the ISS which is contained within a Volatile Usage Agreement (VUA) created for the experiment. 3.0 SAME CARRIER INTERFACES – MICROGRAVITY SCIENCE GLOVEBOX (MSG) 3.1 Power • 120 VDC • 28 VDC • ± 12 VDC • 5 VDC • Switch Control

They are organized by the assembly level, and the order in which they are currently planned to be installed into the MSG.: 1. Fluids Control Box Assembly (67198MABA220) The Fluids Control Box (FCB) installs on the back wall of the MSG in the upper left section. It is a fan cooled enclosure made from aluminum that contains most of the fluids control devices and monitoring devices including solenoids, pressure regulator, pressure transducers and mass flow controller. It interfaces directly with the MSG fluids resources (VES and GN2) and the Power Distribution and Control Unit (PDCU), and distributes the fluids resources accordingly.

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: Please refer to the SAME Fluids Schematic (67198PABA000) for more information on its, and the other fluids system functions. 2. Sample Plate Assembly (Experiment Support Plate Assembly) 67198ABA100 This assembly, when fully integrated, contains all of the major functional systems of SAME. It is a mounting plate which includes the mounting hardware for the Sample Carousel, the Thermal Precipitator Unit (TPU), the Dynamic Diagnostics Assembly (DDA) and the Aging Chamber Assembly (ACA). Permanently mounted to it are: • The Smoke Generation Tube • The Video Camera and Controller • The Sample Positioning system including: o the Sample Turning Module o the sample engagement mechanism o the sample position indicator o the sample positioning lock mechanism o the Sample Carousel mounting system

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 6 3. Dynamic Diagnostics Assembly (DDA) (67198MDBA165) The DDA is attached to the Sample Plate Assembly and the Aging Chamber Assembly by the crew and contains: the ISS and STS smoke detectors and the sampling ports that supply the P-Trak Enclosure and the Commercial Diagnostics Enclosure (and port(s) added for any additional diagnostics required). The DDA has a very low internal volume, and the flow of the sample aerosol through it is controlled by regulating and balancing the requirements of the active diagnostics in the DDA with the exhaust rate of the Aging Chamber piston, as controlled by its mass flow controller. It also contains a port, protected by a HEPA filter, that is connected to the VES for exhaust and purging. 4. Aging Chamber Assembly (67198MABA150) The Aging Chamber Assembly contains the cylindrical, metallic Aging Chamber, the pneumatically activated Inlet and Outlet Gate Valves and the Inlet and Outlet Elbows, which connect to the Smoke Generation Tube and the DDA, respectively. A Rulon piston, internal to the chamber, moves the sample into and out from the internal volume, and that flow is controlled by a mass flow controller which regulates the pressure or vacuum flow accordingly.

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: Sampling ports are provided in the elbows for use by the Thermal Precipitator, and the unit contains a Mixing Fan to insure that the contents are homogenous before disbursal to the DDA. 5. Data Acquisition and Control Unit (DACU) (67198EABA660) The DACU is the central control unit for SAME. The baseline software is resident there, and, although many of the other packages contain their own relay and control cards, ultimately it is the DACU that interfaces with the Ethernet and the MLC to orchestrate the performance of the experiment. It also collects and stores data for subsequent downlink through the MSG systems, and controls the MSG Video Recorder to provide a taped record of the pyrolysis event. 6. P-Trak Enclosure (67198MABA500) The P-Trak Enclosure is a flight hardened assembly containing a TSI P-Trak modified to take advantage of the VES system and to function in a microgravity environment. Although it interfaces with the DDA, the DACU, the Fluids Control Unit and the Power Distribution and Control Unit, it is basically a smart box that can operate independently and store its own data. 7. Commercial Diagnostics Enclosure (CDE) (67198MABA600) The CDE houses two of the SAME diagnostics, the TSI DustTrak and a First Alert ionization smoke detector. Both units have been hardened for flight and have been modified to utilize the VES to drive the sample.

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: The DustTrak has also been modified to utilize MSG air to provide its ‘sheath air’ in order to decrease the amount of aerosol required by the unit. Like P-Trak, the DustTrak portion of this device can operate independently and store its own data. The modified First Alert cannot. 8. Dynamic Diluter (DD) (67198MABA180) The DD is a custom designed component that provides dilution of the aerosol from the DDA before its introduction into the P-Trak (and possibly the DustTrak). It works by utilizing a laminar flow element to measure the amount of sample being introduced and using that information (from a differential pressure transducer) to increase or decrease the diluent flow to achieve the desired concentration. The dilution setpoint may be altered by software and adjusts to the desired setting in approximately 5 seconds. 9. Power Distribution and Control Unit (PDCU) (67198EABA680) The PDCU is the central disbursement point for the commands, power distribution and data collection for SAME. It contains the power converters, main relays and terminal data connections for the entire system and interfaces the DACU with the various systems and devices constituting the experiment.

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 7 10. Sample Carousel Assembly (67198MABB400) The Sample Carousel Assemblies (5) each contain six (6) Sample Tubes that interface the samples to the Smoke Generation Tube and allow the capture of the smoke in the Aging Chamber. Sample Carousels are sequentially installed onto the mounting locations on the Sample Plate Assembly, and the mechanisms contained by it identify the individual sample numbers, rotate the carousel to the correct position and engage the Sample Tube, which allows the sample to be in a position to be energized. The samples themselves are composed of five (5) materials: Teflon, Kapton, Silicone, Cellulose and DiButyl Phthalate (which being a liquid, is contained within a small section of cotton lampwick) in small, cylindrical sections, that are wrapped with coils of wire (baseline: stainless steel) that both provides the heat energy to the sample when energized and measures its temperature (by its varying resistance). These samples are removed from the tubes for weighing, both before and after the experiment (before launch and after being downmassed) to quantify the actual mass loss during pyrolysis. 11. Thermal Precipitator Unit (TPU) (67198MABB300) The TPU is a device that captures actual samples of the aerosol particulate on Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) grids for examination when returned from the ISS.

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: The units (4) are number matched to the samples in the carousel, to take samples from both the Inlet and Outlet Elbows leading to and from the Aging Chamber. 12. Alcohol Wick Storage Container (67198MABD700) The Alcohol Wick Storage Container is a custom manufactured aluminum vessel to contain the alcohol wick required by the P-Trak during the time (launch, non-ops) when it is not in direct use. Only one is nominally required, but two are included to provide one as a backup. 13. Hoses SAME utilizes ISS GN2 and the VES system both as resources for the experiment process and as systems to power its devices. These resources are distributed to the components from the FCU via the hoses, which are nominally operated at +/- 15 psig. In order to conserve weight and volume, and provide ease of operation, acrylic hoses and quick disconnects will be used for the distribution of pressure and vacuum throughout the system (not typical Teflon with stainless steel overbraid). 14. Harnessing All harnessing will conform to applicable standards and be designed to minimize the crew time needed to make the required experiment connections, without sacrificing reliability. 15. SAME Service Kit This is a place holder. SAME has not yet defined any servicing requirements.

text: 4.2 Video Recording Devices Video recordings of the smoke evolution process are very important for establishing proper operation of the test apparatus and for debugging the system operation. Furthermore, the video provides a helpful demonstration of the variability in smoke evolution. Experience with CSD showed dramatic cases where clearly visible smoke streams were not always detectable by the smoke detectors while invisible smoke streams were readily detected. Normal video resolution is acceptable if the smoke is illuminated by forward scattered light from an appropriate light source. Video will be viewed on and recorded by the MSG video Monitor/Recorder. 4.3 On-Orbit Crew Operational Functions The crew will be asked to assemble the experiment from provided subsections, load software, reload Sample Carousels, Thermal Precipitator Modules, and alcohol for the particle counter, enter parameters, initiate the experiment, and disassemble the experiment.

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 8 5.0 SAME SOFTWARE CONTROL 5.1 Software Controlled Operational Functions The DACU is the central point for SAME control. It is ultimately responsible for all experiment operations and interfacing with the environment external to SAME. It contains all of the logic necessary to autonomously operate the experiment as well as receive, validate, and process commands from the MSG. The DACU periodically transmits the status of the Smoke system to the MSG, which then forwards it to the ground. The software can autonomously control the progress of preprogrammed test, manage and store all science and system files on the local data storage medium, control the MSG video recorder capturing Smoke images, and copy the files to the MLC for downlink. The software inside the DACU is also responsible for providing diagnostic information and manual control of all sensors and controls using the GSE port. Please refer to the SAME Baseline Software Requirements Document (SAME-DOC-004) for more detail. 5.2 Data Collection Data is collected and stored in the DACU until it is time to downlink the information. The Thermal Precipitator Module, which collects samples of the smoke, will be bagged and returned for analysis. Sample Carousels are retained so that the samples can be weighed after return to Earth. 6.0 SAME OPERATIONS 6.1 Operations Flow 1.

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: Experiment Setup- The experiment will be shipped in individual subassemblies that will be assembled inside of the MSG. Parts will be inserted through the MSG side ports starting with the upper, back components. After the MSG ports are covered and the rack is returned to nominal position, the Experiment Software is installed onto the MSG Laptop. 2. Perform Experiment- The first steps in performing the experiment are to load the desired Sample Carousel, load or replenish the alcohol wick in the particle counter, and install a new Thermal Precipitator Module. Next, the start-up check out routine is performed. After the uplink parameters are sent, the experiment is initiated. Then, the baseline uplink parameters are modified, as required, for the next test and the experiment is initiated again until all six samples in the Sample Carousel have been used. The next number matched Sample Carousel and Thermal Precipitator Module will then be loaded and the experiment will continue as such until complete. 3. Shutdown and Repack Experiment- When all the Sample Carousels have been used and all the experiments have been performed, the final Sample Carousel and Thermal Precipitator Module will be capped and bagged. In reverse order of installation, the experiment hardware will be repackaged for downmassing.

A 10 7.2 Pressurized Systems The pressure system includes the aging chamber, the system for moving the piston in the aging chamber (valves, regulator, lines, hoses, relief devices) and the Dynamic Diluter. All of the parts will be designed to meet the requirements of NSTS1700.7 ISS addendum, NASA-STD-5003, SSP 30558, and SSP 52005 for pressurized hardware. Pressurized lines and fittings will be designed to a factor of safety of 4.0 X System MDP of 200 psid (ISS N2 limiting pressure). Pressurized system components will be designed to a factor of safety of greater than or equal to 2.5 X System MDP of 200 psid. Down stream of the pressure reduction the MDP is 20 psig. These components are designed with the same factors of safety. See table of components and factors of safety and hazard report SMOKE-04. Materials will be selected and evaluated for stress corrosion and/or fluid compatibility in accordance with SSP 30233, Space Station Requirements for Materials and Processes. In the event of loss of power all solenoids will close including the mass flow controllers, therefore the system will not over pressurize. More detail can be found in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001) specifically hazard report SMOKE-04. 7.3 Structures The SAME experiment is launched in stowage and contained in MSG for on orbit use.

text: The structural aspect of SAME is primarily sealed containers and vented containers. Pressure systems are covered in section 1.2. SAME structural failure is addressed in Hazard Report SMOKE STD 01 in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001). 7.4 Materials The ZIN Tech Engineering Team will assure that reasonable measures have been taken with regard to material selection for the experiment‘s design, and selected materials are safe for the intended manned space flight application in their respective usage environment. A material flammability assessment will be performed per NSTS 22648. The flight unit will be offgas tested. The SAME Project Team will prepare the standard Materials Identification & Usage List (MIUL) and MUA’s. ZIN Engineering will review and approve material evaluation prepared by the SAME Project, and submit it to NASA/GRC/SMAD for concurrence. Upon material evaluation approval, NASA/GRC/SMTD will issue the Material Certification Letter in accordance with the guidelines established in the applicable Material and Processes (M&P) Intercenter Agreement prior to flight hardware fabrication. Further information can be found in Hazard Report SMOKE STD 01 in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001).

text: 7.5 Frangible Materials (Glass) All of the hardware which contains glass will undergo a vibration test in the stowed configuration at workmanship or protoflight levels and a post-test visual inspection to verify ability to survive launch loads. The duct with the video camera lens and LEDs installed will be stowed with clear plastic for crew inspection after launch. 7.6 Release of Experiment By-products into the Cabin Atmosphere The P-Trak needs a cartridge with an alcohol-saturated wick for its operation; therefore, a risk of contaminating the ISS environment has to be considered. The amount of alcohol released will be carefully controlled and limited. The Project Team will submit a Volatile Usage Agreement request to JSC/OC (Material and Processes) for disposition and approval. All payloads are to submit their usage requests to a single approval authority at JSC because alcohol usage is a cumulative risk, and it will be necessary to process VUA through a single approval authority to track the total quantity of alcohol being used. More detail can be found in the safety date package (SMOKE-SDP-001). The pyrolysis products of Teflon currently have a JSC Tox level 3 for 5 minutes after creation. After this point the particles coalesce and drop to tox level 0. A hazard report has been generated to address this issue.

The MSG is the second containment of the smoke if the aging chamber where to leak. Finally the MSG is under a negative pressure which would prevent the smoke from leaking in the event of an MSG leak. Hazard Report SAME-08 has been written and submitted to the PSRP for review.

These lasers are of Class 1 lasers, and the laser beams are fully contained. These items are not removed from their original housings and are used in the applications for which they are intended. There is no crew access to the lasers at any time. The lasers meet ANSI Z136.1-2000 standards for Class 1.
