SAME-DOC-007 1 1.0 INTRODUCTION 1.1 Purpose This document will eventually hold most of the info rmation needed to operate the SAME experiment on ISS from the ground from the TSC. It will also descri be alternate methods of performing tasks when the experiment hardware is not on ISS, but is instead e asily accessible. For now, however, this document is a place to collect miscellaneous operational information and methods that need to be documented and under configuration control. 1.2 Scope TBD. 1.3 Applicable Documents [1] SAME-DOC-005 Software Interface Control Document

SAME-DOC-007 2 2.0 IN-FLIGHT FUNCTIONAL CHECKLIST This is a list of items that should be addressed after the hardware is installed in the MSG and before any samples are tested. Not currently in any order. - Perform piston calibration and alter registry values as necessary. See procedure later in this document. Run a test with heater setpoint below R0 and no use of the thermal precipitors in order to confirm correct calibration. - Figure out good values for STSPumpFailureLowLimit and STSPumpFailureHighLimit registry values. These depend somewhat on atmospheric pressure and should be adjusted for the ISS environment. Correctly set, these values help detect failure of the STS pump. - Log some data with the P-Trak and DustTrak and confirm that their settings are correct. For example: log interval, time constant, and date/time. - Record some video, downlink, and examine. - Experimentally determine the maximum setpoints that the mass flow controller will meet given ISS vacuum and GN2 sources. Determine if any desired inlet velocities or diagnostic combinations are affected. - The registry value, DisableChecksumCheck, can be set to 1 to avoid the startup delay associated with calculating the checksum each time.

- Revisit the decision about whether the heater controller offset correction will be done automatically as part of the test sequence or manually using the HeaterCorrectOffset utility prior to the test sequence. Adjust the CorrectOffset registry value appropriately.

SAME-DOC-007 3 3.0 STARTING THE SOFTWARE 3.1 Ground Computer On the ground computer you’ll need to first log on. Then start TReK with SAME configuration files. Also start SAMEDisplay. More TBD. 3.2 SAME Flight Software The software that controls the system starts automa tically upon power on. Within 30 seconds of turning on 120V power to the system there should be telemetr y data received at the SAMEDisplay application. The GMT will be updating and startup messages will appear in the log window. The Run Mode will change from Startup to Unitialized.

SAME-DOC-007 4 4.0 TEST CHECKLIST This is a list of important things to do or confirm pr ior to, during, and after the running of a sample test. Placement of a highly visible printout of this lis t on console is recommended. Steps depend on whether sample heater offset correction is being done automatically or manually. Check the CorrectOffset registry value to find out (0=manual, >0=automatic). - Once per carousel open the gate valves and turn on the diagnostics for TBD minutes. Downlink the data and verify correctness. The purpose is to collect baseline measurements of the MSG work volume required by the science team. 4.1 With Automatic Heater Offset Correction - Power on the system, wait for telemetry reception. - Send the Initialize command. - If the desired sample is not engaged, engage it using the Self Test command. - Turn on the 12VDC Heater Power. - Note the sample resistance and compare to ground measured resistance. If they differ significantly, TBD. Determine the setpoint. - Look at test parameters and change as necessary. Use manual positioning option, but carousel and sample number must be correct. - Start the test. - When the test pauses check the following: o A “sample type is confirmed” message appears in the log. o The offset correction returned a value less than 50uV in the log. o The sample resistance is still good. Within TBD % of before.

o The desired diagnostics are powered and readings are nominal. o GN2 regulated pressure and vacuum pressure are good. Range is TBD. - If the offset correction returned a value greater than 50uV, abort the test and restart. If the offset is still greater than 50uV, change the CorrectOffset registry value to 0 (manual) and use the manual heater offset correction checklist instead. - Resume the test. - Watch the log for details about when the sample heater will start. When it does, be ready to send an Abort command. - Watch the sample resistance and compare to the desired setpoint and MaxRt. The software will too, and will abort heating if the resistance/temperature gets too high. But watch anyway and send the Abort command in the highly unlikely event of too high resistance/temperature. - After sample aging, during exhaust, watch the output of the diagnostics for unexpected results. - After test is complete, power on any P-Trak or DustTrak that was used and retrieve the latest logged test ids. Turn back off. - As desired, force a transfer of the current housekeeping and log files to the MLC. Their transfer during power down has a slight chance of failing. Doing it here ensures success. - Perform any other desired OS or system maintenance, such as directory listings or self tests. - Disengage the sample.

SAME-DOC-007 5 4.2 With Manual Heater Offset Correction - Power on the system, wait for telemetry reception. - If the desired sample is engaged, DO NOT send the Initialize command. - If the desired sample is not engaged, send Initialize, engage sample using the Self Test command, and send Shutdown command with Restart option to bring system back to uninitialized state. - Send the OSCommand command with parameter ‘/root/HeaterCorrectOffset_g’. If this command returns 0 in the log, then proceed, otherwise repeat until it does. (Look at the value returned, not the details message which always says the same thing.) See section 7.5 for details about the HeaterCorrectOffset utility. - Send the Initialize command. - Turn on the 12VDC Heater Power. - Note the sample resistance and compare to ground measured resistance. If they differ significantly, TBD. Determine the setpoint. - Look at test parameters and change as necessary. Use manual positioning option, but carousel and sample number must be correct. - Start the test. - When the test pauses check the following: o A “sample type is confirmed” message appears in the log. o The sample resistance is still good. Within TBD % of before. o The desired diagnostics are powered and readings are nominal. o GN2 regulated pressure and vacuum pressure are good. Range is TBD. - Resume the test.

- Watch the log for details about when the sample heater will start. When it does, be ready to send an Abort command. - Watch the sample resistance and compare to the desired setpoint and MaxRt. The software will too, and will abort heating if the resistance/temperature gets too high. But watch anyway and send the Abort command in the highly unlikely event of too high resistance/temperature. - After sample aging, during exhaust, watch the output of the diagnostics for unexpected results. - After test is complete, power on any P-Trak or DustTrak that was used and retrieve the latest logged test ids. Turn back off. - As desired, force a transfer of the current housekeeping and log files to the MLC. Their transfer during power down has a slight chance of failing. Doing it here ensures success. - Engage the next desired sample using the SelfTest command. Engaging the next sample here shortens the time for starting the next test. - Perform any other desired OS or system maintenance, such as directory listings or self tests. - Send the Shutdown command with Shutdown option and power off system, or proceed to next test.

SAME-DOC-007 6 5.0 RUNNING A TEST 5.1 Initialization Select the Initialize button on the System tab, sending the Initialize command, and wait until the Run Mode changes from Unitialized to Ready. 5.2 Setting parameters From the Testing tab, select Change… to change to the set of test parameters you want to look at. Create a new test by selecting the CreateNew button. Select Set anywhere in the window to change the parameter for the selected test. The Test Setup group box is the way to choose which di agnostics to use. Select the Pri. or Sec. radio button to see the difference in setup between primary and secondary aging. Heater Control Setpoint should be set after knowing the unheated resistance of a sample, a.k.a. R0. Nominal setpoints are a multiple, Rt/R0, of R0 depending on sample type: Sample Type Setpoint Multiplier, Rt/R0 DBP TBD Kapton 1.380 Lampwick 1.245 Silicone 1.327 Teflon 1.440 To find the R0 of a sample, engage the sample to th e inlet tube either by manual blocking or using the SelfTest command with EngageSample option (on Syst em tab). Then on the Smoke Generation tab turn on the 12 VDC Heater Enable (right click on the ‘ LED’ and select ‘Set On’). Sample Resistance will settle to a valid measurement within 4 seconds.

5.3 Registry File Concerns Assuming you’ve set the test parameters to a specif ic carousel number, sample number, heating setpoint and duration, you may think you are ready to go. Y ou may not be. There are a bunch of sample-related limit checks that may cause an error or warning prior to heating. There are also many timing constants that affect the system behavior. These can be cha nged by selecting Set Registry… on the System tab. See SAME-DOC-005, Software Interface Control Document for key names and descriptions. A system timing simulator, currently located in SAMEFluidMode l.xls, will be available on console to help see the effect of registry value changes. Testing with the engineering unit is also recommended. Alternately, registry values can be changed by editing the registry.txt file on the DACU. This file is located in the /config directory. Also in that dir ectory is registry.orig.txt which contains the original registry settings. Important: Changes to registry values will not take e ffect until you restart the software. Follow the steps for shutting down, below, but use the restart parameter option.

SAME-DOC-007 7 5.4 Running the Test From the Testing tab select Start… and enter the test number to run, if it hasn’t already been entered in the field, and select Send. After sample positioning and aging chamber setup has occurred the test will pause so you can examine the log for any warnings or errors. Then send the Resu me button. The test should proceed to finish. You can abort anytime by sending the Abort command. An abort causes all valves to be turned off as well as all diagnostics. 5.5 Shutdown It is recommended that the system be gracefully shut down using the Shutdown button on the System tab, then cut power about 2 minutes later. Current housek eeping and log files are transferred to the laptop during the first minute. Use the second minute to ensu re that the system did not restart, looking for the restart of low rate telemetry packets and updating GMT. If the system restarts, select Shutdown again or send the OS command with parameter, ‘/bin/shutdown –b’. 5.6 Self-Tests The flight software has a few operations available through the SelfTest command. These may be useful for other than self-test purposes, for instance to engage a sample to the inlet tube to check R0.

Parameters depend on the self test: Self Test Parameter Definition Disengage Carousel no parameters Increment Carousel no parameters, rotates carousel one position Engage Carousel no parameters Dynamic Dilutor Parameter1: setpoint in sccm Parameter2: duration in seconds ISS Detector no parameters Fill Chamber Parameter1>0: Fill rate is this parameter divided by 10 in LPM Parameter1=0: Fill rate is ChamberSelfTestFillRate registry value Parameter2 not used. Exhaust Chamber Parameter1>0: Exhaust rate is this parameter divided by 10 in LPM Parameter1=0: Fill rate is ChamberSelfTestExhaustRate registry value Parameter2>0: Percentage to exhaust. Parameter2=0: Exhaust entire chamber. Sample Heater Parameter1>0: Duration in seconds Parameter1=0: Get previous run’s data and save to file. Do not heat sample. (Useful for aborted heating sequences.) Parameter2: not used. Setpoint ratio, Rt/R0, is SampleHeatingSelfTestRatio registry value. STS Detector no parameters Watchdog Timer no parameters. System will reset in 2 minutes.

SAME-DOC-007 8 6.0 PROCESSING FILES 6.1 Transferring files from DACU to the MLC All files will be automatically transferred from th e DACU to C:\ftp on the MSG laptop. Housekeeping files (.hkp) are transferred on the hour and upon shut down (with either the shutdown or restart option). The Log file is also transferred upon shutdown. P- Trak, DustTrak, and heater files are transferred soon after they are created. P-Trak and DustTrak file s are not automatically created since their data is embedded in the housekeeping data. To explicitly retrie ve logged data select the Transfer Data button on the DustTrak and P-Trak tabs. This should be do ne no more frequently than once per minute because the filename is derived from the GMT, including the latest minute, but not the latest second. If you need the data immediately or a file doesn’t get downlinked for some reason you’ll have to do it manually using one of two methods described here: 6.1.1 Using SAMEDisplay and FTP Cmd command. You’ll need to identify what file you need and the dir ectory it is in. Files are stored in a directory named according to GMT year and day. For instance /data/2006_132/. The .log file will be named 2006_132_00.log in this example. Housekeeping files will be 2006_132_15.hkp, 2006_132_16.hkp, etc. according to the GMT.

With the flight software and SAMEDisplay running (does not need to be Initialized), select the FTP Cmd from the System tab. Type: LCD /data/2006_132, for example, to change local directory (on the DACU) and send the command. Then select FTP Cmd again a nd type: PUT 2006_132_16.hkp, for example, and send the command. Watch your letter case – it matters. 6.1.2 Using SAME processor command line to transfer files For this to work you’ll need a keyboard and mon itor connected to the GSE port on the SAME DACU. Also, verify that the switch on the SAME DACU is sw itched to Override position. This is obviously a ground use only method. From the command line on the GSE monitor (if the so ftware is running you can get another console window by typing <CTRL><ALT>n, where n is 1 or 2), na vigate using cd and ls to the directory with the file you want to transfer. Type: ftp 192.168.1.1 <Enter>. Type: anonymous<Enter> for name and just <Enter> for password. Then at ftp> prompt t ype: bin<Enter>, then t ype: put 2006_ 132_16.hkp, for example. File should end up in C:\SAME Data on laptop. After done transferring file(s), type: bye<Enter> on the DACU. You can also use the two above methods to transfer files to the DACU using GET and get instead of puts. 6.2 Converting Housekeeping file to engineering units Use SAMEFileConverter. More instructions TBD.

SAME-DOC-007 9 7.0 MISCELLANEOUS PROCEDURES AND INFORMATION 7.1 Obtaining a directory listing An example: - OSCommand(‘ls –l /data/2006_237 > /data/dir.txt’). - FTPCommand(‘LCD /data’). - FTPCommand(‘PUT dir.txt’). - Have MSG cadre downlink the file dir.txt. 7.2 Replacing the registry file Normally you would change individual entries usi ng the SetRegistry command. This method could be used to set the registry to a known state, perhaps a f ile under source control, using an uplinked file. And this is the only way I could get the copied-over registry.txt file to ‘take’. If the system is shut down nicely through the shutdown command then it appears to revert to the old registry file. - FTPCommand(‘LCD /config’). - FTPCommand(‘GET registry.new.txt’) - OSCommand(‘cp /config/registry.txt /config/registry.old.txt’) - OSCommand(‘cp /config/registry.new.txt /config/registry.txt’) - Do a hard shutdown: power off - Power on and the new settings should take effect. 7.3 Piston Calibration Piston calibration, a.k.a. piston characterization, is a process of adjusting some registry values so that piston rates and time marks are correct for current conditions.

This process should be performed whenever there is a change of hardware, especially the aging chamber and piston itself; a change of environment, such as the move to the ISS; a change of fluid source strength; or a change of hardware condition, perhaps after many tests have been run. 7.3.1 Inlet Velocity Actual inlet velocity is required to match desired inle t velocity to within +/- 0.5 cm/sec. Actual velocity is not a directly measured value. It is a function of piston bottom to top travel time, chamber volume, and inlet tube diameter. The equation is: t Vv *60*105.2= where, v = actual velocity (cm/sec) V = chamber volume (L) = 5.65 t = piston travel time (seconds) 2.105 = conversion beween LPM and cm/sec Increasing the registry value, FillLeakRateLPM, will in crease the actual velocity. To determine piston travel time, perform the following steps: - Run a test with the desired inlet velocity and no heating (setpoint set below R0 and/or heater duration set to zero and/or no sample engaged.) - Abort the test during or after the aging period. - Obtain the drive side pressure data during chamber fill and graph it.

SAME-DOC-007 10 - Pick the points where the piston begins moving, characterized by the start of increasing pressure, and where the piston stops moving, characterized by drastically decreasing pressure. - Subtract the start time from the stop time and calculate velocity. Adjust FillLeakRateLPM and repeat as necessary. 7.3.2 Sample Heating Start Time Ideally, the start of sample heating is calculated so that the end of sample heating occurs before the piston reaches the top of the chamber. Actually, even before that, so that most of the smoke in the inlet tube at the end of heating enters the chamber as well. And really, even before that, so that some clean air follows the ‘last’ of the smoke and more of the smoke enters the chamber. The amount of the latter clean air is determined by the BackEndCleanAirOffset registry value. Because there is no direct physical measurement of where the piston is in the middle of its stroke, the software must estimate when the stroke begins and how long the stroke will take. Then it can back off from there to determine sample heating stop and start times. The registry values, FillWaita.b, where a.b is 0.0 to 5.0 by 0.5, help compensate for timing inconsis tencies which are a function of fill rate in LPM. (These values were more drastically a function of f ill rate before the FillLeakRateLPM registry value was increased from 0.0.

See section 7.3.1.). Piston chamber fill movement begins by evacuating the the drive side of the piston at a rate of 3.0 LPM until the drive side pressure reaches 13.2 psia. These values have been determined to be reliable, but can be changed if necessary by altering the registry values, FillStartRateLPM and FillStartPressurePSIA. Then the software waits for a period determined by th e desired fill rate, a function of inlet velocity, and the FillWait registry values. For a fill rate of 3.0 the software waits for the value of FillWait3.0. For rates in between, the wait time is interpolated. After wai ting this time the software marks the start of piston movement, logging a message for the user. Sample heating and other start and stop times are based on this mark. To determine the best FillWait registry values, - Perform the following steps for each rate, R= 0.5 to 5.0 by 0.5, and then estimate FillWait0.0 interpolating by hand on a graph of the other values versus rate. - Fill the chamber using the SelfTest command and the rate. - Note when the drive side pressure reaches 13.2 psia. The software issues a “x seconds before piston moving mark” message to indicate this point. The aim of this procedure is to get the ‘x’ right. - Note when the piston reaches the top of the chamber. Visual confirmation is best, but examination of the drive side pressure also works.

The start of the drastic drop in pressure is the point at which the top is reached. Do not rely on the “Aging chamber is filled” log message. This comes only after the FillTopPressurePSIA has been reached. - Subtract the two times to get the time between 13.2 psia and the top, tactual. - Registry value for this rate, a.b is, where, 60*. teLPMFillLeakRaba Vt chamber ideal −= and, chamberV = Chamber volume = 5.65 L FillLeakRateLPM = registry value by this name idealactual ttbFillWaita −=.

SAME-DOC-007 11 7.3.3 Secondary Aging Volume When a secondary aging period and volume are speci fied, the piston must stop a percentage of the distance between the top and bottom of the chamber. There is no direct physical measurement of the running distance, therefore it is estimated from th e exhaust rate over time. The registry value, ExhaustPercentageCorrectionFactor, is applied to the running percentage. To adjust this value, - Perform a SelfTest to exhaust the chamber to a specific percentage. For best results use the exhaust rate and secondary volume that will be used during the actual test. Or use 5 LPM and 50%. - Perform a SelfTest to exhaust the chamber the rest of the way. Use the same rate and 100%. - Calculate the time taken for each portion using log messages or pressure data and figure the percentage of total time taken by the second exhaust. Adjust the registry value and repeat until this percentage is within the desired accuracy of the secondary aging volume percentage. 7.3.4 Exhaust Rate It was verified that the system exhausts at a rate sufficient to achieve overpressure of the diagnostic duct for all combinations of diagnostic use except when usi ng the STS detector with both DustTraks. If this situation changes, the exhaust rate can be increased using the ExhaustOverpressureRate registry value.

7.4 Changing flight software during flight Description: Transfer new version of flight software from MLC to DACU. Uses crew time, SAME Utility Cable, and HyperTerminal application on MLC to perform ftp transfer, backup old flight software, and replace it with the new. Reboots are necessary b ecause the software runs au tomatically on startup and cannot be replaced while running. Therefore, afte r making a backup, the software is removed so that it cannot autostart. Then the new version is copied to the autostart name. Upon reboot, the system finds the autostart name again, the new version of software, and operation proceeds normally. *Note that only the steps marked with an asterisk n eed to be done by the crew. Wait 30 seconds for DACU to reboot. - *At HT, press <Enter> and verify that a prompt, “#”, appears. - *At ‘#’ prompt, type ‘cd /root<ENTER>’. - *Type ‘cp SAME_g.new SAME_g<ENTER>’. Wait for prompt, approx. 20 seconds. - *Type ‘shutdown<ENTER>’. - *Exit HT. - Ground team will confirm new version is running (or check log messages on Crew Display for report of version number), and then shutdown SAME. - *Remove cable. 7.5 Description of HeaterCorrectOffset Utility Sample heater offset correction is a feature of the sample heater microcontroller that reduces measurement error by automatically removing off set voltages from the signal path. After offset correction is performed, all subsequent resistance me asurements will include the o ffset correction. Until the system is powered off, that is. At power up the offset correction is zero. Offset correction should be run for each sample while the sample is engaged with the inlet tube and sample heater contacts. Occasionally the offset correction circuitry produces a co rrection that is obviously too high. The result is that subsequent reports of resistance are lower than ac tual.

This can be detected at the time of the test pause by looking at the sample resistance and by lo oking for the log message indicating the value of the offset correction. It should be approximately 200uV or less. If the offset correction at the time of the test pause is too high, then the test must be aborted and restarted to give the offset correction circuitry a second chan ce. To avoid this time-consuming detour a utility separate from the flight software has been developed. It is HeaterCorrectOffset_g in the /root directory of the DACU. It can be run from the flight software by sending the OSCommand command with a parameter of ‘/root/HeaterCorrectOffset_g’. The HeaterCorrectOffset utility app lies 12VDC to the sample heater , waits a few seconds, and then requests an offset correction from the heater microcontro ller. If the returned off set is in range then the utility exits, otherwise it requests the offset correction ag ain for several times until it is in range. Either way, 12VDC is removed from the sample heater befo re the utility exists. As long as system power (not 12VDC) remains applied, the offset correction initiated by the utility will be used by the flight software. If the utility fails to correct the offset to within the desired range then it returns a -1 (which is reported in the flight software log as 65280), otherwise it returns a zero to indicate success.

There is one caveat to running the HeaterCorrectOffset utility. The flight software must be either not running, which will not occur during flight, or must be in the uninitialized state. Once the software is initialized the utility cannot gain serial access to the heater micr ocontroller. Thus the sequence gymnastics in section 4.0. Additionally, if the HeaterCorrectOffset utility is used, then offset correction prior to the test pause should be disabled. Otherwise an incorrect correction he re will negate the use of the utility. Setting the CorrectOffset registry value to zero will disable au tomatic offset correction during the test, allowing the value created by the HeaterCorrectOffset utility to be used.

SAME-DOC-007 13 For advanced users, the HeaterCorrectOffset uti lity is configurable via its own registry file, /config/HeaterCorrectOffsetRegistry.txt, on the DACU. Changes on the flight system can be made by uplinking a new file. Parameters are as follows: Key Name Description Default Value Units Data Type HCOMaxOffset Maximum allowa ble offset. If above this value the utility retries the correction. 200 microvolts float HCORetries Number of times to retry the correction before returning -1. 3 n/a short HCOSleep1Msec This key plus next key is time to wait between turning on the 12VDC and requesting an offset correction. 3000 milliseconds ushort HCOSleep2Msec Time to wait between retries. 2000 milliseconds ushort As stated before, the HeaterCorrectOffset utility report s success or failure back to the flight software. More details, including the correction factor and resi stance measurement immediately after for each retry can be found in a log file in /data/HeaterCorrectOffset on the DACU. Beware that this file will be named the same as the current day’s flight software l og, but it will not be automatically downlinked upon shutdown. 7.6 Transfer and Installation of Crew Interface application FTPCommand(‘LCD /crewinterface’) FTPCommand(‘PUT SAMECrewInterfaceX.YInstall.exe’), where X.Y is the version.

The transfer takes about 1.5 minutes and the file should end up in c:\ftp on the MLC. An EDLFSerialPort Incorrect Checksum error may appear in the log. It can be ignored. At this point the MSG cadre will use their commands to run the install file. The format is: SAMECrewInterfaceX.YInstall.exe /SP- /VERYSILENT ,where X.Y is the version number. No user interaction is required with these options. The crew interface and support files will be installed in c:\01 on the laptop. See SAME-DOC-008, Crew Interface Description; SAME-PRO-002, Software Installation Procedure; and SAME-DOC-011, Flight Software VDD, for more information. The crew interface and support files are uninstalled by the MSG using the following: c:\01\unins000.exe /SILENT 7.7 Use of tar utility The tar utility can be used to assemble or disassemble collections of files on the DACU, much like WinZip does on a PC. It may be useful to tar a collection of files into one file prior to downlink. The executable is located in the /root directory on the DACU and therefore should be able to execute from any local directory. It is not necessary to specify the path to tar. Use the OSCommand and parameters according to http://www.qnx.com/developers/docs/6.3.0/neutrino/utilities/t/tar.html.

SAME-DOC-007 14 8.0 KNOWN ISSUES - Aborting a test occasionally causes the software to restart. If this should happen you’ll need to reissue the Initialize command. - Try to avoid running a test sequence through the change of hour (i.e. 12:45-13:05). Transfer of the housekeeping file at the top of the hour takes a good bit of processor time and the processor is close to 100% capacity, possibly affecting diagnostic measurement retrieval. - It is recommended that the system be gracefully shut down using the Shutdown button on the System tab, then cut power about 2 minutes later. However, about 20% of the time the software will hang or restart before completely shutting down. If it restarts, issue the Shutdown command again or issue the OS command with parameter, ‘/bin/shutdown –b’. If it hangs (you may only know this if you have a monitor connected to the GSE port) a hard power off will have to suffice. The operating system will clean up any file ‘litter’ on the next power up. - Maximum inlet velocity with the FillLeakRateLPM registry value equal to 0.30 is 9.8 cm/sec. Above this the software does not correctly use the FillWait registry values to time chamber fill operations, including sample heating start time. 10.0 cm/sec can be achieved if FillLeakRateLPM is 0.25 LPM or less.

But timing is affected in other ways and ground testing or flight testing without sample heating is recommended. - Whenever the P-Trak is on, the DACU requests a measurement from it once per second. Occasionally the P-Trak does not respond with a measurement and the DACU substitutes a -999 value instead to mark this occurance. If the P-Trak is logging during this time, that missing data can be recovered by issuing the Transfer Data command to retrieve the logged data. It is recommended that this be done for each test, soon (within days) after the test is complete. - The P-Trak memory can hold approximately 60 20-minute tests. When all memory is used the unit does not respond with any serial measurements while logging. In other words, continuous - 999 readings is one indicator of full memory. It is suggested that memory be cleared after 50 tests to be safe. - Sample heater offset correction occasionally produces an incorrect correction factor. The result is that reported sample resistance is lower than actual. For more information see section 7.5. - Using ground support equipment there was insufficient fluid flow during chamber exhaust to maintain overpressure of the diagnostic duct, as required, when the STS detector and both DustTraks are in use. When the STS detector is used it is recommended that at most one DustTrak is used.

- If the heater gives an “Abort on MaxRt” error, the system must be power cycled before proceeding. Otherwise, as will be apparent, the resistance measurement will be in error. - When specifying inlet velocities below 2 cm/sec, the FillWait registry values may not be accurate. The registry value, BackEndCleanAirOffset, must be adjusted to ensure correct heater timing. For 1 cm/sec, a value of 170 seconds is good. But run a test with no heating to be sure. - During ground testing the connection between the DACU and the MSGSimulator occasionally drops out. Packet count numbers of the MSGSimulator no longer increment and change from green to blue. To reestablish the connection deactivate it and activate it again.

SAME-DOC-003 Rev A 1 1.0 INTRODUCTION The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) instrument is an experiment payload planned for the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) located on the International Space Station (ISS). Thr oughout this document the term “project” is used to refer to the SAME project in its role as payload developer. 1.1 Purpose The purpose of this Software Description Document is three-fold: (1) to describe the Software Management Plan (SMP) for the project (2) to identify what product specification and procedure documentation will be produced as part of the software effort for the project, and (3) to identify and describe the records that will be produced as part of the software effort. This document is inte nded to be used as a roadmap of the software development effort, describing some aspects of the road within the document itself and, as applicable, pointing to other software documents and records which will be completed as the project progresses. The basis for this document, including structure, are two Glenn Research Center (GRC) Manuals, GRC - P2.6.4 and GRC -M2.6.4. Refer to these documents for more detailed background information and terminology definitions. 1.2 Scope This Software Description Document establishes the project's management processes for the software to be developed by the project to satisfy its requirements.

It also contains requirements to be satisfied by the providers of all software purchased, contractually acquired, developed, or maintained for the support or execution of the project. And e xcept for software and hardware interfaces used to estimate capabilities and schedules for the availability of support resources, it does not apply to software applications that provide company-wide capabilities not specific to this project. The term "software" as used in this document includes code, documentation, associated data, and "firmware", which is software installed in a medium that cannot be dynamically changed. The project software is comprised of several software “packages”, each executing on a separate platform. Located within the MSG will be a microcontroller-based data acquisition and control unit (DACU) that is responsible for direct control of the experiment. Connected to this controlle r is the MSG Laptop Computer (MLC) which will contain software to provide a crew interface into the DACU. Ground support software will be developed to collect and analyze on -orbit data at the GRC Telescience Support Center (TS C). Test software may be dev eloped to assist in the development and testing of hardware subsystems. This document is applicable to all of these packages. Any s pecific exceptions will be identified in the appropriate section.

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 2 2.0 INSTRUMENT OVERVIEW The SAME instrument is designed to quantify the size and distribution of smoke particulate in low gravity so that this information is available for the future design of effective low gravity smoke det ectors. The instrument will also be used to evaluate the performance of two existing U.S. spacecraft smoke detectors and one commercial smoke detector. Measurements will be made for the smoke from several materials found in spacecraft considering the effects of sample temperature, air flow, smoke residence time and aging. The primary targets are materials that produce liquid smoke particulate but solid smoke producers will also be considered. Figure 1 SAME Instrument Assembly Inside MSG WV The instrument is installed and operated in the MSG Work Volume (WV) which provides a minimal level of containment (see Figure 1). A general description of the major subsystems follows below. See SAME-DOC-001, Concept Description Document, for more detail. • Sample Carousel Turning Module, Sample Carousel and Heater Wire Coil These components are used to select and heat a sample in order to generate smoke. • Camera A camera and light(s) are mounted to see the sample and production of smoke. • Aging Chamber The aging chamber has a piston and two gate valves for holding the smoke for a time before releasing it downstream.

The piston is moved by pressure and vacuum provided by MSG and controlled by SAME. • Thermal Precipitator Module This assembly collects samples of smoke on TEM grids for post-flight inspection. It has access to smoke before and after the aging chamber. Aging Chamber Data Acquisition and Control Unit (DACU) Power Distribution and Control Unit Thermal Precipitator Module Sample Carousel Smoke Inlet Duct ISS Smoke Detector STS Smoke Detector Carousel Mounting Brackets Camera Controller P-Trak Enclosure Dynamic Dilutor Commercial Diagnostics Enclosure Fluid Control Unit

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 3 • Smoke Diagnostics After the aging chamber, the smoke is passed to several diagnostics: the TSI P-Trak™ particle concentration counter, the TSI DustTrak™ , a residential-grade ionization detector, the ISS photoelectric smoke detector and the STS ionization smoke detector. • Fluids Control Unit Pressure and vacuum supplied by MSG is controlled for smoke aging chamber piston movement and for all other fluid flow to and from the diagnostic equipment. • System Diagnostics Besides the diagnostic instruments measuring smoke characteristics, there are pressure transducers, temperature gauges, and voltage and current sensors to monitor system performance. • External Interfaces External interfaces provided by MSG include power, video recording, temperature control, post - pyrolization venting, nitrogen and air supply/vacuum, an RS-422 interface for commanding and telemetry, ethernet for file transfer, and a laptop for crew access to the SAME experiment. A SAMS unit measures local µg and vibrations and forwards that data to the ground requiring no SAME or MSG processing. • Avionics Contained in the Data Acquisition Control Unit (DACU) box, the SAME avionics conduct automated experiments, controlling the other sub-systems to produce and analyze the smoke. Commands from the ground are processed.

Experiment data is saved to files on a local storage medium and forwarded to MSG for subsequent downlink. Housekeeping data is downlinked every second and supplied to MSG. Off - nominal conditions are reported to MSG and the ground. In addition, a means for the crew to access SAME data and control is provided.

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 4 3.0 AVIONICS OVERVIEW SAME avionics are located in the DACU within the MSG Work Volume (WV). Cables will stretch to the SAME diagnostic hardware for control and feedback, to J311 of the WV for command and data transfer, and to J404 of the WV for ethernet connection to the MSG laptop computer (MLC) for file transfer and crew display operation. There is also a cable for the camera. 3.1 Data Interfaces To interface to the MSG, and subsequently to ground systems, the DACU CPU will communicate primarily to the MSG Rack Controller, also known as the SPLC (Standard Payload Computer) using an RS-422 interface (see Figure 2). SAME will use this interface to receive uplink commands and send health and status (H&S) data and low rate telemetry (LRT) data. Figure 2 SAME to MSG Data Interfaces Payload commands are transmitted from the ground through the ISS Payload MDM and eventually to the SPLC via MIL-STD-1553. The SPLC abstracts this interface from the payload developer, relieving the burden of knowing the details about the 1553 bus and command validation. A packet containing SAME health and status is automatically transmitted in the reverse direction on the 1553 bus and is received on the ground. Also included in the payload health and status packet is the Experiment Control Word or ECW, a single dedicated memory word that represents the status of the payload.

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 5 File-based SAME science data such as experiment measurement data and instrument ancillary data will be transferred to the MLC using FTP utilizing a 10BaseT ethernet connection. Once these files are stored on the MLC, the MSG Operations Team at the Payload Operations Integration Center (POIC) will periodically initiate their downlink and forward them to the SAME Operations Team. Since SAME is not permitted to transmit data on the ISS LAN, the DACU will automatically switch the active network connection fro m the MLC to SAME and ISS using a custom designed ethernet switch when the FTP transfer is required. In its normal state, the MLC will be connected to ISS LAN. The camera looking at the SAME sample is hooked up via an NTSC cable to a feedthrough inside the WV which is then patched on the outside to a video recorder channel in the video drawer. 3.2 DACU Overview The DACU is the central point for SAME control. It is ultimately responsible for all experiment operations and interfacing with the environment external to SAME. It contains all of the logic necessary to autonomously operate experiments. A brief list of its major responsibilities is as follows: 1. Receive, validate and process commands from the MSG. 2. Periodically transmit SAME system status and select parameters to the MSG. 3. Transmit completed and requested data files to the MLC via FTP. 4.

Manage and store all science and system files on the local data storage medium. 5. Autonomously control the progress of preprogrammed tests. 6. Provide diagnostic information and manual control of all sensors and controls using the GSE port. 7. Control the MSG video recorder(s) capturing SAME images. 8. React to sensor(s) out of tolerance by notifying MSG and ground systems, and performing software inhibits or other actions as appropriate. 3.3 Crew Display Overview During long periods of LOS or failure of telemetry, it is beneficial to provide limited visibility into SAME operation. Payloads may utilize the MLC to present payload status to the crew and provide a mechanism to control the payload directly from it. Two options for providing the SAME Crew Display are possible. Option 1 is the preferred solution at this time because of a likely delay in an upgrade to provide a dedicated ethernet link between the MLC and an experiment. 3.3.1 Option 1 - Custom Win32 or Java Based Application All data transmitted to the SPLC via H&S and LRT is also transmitted to the MLC via the MSG 1553 bus, and is therefore available on the MLC. SAME may develop a custom Win32-based or Java-based application that displays a limited set of the SAME downlink data for the crew to see and provides commanding to the SAME instrument.

3.3.2 Option 2 - Embedded Web Pages A dedicated ethernet interface between the MLC and SAME may be leveraged to provide a web-based interface into the DACU using the MLC native web browser. The operating system running on the DACU is capable of running an embedded web-server such as Apache or NASA’s Tempest servers.

A copy of these data files will automatically be forwarded to the MLC via FTP on a point-to-point cross-wired ethernet cable. The SAME Operations Team will submit a request to the MSG Team at MSFC to downlink the files on the M LC at the earliest possible time. Because the connection is made directly to the MLC, no bandwidth restrictions are necessary to ensure ISS LAN resource availability. 4.2.2.1 FTP Usage [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-2-1-1] All data files stored on the DACU local storage shall be automatically forwarded to the MLC via FTP for backup and downlink. 4.2.2.2 Network Details [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-2-2-1] A dedicated standard 802.3 (10BaseT) ethernet connection from the MLC to the DACU shall be used to perform the FTP transfer. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-2-2-2] Communications with the FTP server shall be done utilizing a server IP address of 192.168.1.1, port 21.

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 9 4.3 Data Storage Requirements The data storage requirements reflect two main needs. First, that a record of all status, measurements and events is preserved beyond the flight of the instrument. And second, that individual values of status, measurements or events can be easily located in stored data. 4.3.1 Storage Media [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-1-1-1] The DACU shall store all files on a media that can preserve all generated files for extraction after payload down-mass. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-1-1-2] The storage media shall have a capacity of at least 520 megabytes. 4.3.2 File Conventions 4.3.2.1 Directory Structure Because the execution of ISS instrument experiments are highly scheduled, the date and time that procedures and ground commanding is performed is usually reliably recorded by NASA cadre and experiment ground operation teams. As such, finding the data files for a previously run experiment or for a particular logged event is facilitated by a data storage structure based on the date. Therefore, [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-2-1-1] All files created shall be organized into a hierarchical directory structure based on the date that files were created. 4.3.2.2 File Names [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-2-2-1] All files created shall have unique file names.

4.3.3 Stored Data 4.3.3.1 Housekeeping Data [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-1-1] Once per second data relating to the status of the instrument shall be stored to a file. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-1-2] Each second of housekeeping data stored to a file shall be time-tagged. 4.3.3.2 Messages [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-2-1] Messages generated by the instrument shall be stored to a file. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-2-2] Each message stored to a file shall be time-tagged. 4.3.3.3 Experiment Results [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-3-1] Experiment results shall be stored to a file [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-3-2] Experiment results stored to a file shall be time-tagged. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-3-3] DELETED.

The specific payload conditions that result in warning and caution levels are determined by the Payload Safety Review Panel (PSRP) during Phased Safety Reviews. Smoke Experiment aka Characterization of Smoke Particulate for Spacecraft Fire Detection Engineering Report Characterization of Ignitor Wire Candidates Submitted by: ZIN Technologies, Inc Len Miller April 2002

SMOKE Experiment Ignitor WIre Characterization Study April 2002 Purpose: The purpose of this report is to document the results of a study conducted in search of the ideal type of wire to be used for the hot wire ignitors for the Smoke Experiment. Objective: The objective of this study was to find a wire with a consistent, linear resistance versus temperature characteristic and with a “significant” slope. Scope: This study was conducted in the Phase A Laboratory (Bldg 77, Room 154A) on commercially available wire. The ignitor manufacturing technique and the pyrolization of samples is beyond the scope of this study. Procedure: Each type of wire was mounted on a test fixture. The test fixture was then placed into a ThermCraft laboratory oven. The oven was programmed to ramp up to a set point, hold the set point for fifteen minutes, and then ramp to the next set point until the final temperature of approximately 800 oC was attained. (See oven cycle graph in Appendix C.) Resistance readings were taken near the end of each “dwell” period. Several of the wire types were subjected to additional tests to examine the effects of the previous thermal cycle(s). The test fixture held approximately thirty-four inches (0.86 meters) of wire. A stainless steel sheathed type-k thermocouple (Omega Part No. KQSS-116U-24) was placed inside the oven in close proximity to the wire under test.

Leads of high temperature furnace wire (#18 AWG) were brought out of the oven to enable the test conductor to measure the resistance of the wire under test. The resistance of the leads and the terminations was characterized by subjection the fixture and leads to a thermal cycle with a copper bus bar shorting the terminals of the fixture. The fixture resistance was subtracted from the total resistance reading for each test point to determine the net resistance of the wire under test. The results were recorded in an Excel Workbook. Several different data plots were prepared and studied.

SMOKE Experiment Ignitor WIre Characterization Study April 2002 Summary and Conclusions: This study examined the characteristics of eight types of wire: anodized mild steel, pure iron, Alomega (similar to Alumel), -Stainless steel, pure platinum, platinum-rhodium, tungster-5%rhenium, and tungsten-26%rhenium. Traditional heating wires, Nichrome and Kanthal were also included for comparison. Pure platinum has close-to-ideal characteristics. However the cost of the material may be prohibitive. Alomega and stainless steel ran a close second. Mild steel, iron and tungsten-composites oxidized in the oven and their characteristics changed significantly from one thermal cycle to the next. Nichrome and Kanthal have too flat a slope to meet the objectives. Further testing will be conducted to determine the optimum wire type and wire diameter. Representative test samples will by pyrolized using various ignitor configurations. The quality and quantity of the smoke will be visually evaluated. Test Results: The tests were conducted in the Phase A Lab from February 6, 2002 through March 20 2002, by Len Miller and Nathan Funk of Zin Technologies, Inc. The individual results for each test were tabulated and plotted. For those wires subjected to more than one thermal cycle, the comparative results were plotted. Finally, an overall plot of the combined results was prepared.

The entire Excel Workbook, with tabulated test results and plots thereof, is included in Appendix A of this report. Photographs of the laboratory apparatus are in Appendix B and a graph of the thermal cycle is in Appendix C.

Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER) Abstract Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER) is an extension or continuation of Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), conducted in space from September 9 to October 5, 2007. On the success of SAME, SAMER included the following modifications: 1) a new test sample material Pyrell ®, an intumescent fireretardant foam by Foamex was introduced to replace DBP samples, 2) test condition ranges was extended to include higher heating temperature and no-flow conditions, and 3) a new instrument, M-pass, developed in-house GRC, was used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures used in SAME. SAMER flight tests were conducted from July 16, to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points. As a part of SAMER effort, three major post–flight ground tests were performed: the SAMER apparatus flow tests to obtain accurate dilution ratio data, the TEM tests to obtain the 1-g counterpart of TEM samples and a batch of SMPS tests to examine the validity of the lognormal distribution assumption of aerosol particle size for the tested materials.

Based on the results of both SAMER flight and ground-based tests, it is concluded that the moment method in conjunction the lognormal distribution assumption is a valid and effective approach to characterization of the aerosol encountered in space vehicles. Particle size distributio ns of aerosol produced from 5 tested materials commonly found in space crafts were identified. Introduction Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER) is one of the awarded Rapid Turn Around (RTA) projects, solicited by NASA Headquarters in June 2009. SAMER is an extension or continuation of Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), which was conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) onboard the International Space Station (ISS) from September 9 to October 5, 2007. Generally speaking, SAME experiments were completed successfully in that the apparatus developed for the experiments functioned well and desired data from instruments were obtained. However, there was a major problem of the SAME experiments. After the thermal precipitators returned to the ground, it was found that all the TEM grids were severely contaminated with some unidentified foreign particles, making these grids unusable although some of them showed shapes of certain types of smoke particles.

Based on the experience gained from SAME, SAMER included the following modifications: 1) a new test material, Pyrell®, an intumescent fire-retardant foam by Foamex, was introduced to repl ace DBP samples, 2) test conditions were broadened including higher heating temperatures and no-flow during sample heating time, and 3) a new instrument, M-pass, developed in-house GRC, was used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures that includes a DustTrak and an ionization detector used in SAME. SAMER flight tests were conducted from July 16, to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points. After SAMER flight tests, three major post–flight ground tests were performed to improve data reduction process and to validate the lognormal distribution assumption, the key to the moment method employed by SAME and SAMER. The first ground-based test is the SAMER apparatu s flow tests. The objective of the test is to obtain accurate dilution ratio data of the P-trak and Dusttrak so that the accuracy of aerosol concentration can be improved. The second batch of ground tests was the TEM tests which were conducted under exactly the same conditions as those for the SAMER flight tests so that the gravity effects on the TEM samples can be identified.

The third batch of ground tests was to a SMPS apparatus to obtain the actual particle size distribution under the same condition as the SAMER flight tests. The objective of these tests is to ex amine the validity of lognormal particle size distribution assumption. Besides these ground tests, there were two improvements in the data reduction procedures. One is to derive sample heating temperatures from the logged engineering data so th at each test can be characterized by the sample heating temperature instead of R t/R0 as has always been used. It was reali zed that even two tests use the same R t/R0, the sample heating temperatures can be quite different. Charac terizing a test with sample heating temperature makes it

easier to understand the particle generation from the view point of material pyrolysis. The second improvement is to device a method of calculating the percentage of cumulative moment detected by an instrument that has a limited particle size detection range. This development allows us to improve uncertainty analysis of the results we obtained. Since the apparatus used in SAMER is mostly unchanged from that of SAME and the basic approach – the moment method – used by the two experiments are the same, in this report, these two parts – the apparatus and the moment methods – will not be repeated. What w ill be included in this final report are the newly added part, the improved data reduction methods and the new results of particle distributions. As desc ribed above, the count mean diameter and the diameter of average mass measurements are independent of the nature of the size distribution however, the calculation of the geometric mean diameter and the geometric standard deviation ( σg) depend on the assumption of a log-normal distribution. This assumption cannot be directly tested with the available da ta since this would require a device that can separate the particles into size bins. However, there are two indications that the distribution can be approximated by a lognormal distribution. In the cases listed below, the count mean diameter is less than the diameter of average mass which is a necessary condition for a log-normal distribution (See Fig. 1). The second indication is that the geometric standard deviations are all physically reasonable (i.e. greater than 1 (see Eq. 3) and less than approximately 3.5 which is the practical limit on the magnitude of aerosol ge ometric standard deviation). The aging results show a substantial increase in the observed diam eters. As expected the increase in th e count mean diameter is greater than the corresponding increase in th e diameter of average mass. This can be understood since coagulation consists of particle collisions joining two particles.

For a polydisper se aerosol, these collisions usually involve the collision of one of the smallest (high mobility) particles with the larg est (high cross-section) par ticles. This collision has little effect on the size of the large particle but it removes the smaller particles from the size distribution. This has a larger effect on the count mean diameter since it is linear in diameter while the diameter of average mass varies with the cube root of the diameter. Impact of flow on particle morphology As the samples are heated by the wire, chemical bonds are broken and gaseous products are released via pyrolysis. These products may include partially oxidized species resulting from the reaction with oxygen. As the gases move from the wire, the temperature and species concentration will decrease as a result of conduction/diffusion and convection. With the decrease in temperature, the super saturation ratio of the pyrolysis gas will pass a critical stage and nucleation of smoke particles will occur. These smoke nuclei grow rapidly from the condensation of the pyrolysis gases. The time scale for the nucleation and condensation is on the order of miliseconds or less.

Over a longer time scale, the growing smoke particles undergoing Brownian motion collide and stick together in a process known as coagulation. This process may continue for time scales of up to thousand seconds. If the particles are liquid, the colliding particles will coalesce and form larger droplets. This is the case for the lampwick, silicone rubber, and Kapton smokes (Fig. 11). If the particles are solid, they will retain their structure as they stick resulting in an agglomerate structure composed of many primary particles connected in a low density fractal-like structure. This is the case for the Teflon and Pyrell smokes (Fig. 11). Key parameters affecting the smoke properties of the smoke produced here are the low-gravity condition, the convective flow past the heated wire, the wire temperature, and the aging time. As the wire temperature increases, more of the sample will be pyrolyzed and these gases will subsequently condense on the nuclei leading to a larger mass concentration of the aerosol and a larger diameter of average mass. An increase in the convective flow for a fixed wire temperature is expected to result in an increase in the pyrolysis rate and thus an increase in the mass concentration of the aerosol. Some results follow this trend with silicone rubber, lampwick, and Pyrell increasing slightly with flow while Teflon and Kapton decrease.

A possible explanation is that holding the wire temperature fixed does not necessarily mean that the sample surface temperature distribution is precisely the same at different air flow speeds. Although these are expected to be small variations, given the exponential dependence of the pyrolysis kinetics on temperature, changes in the heat transport environment could change the sample surface temperature between the wire coils. A case of special interest is the case of zero-flow. The transport for the zero-flow case in μ-g is controlled by molecular diffusion and thermal expansion. Over a period of 60 seconds, the gases would diffuse a distance on the order of 4 cm. Assuming a cubical geometry this would correspond to the smoke being confined to a volume of about 64 cm3 rather than being diluted in the 6000 cm3 piston. If the same number of particles is generated as for the flow case, the initial concentration will be on the order of 50 times higher for the zero-flow case. SAME Smoke-in-Drums Ground-Based Experiment In order to assess whether the size distribution of the smoke is lognormal, detailed particle size distributions were measured with a reference instrument. This cannot be accomplished in low gravity, so this investigation was performed with the ground-based engineering SAME hard ware which is identical to the setup on the ISS, incorporating the flight aerosol instruments which had been returned to earth. A Scanning Mobility Particle Sizer (SMPS) Spectrometer (3936, TSI, Shoreview, MN, USA) was used as the reference instrument in validation experiment. The SMPS requires a two minute scan through a range of voltages to acquire a high resolution particle size distribution; however, the duration of smoke supplied from the SAME aging chamber is at most 30 seconds. Therefore, the smoke was collected in an intermediate container which served two purposes. The first purpose was to sufficiently dilute the smoke from the SAME chamber in order to effectively stop coagulation (aging) of the smoke particles during the SMPS scans.

The second purpos e was to have a large enough quantity of dilute smoke for multiple SMPS scans. A 55 gallon drum was chosen for this purpose and the SAME smoke-in-drums setup was developed to enable SMPS measurements on a portion of the smoke output from the SAME piston chamber. The configuration is shown in Figure 14, which shows the or iginal SAME hardware inside the dashed outline. One DustTrak™ was removed from the original SAME configuration and its portion of the smoke sample was diverted from the setup to one of two drums which hold the diluted smoke during multiple 2-minute SMPS measurements. One drum collected fresh smoke from the heated sample material and the other drum was filled after a controlled aging period in the piston chamber. Thus both aged and unaged smoke could be measured with the SMPS. Drum Hardware and Experimental Process The two 55 gallon drums were minimally modified for use in the experiment as follows: A muffin fan was bolted to the circular drum floor opposite the removable lid. All other modifications were made to the lid, including feedthrough adapters for tubing and the electrical fan cord, and mounted HEPA filters through which clean air was provided for purging. A four-way crossover valve enable d the drum to be either filled with smoke via a vacuum pump preceded by a flow-controlling orifice, or bypassed by the smoke, which effectively isolated the SAME hardware from high pressure during the drum purging process. Transfer of un-aged smoke into the drum began when the SAME software commanded the valve opening and lowered the piston in the aging chamber causing half of the chamber volume to be expelled (3 liters), with the remainder of the smoke retained in the chamber and allowed to age for 12 minutes. The flow rate into the drum was 1.7 L/min, matching the flow rate of the DustTrak™ instrument that the drums replaced. It took less than 2 minut es to transfer the smoke sample into the drum.

Tubing from the SAME hardware to the drums was less than one meter in order to minimize transport losses of smoke particles. Initial calculations from previous SAME data indi cated that for all materials, the aerosol concentration in the drum would be less than 2 × 10 4 particles/cm3, which is below the rule-of-thumb threshold concentration of 106 particles/cm3. Below this level, coagulation can be neglected since it will occur at a very slow rate. 15 Thus it could be assumed that very little aging took place in th e drum during the SMPS measurements of un-aged smoke. The drum concentration was well within the counting range of the SMPS so no additional dilution was required for

the measurements. During each SMPS sample, the volume of air removed was between 0.5 % and 1.5 % of the drum volume and a correspondingly small number of particles were removed so the drum aerosol concentration was relatively constant during the measurements. Any make-up air needed during the sampling was drawn in through the HEPA filters on the drum lid. The fan in the drum was used to mix the smoke and prevent stratification which could skew the SMPS measurements. First, a 10:1 sheath -to-aerosol flow ratio was used for three consecutive measurements with high fidelity giving particle sizes up to 660 nm. Three subsequent samples were taken with a flow rate ratio of 5:1, in order to reach the largest meas urable SMPS particle size of 1000 nm. Considering that aging increases particle size, the high er flow rate ratio (smaller range) give s results for only a portion of the true aged size distribution for most materials in this experiment. Therefore the larger range is important for measurements in spite of the low resolution. After six SMPS scans at two different flow rates, the drum was purged with a continuous flow of HEPA-filtered house air at appr oximately 309 kPa-g (45 psig), which was exhausted into a fume hood. An additional P-Trak™ was used to indicate when the drum concentration was below 30 particles/cm3, which was considered ‘clean’.

One set of SMPS measurements for one smoke sample (both aged and unaged) was accomplished in approximately 30 minutes. Limitations of Aerosol Instrument Measurement Ranges Calibration of SAME instruments was intended to empirically account for differences in the ranges of the instruments. In the ground valida tion tests, however, the truncated distribution formula (equation 13) can shed light on th e limitations and unce rtainty of the SMPS measurement range for the fuels te sted. Particularly when the particle size distributions are converted to surface area or volume distributions, the percentage of the distribution that is lacking can be significant. Furthermore, the upper end of the SMPS size distribution measurement may not be as reliable because it can be affected by poor counting statistics and these bins are more susceptible to multiple charge correction errors.

Therefore it is prudent to compare a more conservative upper SMPS limit of 700 nm along with the full recorded range to 1000 nm, to see the effect of the SMPS measuremen t range. Log-probability Plot The log-probability plot is a graphical technique used to assess lognormality of an aerosol. Discrete data from the SMPS size bins and TEM size distributions are plotted on the probability scale.

Lognormal distributions will be a straight line, and volume and number size distributions should be parallel, indicating that σg is the same for both distributions but with different means. Extremes on the graphs can be neglected in the log probability plots for number distributions when they deviate from the straight line fit for 5% or less of the extremes of the probability scale (Hinds, 1999). For the SMPS data, these deviations are the result of poor counting statistics in the large diameter tail and lack of measurement range (for lamp wick and silicone), which particularly affects the volume distribution plots. Thus the volume distribution plot will display a line that is slightly curved at the large sizes, which corresponds to a lack of linearity of the number distribution line beyond 95% of the distribution. Sample heating temperature derivation Sample heating temperature is one of the key parameters that dictate the properties of generated smoke particles. When studying effects of gravity on the smoke properties, we want to compare smokes generated at the same temperature. For SAME and SAMER, during a test, the so ftware controls the temperature via the resistance of heating wire. It is true that for the same wire coil, co nstant wire resistance means constant wire temperature. Traditionally, test conditions are specified by Rt/R0, the ratio between the resistance of heated wire over the resistance of the wire at room temper ature. Thus, before each run, the samp le wire resistance is measured, then multiplied by this parameter to get the target resistance for the control circuitry. Although, Rt/R0 can uniquely define the temperature, it is not clear what actual sample temperature is. Since the wire resistance is one of the parameters that are logged in the en gineering data sheet which makes it possible to derive actual temperature from the logged resistances. However, when deriving wire temperatures, one has to take the fact into account that the wire length varies from sample to sample and so called room temperature varies too.

After the heating temperatures were obtained, it is surprising that for the same R t/R0, the actual heating temperature di fference can be as large as 30 degrees Celsius. The following is how this is carried out. SAME heater temperature modeling.

Objective: It was identified that each sample has a significant length of leading section of the resistive wire. This section does not touch the sample material and is exposed in air flow. Thus the temperature of this leading section is different from the portion of the wire that contacts the sample material. The control circuitry only controls the total resistance of the heating wire, not individual portion of the wire. Our goal is to find the temperature of the wire that is in contact with the sample material. Formulation: Hypothesis: the temperature difference between the two portions of the wire is caused by different convection heat transfer from the two. The wire that is in contact with the sample has less heat loss from the convection heat transfer because about half of its surface area is covered by the sample material. Assumptions and simplifications: 1) Assume the entire wire consists of two distinct portions, one is in air (portion 1) and the other (portion 2) is in touch with the sample so that only half of the wire area is exposed to air. 2) Uniform cross section area of the wire, so the resistance is proportional to the length and the resistivity of the wire. 3) Resistivity is a known function of temperature. 4) Temperature distribution inside wire is uniform. 5) Newton convective heat transfer equation applies to both sections but with different coefficients.

Although the port 2 is half exposed in air where convective equation works and half in contact with sample where transient conduction heat transfer should be used, for the sake of simplicity, we lump the two mechanisms together and use convection only with a modified heat transfer coefficient. I. Introduction ppropriate design of fire detection systems requires knowledge of both the expected signature of the events to be detected and the background levels of the measured parameters. Terrestrial fire detection systems have been developed based on extensive study of terrestrial fires. 1, 2 Unfortunately there is no corresponding data set for spacecraft fires and consequently the fire detectors in current spacecraft were developed based upon terrestrial designs. There are a number of factors that can be expected to affect the particle size distribution of the smoke from spacecraft fires. The absence of buoyant flow in low-gravit y increases the residence time in microgravity fires and increases the transit time from the reaction zone to the detector. 3 Microgravity fires have been found to have radically different structure from their normal-gravity (a.k.a. 1-g) counterparts. The limited options available to respond to a spacecraft fire increase the importance of early detection. Finally the materials used in spacecraft are different from typical terrestrial applications where smoke properties were previously evaluated. All of these effects can be expected to change the smoke particle size distribution. The objective of this work was to make sufficient measurements of smoke from spacecraft fires to enable improved design of future detectors.

Smoke Background Smoke is a general term that encompasses aerosol materials produced by a number of processes. In particular it can include unburned, recondensed, original polymer or pyrolysis products that can be either liquid or solid, hydrocarbon soot, condensed water vapor, and ash particles. Soot particles dominate the smoke particulate in established flaming fires while unburned pyrolysis produc ts and recondensed polymer fragments are produced by smoldering and pyrolysis in the early stage of fire growth. Given the constrained space on any spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not es tablished flaming fires; consequently, the primary target for detection is the pyrolysis products and not the soot. Prior spacecraft systems are summarized in more detail in papers by Friedman and Urban. 4, 5 In the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo missions, the crew quarters were limited and mission durations were short, consequently it was considered reasonable that the astronauts would rapidly detect any fire. The Skylab module, however, included approximately 30 UV-sensing fire detectors. 4 These devices were limited to line-of-sight and were reported to have difficulties with false alarms.

The Space Shuttle Detectors were based upon ioni zation fire detector technology, the most advanced technology available at the time and used an inertial separator designed to eliminate particles larger than 1-2 micrometers. The International Space Station (ISS) smoke de tectors use near-IR forward scattering, rendering them most sensitive to particles larger than a mi crometer, outside of the range of sensitivity of the shuttle detector. As described by Friedman4 there have been six overheat and failed component events in the NASA Orbiter fleet in addition to several similar incidents that have occurr ed on the ISS. None of these events spread into a real fire but as mission durations increase, the likelihood of failures increases. The experience on Mir in 1997 has shown that failure of oxygen generation systems can have significant consequences. As a result, improved understanding of spacecraft fire detection is critically needed.6 Previous work on smoke particles from low-gravity sources by Urban et al. 5 found that the particulate produced by low-gravity flames (soot or unburned fuel particles) tends to have larger size particles than in normal gravity.

Results from the CSD (Comparative Soot Diagnostics) Experiment 5 which studied smoke properties in low-gravity from several spacecraft materials suggested that liquid smoke particles could achieve sizes larger than 1 µm while solid particulate remained in the sub-micrometer range. However, the CSD experiment did not produce sufficient data concerning the size of the liquid smoke particles to guide detector design. The combined impact of these limited results and theoretical predictions is that, as opposed to extrapolation from 1-g data, direct knowledge of low-g combustion particulate is needed for more confident design of smoke detectors for spacecraft. II. SAME Experiment To address the limited data from the CSD experiment concerning the likely size of spacecraft smoke particulate, another experiment was developed: the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). The SAME experiment sought to avoid the problems experienced by the CSD experiment by obtaining the particulate size statistics on-orbit with a reduced dependence upon sample return to Earth. This is a challenging endeavor because existing aerosol instrumentation is typically large, incompatible with spacecraft experiment constraints, and some systems require substantial sample return to Earth.

As will be described below, an alternative approach was employed that used three discrete instruments to measure separate moments of the size distribution. When combined, these moments provide useful aggregate statistics of the size distribution. The measurements were made using smoke generated by overheated spacecraft materials in much the same manner as the CSD experiment however the sample temperature, flow field, and particle aging time were more rigorously controlled in the SAME experiment. G. Experimental Results Over 100 sample materials were tested. These were comprised of samples of 6 materials: Teflon™, Kapton™, Pyrell™, silicone rubber, cellulose (lamp wick), and dibutyl-phthalate deposited on a porous wick. The test conditions included multiple sample temperatures and air flow rates. The baseline air flow rate was 8 cm/s with runs conducted at rates down to 2 cm/s with a limited set conducted with no airflow while the sample was heated. The sample temperatures were based on the pyrolysis properties of the material and were thus material specific. The baseline temperature was selected to produce 1 to 2 mg of weight loss in 60 seconds and have reasonable signal on each of the moment instruments. To examine the effect of sample temper ature, additional higher temperature conditions were also selected that would not saturate th e moment instruments. The TEM girds recovered from the thermal precipitators on SAME-1 were unfortunately cont aminated with extraneous particles whose origin is currently under investigation. For SAME-2 more rigorous assembly controls were followed and numerous good particle images were obtained. For typical runs, the partic le concentrations were a few million particles / cc and the mass concentrations were 2 to 15 mg/m 3 however there were runs with fewer particles.

For these conditions, the typical numbers of particles sampled by the instruments were in the billions although for the test with the lowest particle concentrations the sample sizes were of the order of several million particles. 1. Moment Instrument Results Geometric mean, count mean, and average mass diameter re sults from the moment instruments for baseline runs are presented in Table 1. As desc ribed above, the count mean diameter and the diameter of average mass measurements are independent of the nature of the size distribution however, the calculation of the geometric mean diameter and the geometric standard deviation ( σg) depend on the assumption of a log-normal distribution. This assumption cannot be directly tested with the available da ta since this would require a device that can separate the particles into size bins, However, there are two indications that the distribution can be approximated by a lognormal distribution. In the cases listed below, the count mean diameter is less than the diameter of average mass which is a necessary condition for a log-normal distribution (See Fig. 1). The second indication is that the geometric standard deviations are all physically reasonable (i.e. greater than 1 (see Eq. 3) and less than approximately 3.5 which is the practical limit on the magnitude of aerosol ge ometric standard deviation).

The aging results show a substantial increase in the observed diam eters. As expected the increase in th e count mean diameter is greater than the corresponding increase in th e diameter of average mass. This can be understood since coagulation consists of particle collisions joining two particles. For a polydisper se aerosol, these collisions usually involve the collision of one of the smallest (high mobility) particles with the larg est (high cross-section) par ticles. This collision has little effect on the size of the large particle but it removes the smaller particles from the size distribution. This has a larger effect on the count mean diameter since it is linear in diameter while the diameter of average mass varies with the cube root of the diameter.
