2. MPASS Results The MPASS was included in SAME-2 to demonstrate the effectiveness of a two-moment smoke detector. Because of how they are used, a smoke detector is not calibrated for speci fic materials and instead has a single calibration for all conditions. The objective is to maintain a flat sensor response, regardless of the type of smoke or the particle size so the signal is proportional only to a se lected moment (e.g. mass or number concentration). The approach used was to derive correlations to predict the smoke number concentration and mass concentration from the MPASS output. This correlation was made using the other SAME measurements (number and mass concentration) as a reference. A least-squares, third-order, correlation was computed on all test points with a signal to noise ratio greater than 2 independent of all other parameters (e.g. material, heating rate, and aging time). The results are shown in figures 9 and 10, for prediction of the mass concentration and the number concentration, respectively. Ideally th ese response graphs should be horizont al lines. The norm alized output is plotted along with the normalized correlation result as a function of geometric m ean diameter. Ideally the normalized result should be horizontal lines.

The uniformity of response (scatter) is expressed by the least squares variance relative to the mean ( Δ) and is shown in the legend. Both figures show that the correlation decreases the relative variance by roughly a factor of at least 2 relative to that provided by a conventional single-output sensor. The resulting variance for the mass response is substantially lower than for the number concentration. This is consistent with the fact that the original optimizati on of the MPASS was to mass concentration not to number concentration. Thus with appropriate processing, the MPASS output can be proportional to either the number concentration or the mass concentration over a wide range of particle sizes and material compositions. This independence demonstrates that by combining 2 moments the MPASS is able to scale its response to the particle size being sampled giving a more accurate indication of the amount of smoke present than a single moment detector. The MPASS therefore has the ability to discern the difference between a strong signal from a high smoke concentration and a strong signal from a lower concentration of very large dust particles, a feature which can minimize false smoke detector alarms. 3. TEM Results Overall, 72 particle samples were taken on Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) grids using the thermal precipitator. These samples were imaged with a TEM to evaluate the particle morphology as a function of flow conditions, material and heating level. Overall, silicone rubber and DBP presented no particles that were visible via TEM, presumably because the particles were condensed liquid that evaporated before they could be imaged in the TEM. Figure 11 presents typical images for the major materials. As seen in Table 1, aging did increase the average partic le size, however this level of change is not readily visible in the TEM images, instead the mo st visible change is the disappearance of the smallest particles. (Fig 12) As described in the discussion of Table 1, this is consistent with expectations since the smaller particles have the highest mobility and consequently are readily incorporated in to the larger particles. Particularly for the semi-liquid particles, this absorption of the smallest particles into larger particles is expected to have little or no apparent effect on the size of the larger particles b ecause the diameter is the cube root of the volume. In th e case of non-liquid particles, the smallest particles will ne vertheless be unlikely to be visible via TEM when they are attached to larger particles.

4. Impact of flow on particle morphology As the samples are heated by the wire, chemical bonds are broken and gaseous products are released via pyrolysis. These products may include partially oxidized species resulting from the reaction with oxygen. As the gases move from the wire, the temperature and species concentration will decrease as a result of conduction/diffusion and convection. With the decrease in temperature, the super saturation ratio of the pyrolysis gas will pass a critical stage and nucleation of smoke particles will occur. These smoke nuclei grow rapidly from the condensation of the pyrolysis gases. The time scale for the nucleation and condensation is on the order of ms or less. Over a longer time scale, the growing smoke particles undergoing Brownian motion collide and stick together in a process known as coagulation. This process may continue for time scales of up to 103 s. If the particles are liquid, the colliding particles will coalesce and form larger droplets. This is the case for the lampwick, silicone rubber, and Kapton smokes (Fig. 11). If the particles are solid, they will retain their structure as they stick resulting in an agglomerate structure composed of many primary particles connected in a low density fractallike structure. This is the case for the Teflon and Pyrell smokes (Fig. 11).

Key parameters affecting the smoke properties of the smoke produced here are the low-gravity condition, the convective flow past the heated wire, the wire temperature, and the aging time. As the wire temperature increases, more of the sample will be pyrolyzed and these gases will subsequently condense on the nuclei leading to a larger mass concentration of the aerosol and a larger diameter of average mass. An increase in the convective flow for a fixed wire temperature is expected to result in an increase in the pyrolysis rate and thus an increase in the mass concentration of the aerosol. Some results follow this trend with silicone rubber, lampwick, and Pyrell increasing slightly with flow while Teflon and Kapton decrease. A possible explanation is that holding the wire temperature fixed does not necessarily mean that the sample surface temperature distribution is precisely the same at different air flow speeds. Although these are expected to be small variations, given the exponential dependence of the pyrolysis kinetics on temperature, changes in the heat transport environment could change the sample surface temperature between the wire coils. Length scale 2 μm Figure 12: TEM images showing the effect of aging for Kapton (Run 62) and Pyrell (Run 63). From Left to right, unaged Kapton, aged Kapton, unaged Pyrell, aged Pyrell.

A case of special interest is the case of zero-flow. The transport for the zero-flow case in μ-g is controlled by molecular diffusion and thermal expansion. Over a period of 60 seconds, the gases would diffuse a distance on the order of 4 cm. Assuming a cubical geometry this would correspond to the smoke being confined to a volume of about 64 cm3 rather than being diluted in the 6000 cm3 piston. If the same number of particles is generated as for the flow case, the initial concentration will be on the order of 50 times higher for the zero-flow case. This is expected to lead to more coagulation and a larger particle size. It is found for all of the materials the diameter of average mass is 30 % to 40 % larger for the zero-flow tests compared to the flow tests. The zero flow condition was not in the original design of the SAME hardware but was examined for 11 tests by modifying the valve operation in the SAME hardware. This resulted in a very high concentration of particulate where the aging process was accelerated compared to that in the aging chamber at dilute conditions. An unfortunate side effect was that approximately half the smoke was lost from the system because it diffused out of the inlet into the MSG volume. As a result the total particle counts were lower than normal and the TEM grids had few particles.

It is important to recognize that this condition is unique to low-gravity scenarios. If one performed the same experiment at 1-g, the buoyancy of the rising gases would greatly increase the mixing zone. So the larger particle diameters observed in these zero-flow conditions are important to consider in the development of improved fire detection equipment for space vehicles. For the zero-flow case, the heat is transported primarily by conduction rather than convection. This is likely to result in a significant increase in the gas temperature relative to the case with 8 cm/s air flow. A striking effect of this temperature change is the change in the morphology of the Pyrell smoke from fractal-like clusters with up to 30 primary spheres for the case with a flow of 8 cm/s to spherical particles for the zero-flow condition (Fig 13). The results from the SAME experiment indicate that su bstantial differences in the size distributions of the smoke particles are evident for the five spacecraft material s that were tested. For the conditions of the SAME experiment, all samples produced significant numbers of sub-micron particulate that are readily detected using an ionization smoke detector. However, the aging results sugg est that some materials such as silicone rubber can produce smoke that can reach sizes better detected by light scattering techniques. The zero flow conditions produced smoke particles that were 2 to 3 times larger than those produced at the nominal 8 cm/s flow rate. Since spacecraft fire conditions include an even wider array of materials than those tested here and a broader range of flow and temperature conditions, broad smoke aerosol size distributions can be expected from credible pre-fire overheat events. These results suggest that detection methods that can measure more than one moment of the size distribution may show more successful detection and false alarm rejec tion than single moment detectors. The results from the prototype 2-moment detector (MPASS) were very encouraging in this respect with the technique showing real potential as a means to respond to a broad particle range while avoiding excessive false alarms from nuisance sources.

The TEM result demonstrated that fire particulate can be expected to have a broad range of morphologies influenced by heating rate, material and flow conditions. IV. A 3 2.2 SAME Experiment Background Since the very beginning of the manned space flight program, NASA engineers and scientists have gone to great lengths to prevent fires from occurring on spacecraft. They have done this by adapting fire safety systems and procedures developed on Earth to the unique conditions and operating environment of spacecraft. However, microgravity combustion experiments have shown that fire can behave very differently in space and the best methods to prevent, detect, and extinguish fires on a spacecraft may be very different than those used on Earth. In 2000, NASA's Bioastronautics Initiative began with the objective of ensuring and enhancing the health, safety, and performance of humans in space. As part of this effort, the Life Support and Habitation Branch at NASA Glenn Research Center is responsible for developing and implementing a research plan to significantly improve fire safety on spacecraft and in space habitats. This goal will be achieved by applying a significant amount of fundamental knowledge and the experimental capability of microgravity research to spacecraft fire safety questions. Spacecraft smoke detectors must detect smoke with a variety of particulate types. Hydrocarbon fuels typically produce soot, while overheated plastics produce droplets of recondensed polymer fragments.

text: Paper and silicone rubber produce a smoke that is composed of liquid droplets of recondensed pyrolysis products. Differences in the nucleation and growth processes for these different types of smokes create particles that have different sizes and properties. The Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) experiment that flew in the Glovebox on STS-75 demonstrated that the smokes with solid particulates created in microgravity formed longer chains, and aggregated into larger particles than those created in normal Earth gravity. This is surmised to have occurred because of the increased residence time in the high concentration smoke regions and to have affected the responses of the two spacecraft smoke detectors (ISS and STS) utilized in that experiment. To develop smoke detectors that are sensitive to the type and size of smoke particles that will be encountered in microgravity and to allow them to distinguish between dust and smoke, better knowledge of the size distribution and morphology of the particulates is required. 2.3 SAME Experiment Objectives The major goal of this experiment is to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulates achieve in microgravity and to relate the droplet size and distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment.

text: This will be accomplished by extending the Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) concept to provide a particulate count and mass density determination to the diagnostic array used to analyze these liquid smokes. The experimental design and practical application of this data will be enhanced by the development of a numerical code that will predict the smoke droplet growth as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment. The SAME experiment has the following (listed) objectives: 1. Make measurements of three moments of the particle size distribution for the μg smoke from several materials found in spacecraft considering the effects of sample temperature, air flow, smoke residence time (near the source) and smoke aging. The primary targets are materials that produce liquid smoke particulate but solid smoke producers will also be considered. 2. Make measurements of the effect of µg and 1-g on the size distribution of liquid aerosol smokes (using an idealized smoke e.g. DBT) to provide data for numerical model comparison. 3. A 4 2.5 The SAME Risk mitigation experiment – DAFT The objective for the risk mitigation experiment, DAFT (Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test), is to provide a microgravity technology demonstration of the P-Trak Ultrafine Particle Counter manufactured by TSI. The P-Trak is a hand held air quality monitor which is capable of counting particles whose mean diameter is in the range of 1.0 to 0.05 microns. After extensive market research performed by both the Engineering and Science teams, it has been determined that the PTrak is the only commercially available hardware that can perform this particle count while maintaining the weight, resource, and space limitations for an MSG experiment. P-Trak measures particle number concentrations in real-time while storing that data in a memory maintained by an onboard battery. These measurements are made in units of particles per cubic centimeter (pt/cm3) versus traditional aerosol measurements of milligrams per cubic meter (mg/m3) made by photometers. P-Trak operates by using the particles in the aerosol as seeds to condense droplets of alcohol (a condensate nuclei counter). These droplets have many times the average diameter of the original particles, and may, therefore, be easily counted with standard optical techniques.

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: The potential problem is that these droplets are directed through a nozzle to facilitate the counting, and some of these droplets (a predictable percentage) collide with the walls and form a film. In a gravity environment, this film is recycled by ‘falling’ down hill. In microgravity, the distinct possibility exists that these droplets will form a film that will bridge and block the nozzle, effectively plugging the flow of droplets and preventing the device from functioning, or obscuring the optics. Furthermore, there is some concern that the droplets inside the optics chamber may get trapped in an internal circular motion and be counted more than once, producing an erroneously high count. The modification that was implemented in order to counteract these potential problems was: 60. 0.006” grooves were machined down the length of the inside of the condenser. These grooves were designed to provide a mechanism in which the smoke particle/ alcohol mixture can wick its way back to reservoir end to simulate the effects of gravity, hence, inhibiting the possibility of the fluid to inhibit the functioning of the unit.

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: The modifications to account for and eliminate this problem have been devised and implemented, however, it is not possible to test the effectiveness of these modifications in any of the available ground based facilities and/or the KC-135 due to the duration of the nominal operation time required (minutes per instance). This testing, and the verification of the accuracy of the instrument functions on orbit, are the core of the DAFT experiment. Two P-Trak units are included in DAFT flight hardware, one being only flight hardened, and the other with the modified condenser and flight hardened. To successfully accomplish P-Trak functional demonstration, additional hardware (which will not be explained in detail here) has to be delivered to the ISS. This hardware includes a dust concentration monitor (DustTrak), data cables, fill assembly, sample bag assemblies, sample holders, virtual impactor, alcohol reservoir, battery packs, a HEPA filter assembly, and appropriate tubing. The P-Trak utilizes isopropyl alcohol as a condensate, and its use must therefore, be carefully monitored and requires a specific agreement for that use on the ISS which is contained within a Volatile Usage Agreement (VUA) created for the experiment. 3.0 SAME CARRIER INTERFACES – MICROGRAVITY SCIENCE GLOVEBOX (MSG) 3.1 Power • 120 VDC • 28 VDC • ± 12 VDC • 5 VDC • Switch Control

They are organized by the assembly level, and the order in which they are currently planned to be installed into the MSG.: 1. Fluids Control Box Assembly (67198MABA220) The Fluids Control Box (FCB) installs on the back wall of the MSG in the upper left section. It is a fan cooled enclosure made from aluminum that contains most of the fluids control devices and monitoring devices including solenoids, pressure regulator, pressure transducers and mass flow controller. It interfaces directly with the MSG fluids resources (VES and GN2) and the Power Distribution and Control Unit (PDCU), and distributes the fluids resources accordingly.

text: Please refer to the SAME Fluids Schematic (67198PABA000) for more information on its, and the other fluids system functions. 2. Sample Plate Assembly (Experiment Support Plate Assembly) 67198ABA100 This assembly, when fully integrated, contains all of the major functional systems of SAME. It is a mounting plate which includes the mounting hardware for the Sample Carousel, the Thermal Precipitator Unit (TPU), the Dynamic Diagnostics Assembly (DDA) and the Aging Chamber Assembly (ACA). Permanently mounted to it are: • The Smoke Generation Tube • The Video Camera and Controller • The Sample Positioning system including: o the Sample Turning Module o the sample engagement mechanism o the sample position indicator o the sample positioning lock mechanism o the Sample Carousel mounting system

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 6 3. Dynamic Diagnostics Assembly (DDA) (67198MDBA165) The DDA is attached to the Sample Plate Assembly and the Aging Chamber Assembly by the crew and contains: the ISS and STS smoke detectors and the sampling ports that supply the P-Trak Enclosure and the Commercial Diagnostics Enclosure (and port(s) added for any additional diagnostics required). The DDA has a very low internal volume, and the flow of the sample aerosol through it is controlled by regulating and balancing the requirements of the active diagnostics in the DDA with the exhaust rate of the Aging Chamber piston, as controlled by its mass flow controller. It also contains a port, protected by a HEPA filter, that is connected to the VES for exhaust and purging. 4. Aging Chamber Assembly (67198MABA150) The Aging Chamber Assembly contains the cylindrical, metallic Aging Chamber, the pneumatically activated Inlet and Outlet Gate Valves and the Inlet and Outlet Elbows, which connect to the Smoke Generation Tube and the DDA, respectively. A Rulon piston, internal to the chamber, moves the sample into and out from the internal volume, and that flow is controlled by a mass flow controller which regulates the pressure or vacuum flow accordingly.

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: Sampling ports are provided in the elbows for use by the Thermal Precipitator, and the unit contains a Mixing Fan to insure that the contents are homogenous before disbursal to the DDA. 5. Data Acquisition and Control Unit (DACU) (67198EABA660) The DACU is the central control unit for SAME. The baseline software is resident there, and, although many of the other packages contain their own relay and control cards, ultimately it is the DACU that interfaces with the Ethernet and the MLC to orchestrate the performance of the experiment. It also collects and stores data for subsequent downlink through the MSG systems, and controls the MSG Video Recorder to provide a taped record of the pyrolysis event. 6. P-Trak Enclosure (67198MABA500) The P-Trak Enclosure is a flight hardened assembly containing a TSI P-Trak modified to take advantage of the VES system and to function in a microgravity environment. Although it interfaces with the DDA, the DACU, the Fluids Control Unit and the Power Distribution and Control Unit, it is basically a smart box that can operate independently and store its own data. 7. Commercial Diagnostics Enclosure (CDE) (67198MABA600) The CDE houses two of the SAME diagnostics, the TSI DustTrak and a First Alert ionization smoke detector. Both units have been hardened for flight and have been modified to utilize the VES to drive the sample.

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: The DustTrak has also been modified to utilize MSG air to provide its ‘sheath air’ in order to decrease the amount of aerosol required by the unit. Like P-Trak, the DustTrak portion of this device can operate independently and store its own data. The modified First Alert cannot. 8. Dynamic Diluter (DD) (67198MABA180) The DD is a custom designed component that provides dilution of the aerosol from the DDA before its introduction into the P-Trak (and possibly the DustTrak). It works by utilizing a laminar flow element to measure the amount of sample being introduced and using that information (from a differential pressure transducer) to increase or decrease the diluent flow to achieve the desired concentration. The dilution setpoint may be altered by software and adjusts to the desired setting in approximately 5 seconds. 9. Power Distribution and Control Unit (PDCU) (67198EABA680) The PDCU is the central disbursement point for the commands, power distribution and data collection for SAME. It contains the power converters, main relays and terminal data connections for the entire system and interfaces the DACU with the various systems and devices constituting the experiment.

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 7 10. Sample Carousel Assembly (67198MABB400) The Sample Carousel Assemblies (5) each contain six (6) Sample Tubes that interface the samples to the Smoke Generation Tube and allow the capture of the smoke in the Aging Chamber. Sample Carousels are sequentially installed onto the mounting locations on the Sample Plate Assembly, and the mechanisms contained by it identify the individual sample numbers, rotate the carousel to the correct position and engage the Sample Tube, which allows the sample to be in a position to be energized. The samples themselves are composed of five (5) materials: Teflon, Kapton, Silicone, Cellulose and DiButyl Phthalate (which being a liquid, is contained within a small section of cotton lampwick) in small, cylindrical sections, that are wrapped with coils of wire (baseline: stainless steel) that both provides the heat energy to the sample when energized and measures its temperature (by its varying resistance). These samples are removed from the tubes for weighing, both before and after the experiment (before launch and after being downmassed) to quantify the actual mass loss during pyrolysis. 11. Thermal Precipitator Unit (TPU) (67198MABB300) The TPU is a device that captures actual samples of the aerosol particulate on Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) grids for examination when returned from the ISS.

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: The units (4) are number matched to the samples in the carousel, to take samples from both the Inlet and Outlet Elbows leading to and from the Aging Chamber. 12. Alcohol Wick Storage Container (67198MABD700) The Alcohol Wick Storage Container is a custom manufactured aluminum vessel to contain the alcohol wick required by the P-Trak during the time (launch, non-ops) when it is not in direct use. Only one is nominally required, but two are included to provide one as a backup. 13. Hoses SAME utilizes ISS GN2 and the VES system both as resources for the experiment process and as systems to power its devices. These resources are distributed to the components from the FCU via the hoses, which are nominally operated at +/- 15 psig. In order to conserve weight and volume, and provide ease of operation, acrylic hoses and quick disconnects will be used for the distribution of pressure and vacuum throughout the system (not typical Teflon with stainless steel overbraid). 14. Harnessing All harnessing will conform to applicable standards and be designed to minimize the crew time needed to make the required experiment connections, without sacrificing reliability. 15. SAME Service Kit This is a place holder. SAME has not yet defined any servicing requirements.

text: 4.2 Video Recording Devices Video recordings of the smoke evolution process are very important for establishing proper operation of the test apparatus and for debugging the system operation. Furthermore, the video provides a helpful demonstration of the variability in smoke evolution. Experience with CSD showed dramatic cases where clearly visible smoke streams were not always detectable by the smoke detectors while invisible smoke streams were readily detected. Normal video resolution is acceptable if the smoke is illuminated by forward scattered light from an appropriate light source. Video will be viewed on and recorded by the MSG video Monitor/Recorder. 4.3 On-Orbit Crew Operational Functions The crew will be asked to assemble the experiment from provided subsections, load software, reload Sample Carousels, Thermal Precipitator Modules, and alcohol for the particle counter, enter parameters, initiate the experiment, and disassemble the experiment.

text: SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 8 5.0 SAME SOFTWARE CONTROL 5.1 Software Controlled Operational Functions The DACU is the central point for SAME control. It is ultimately responsible for all experiment operations and interfacing with the environment external to SAME. It contains all of the logic necessary to autonomously operate the experiment as well as receive, validate, and process commands from the MSG. The DACU periodically transmits the status of the Smoke system to the MSG, which then forwards it to the ground. The software can autonomously control the progress of preprogrammed test, manage and store all science and system files on the local data storage medium, control the MSG video recorder capturing Smoke images, and copy the files to the MLC for downlink. The software inside the DACU is also responsible for providing diagnostic information and manual control of all sensors and controls using the GSE port. Please refer to the SAME Baseline Software Requirements Document (SAME-DOC-004) for more detail. 5.2 Data Collection Data is collected and stored in the DACU until it is time to downlink the information. The Thermal Precipitator Module, which collects samples of the smoke, will be bagged and returned for analysis. Sample Carousels are retained so that the samples can be weighed after return to Earth. 6.0 SAME OPERATIONS 6.1 Operations Flow 1.

document: SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text: Experiment Setup- The experiment will be shipped in individual subassemblies that will be assembled inside of the MSG. Parts will be inserted through the MSG side ports starting with the upper, back components. After the MSG ports are covered and the rack is returned to nominal position, the Experiment Software is installed onto the MSG Laptop. 2. Perform Experiment- The first steps in performing the experiment are to load the desired Sample Carousel, load or replenish the alcohol wick in the particle counter, and install a new Thermal Precipitator Module. Next, the start-up check out routine is performed. After the uplink parameters are sent, the experiment is initiated. Then, the baseline uplink parameters are modified, as required, for the next test and the experiment is initiated again until all six samples in the Sample Carousel have been used. The next number matched Sample Carousel and Thermal Precipitator Module will then be loaded and the experiment will continue as such until complete. 3. Shutdown and Repack Experiment- When all the Sample Carousels have been used and all the experiments have been performed, the final Sample Carousel and Thermal Precipitator Module will be capped and bagged. In reverse order of installation, the experiment hardware will be repackaged for downmassing.

A 10 7.2 Pressurized Systems The pressure system includes the aging chamber, the system for moving the piston in the aging chamber (valves, regulator, lines, hoses, relief devices) and the Dynamic Diluter. All of the parts will be designed to meet the requirements of NSTS1700.7 ISS addendum, NASA-STD-5003, SSP 30558, and SSP 52005 for pressurized hardware. Pressurized lines and fittings will be designed to a factor of safety of 4.0 X System MDP of 200 psid (ISS N2 limiting pressure). Pressurized system components will be designed to a factor of safety of greater than or equal to 2.5 X System MDP of 200 psid. Down stream of the pressure reduction the MDP is 20 psig. These components are designed with the same factors of safety. See table of components and factors of safety and hazard report SMOKE-04. Materials will be selected and evaluated for stress corrosion and/or fluid compatibility in accordance with SSP 30233, Space Station Requirements for Materials and Processes. In the event of loss of power all solenoids will close including the mass flow controllers, therefore the system will not over pressurize. More detail can be found in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001) specifically hazard report SMOKE-04. 7.3 Structures The SAME experiment is launched in stowage and contained in MSG for on orbit use.

SAME structural failure is addressed in Hazard Report SMOKE STD 01 in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001). 7.4 Materials The ZIN Tech Engineering Team will assure that reasonable measures have been taken with regard to material selection for the experiment‘s design, and selected materials are safe for the intended manned space flight application in their respective usage environment. A material flammability assessment will be performed per NSTS 22648. The flight unit will be offgas tested. The SAME Project Team will prepare the standard Materials Identification & Usage List (MIUL) and MUA’s. ZIN Engineering will review and approve material evaluation prepared by the SAME Project, and submit it to NASA/GRC/SMAD for concurrence. Upon material evaluation approval, NASA/GRC/SMTD will issue the Material Certification Letter in accordance with the guidelines established in the applicable Material and Processes (M&P) Intercenter Agreement prior to flight hardware fabrication. Further information can be found in Hazard Report SMOKE STD 01 in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001).

text: 7.5 Frangible Materials (Glass) All of the hardware which contains glass will undergo a vibration test in the stowed configuration at workmanship or protoflight levels and a post-test visual inspection to verify ability to survive launch loads. The duct with the video camera lens and LEDs installed will be stowed with clear plastic for crew inspection after launch. 7.6 Release of Experiment By-products into the Cabin Atmosphere The P-Trak needs a cartridge with an alcohol-saturated wick for its operation; therefore, a risk of contaminating the ISS environment has to be considered. The amount of alcohol released will be carefully controlled and limited. The Project Team will submit a Volatile Usage Agreement request to JSC/OC (Material and Processes) for disposition and approval. All payloads are to submit their usage requests to a single approval authority at JSC because alcohol usage is a cumulative risk, and it will be necessary to process VUA through a single approval authority to track the total quantity of alcohol being used. More detail can be found in the safety date package (SMOKE-SDP-001). The pyrolysis products of Teflon currently have a JSC Tox level 3 for 5 minutes after creation. After this point the particles coalesce and drop to tox level 0. A hazard report has been generated to address this issue.

text: The smoke is contained in the smoke tube and aging chamber for 5 minutes. All the smoke is expelled through HEPA filters, some of which dumps into the ISS vent the rest of it into the MSG. The MSG is the second containment of the smoke if the aging chamber where to leak. Finally the MSG is under a negative pressure which would prevent the smoke from leaking in the event of an MSG leak. Hazard Report SAME-08 has been written and submitted to the PSRP for review.

SAME-DOC-008 Rev A 1 1.0 INTRODUCTION Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) is an experiment payload planned for the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) located on the International Space Station (ISS). The Crew Disp lay (a.k.a. Human-Computer Interface or HCI) will operate on the MSG Laptop Computer MLC. It provides the crew with information about the current status of the experiment and an ability to issue commands to control the system. The crew interface for SAME is intended to be used only in off-nominal conditions. The nominal operation of the experiment will occur via ground commanding. 1.1 Purpose The purpose of this document is to describe the SAME Crew Display and to: 1) Provide details about the implementation of the SAME Crew Display requirements found in SAME-DOC004, Section 7.0 2) Satisfy the Preliminary and Candidate Display Deliveries as required for the Payload Display Review Team (PDRT) 1.2 Scope This document is limited to the operation of the SAME Crew Display. Issues concerning general operation of the experiment via the software operating on the DACU or ground systems are not discussed here.

SAME-DOC-008 Rev A 2 2.0 CREW INTERFACE 2.1 Purpose The purpose of the crew interface on SAME is to provide some basic information about the status of the experiment during off-nominal conditions, especially in case of loss of data telemetry and/or commanding from and to the ground. This information is minimal in nature. It represents the basic information that a crew member may be asked to report and commands they are asked to issue during off-nominal conditions. Section 3.0 provides flow diagrams showing the typical use of the crew interface. In summary, those uses are: • Commanding and Telemetry Check. Verification of SAME data transmittal and command reception. • Sample Positioning Check. Used to debug unexpected sample positioning behavior that could use a crew member’s eye. • Gate Valve Check. Used to debug unexpected gate valve behavior. • P-Trak Configure. Execute specified commands and verify specified results on the P-Trak to achieve reconfiguration and/or debugging. • Commercial Diagnostics Configure. Execute specified commands and verify specified results on the Commercial Diagnostics unit to achieve reconfiguration and/or debugging. • Attended Operations. Ability to power-up the SAME DACU, initialize the instrument, run a specified test, and shut down.

SAME-DOC-008 Rev A 4 2.2.3 Payload Status Area This is an area reserved in the DGCS for payloads to present critical information that is shown at all times. SAME will use this area to display information about the experiment and testing status. The Run Mode field displays the current running status of the SAME experiment. Possible values are: STARTUP The DACU software is starting UNINITIALIZED The DACU software is waiting for the System Initialize command STANDBY The DACU software has been successfully initialized and is waiting for commands and is emitting housekeeping data. TEST RUNNING A test is currently in progress TEST PAUSED A test is paused SHUTDOWN The DACU software is in the process of shutting down. Table 2 - Run Mode Values The OK Status indicator replicates the physical LED labeled OK on the DACU housing. It represents the physical status of the experiment. When the indicator is lit the system is operational (e,g, powered, booted, ready to run); unlit indicates the system is not operational (e.g. not powered, in error). The Test Number field displays the current test number the DACU is running or prepared to run. The Elapsed Time field displays how long the current test has been running (HH:MM:SS). If no test is running the field will be blank The GPS field is required by SSP50313. It provides a time reference for payload operations.

2.2.4 Status Bar The latest information message received from the DACU will be displayed here. In addition, it is added to the general message log (see 2.2.6). The message is specific to SAME and is composed of four comma-separated parts. The first part is the GPS time the message was generated on the DACU. Next is the level of the message which is either INFO or ERROR. This is followed by the message text and optional detail text. The last two fields make up the Description field in the general message log. Timestamp Message Text Details Level Description

SAME-DOC-008 Rev A 5 2.2.5 Workspace The workspace area is used for displaying information and controls for a given function. The contents will change based on the primary function selected. 2.2.5.1 Welcome Screen The welcome screen is the first thing displayed when the crew display is started. There is no real content display, but it serves the purpose of positively identifying the SAME experiment. Once the operator selects a function from the primary button panel, the workspace will change to the new display. There is no way of displaying the welcome screen again without exiting and restarting the program. Figure 2 - Welcome Screen

SAME-DOC-008 Rev A 6 2.2.5.2 Status Screen The summary status display is shown when the operator presses the Status button. It shows information about the state of SAME in addition to what is shown in the Payload Status Area (see 2.2.3). Figure 3 - Status Screen 2.2.5.2.1 Sample Positioning Group The sample group consists of 3 fields. The Sample Number field is the number of the sample within the carousel being tested at that time. The Carousel Number field is the number of the carousel that is installed. A carousel holds six samples. The combination of the carousel and sample number uniquely identifies a particular test item. The Resistance field displays the measured resistance of the heater wire coil for the sample. This is used as a unique physical indicator of which sample is being tested. 2.2.5.2.2 SAME Power Group MSG provides SAME with 120VDC. SAME converts this into 5 separate voltages using DC/DC converters. The SAME Power group consists of fields indicating the state of the 5 voltages. For all voltages, the possible state include ON and OFF. SAME-DOC-007 1 1.0 INTRODUCTION 1.1 Purpose This document will eventually hold most of the info rmation needed to operate the SAME experiment on ISS from the ground from the TSC. It will also descri be alternate methods of performing tasks when the experiment hardware is not on ISS, but is instead e asily accessible. For now, however, this document is a place to collect miscellaneous operational information and methods that need to be documented and under configuration control. 1.2 Scope TBD. 1.3 Applicable Documents [1] SAME-DOC-005 Software Interface Control Document

SAME-DOC-007 2 2.0 IN-FLIGHT FUNCTIONAL CHECKLIST This is a list of items that should be addressed after the hardware is installed in the MSG and before any samples are tested. Not currently in any order. - Perform piston calibration and alter registry values as necessary. See procedure later in this document. Run a test with heater setpoint below R0 and no use of the thermal precipitors in order to confirm correct calibration. - Figure out good values for STSPumpFailureLowLimit and STSPumpFailureHighLimit registry values. These depend somewhat on atmospheric pressure and should be adjusted for the ISS environment. Correctly set, these values help detect failure of the STS pump. - Log some data with the P-Trak and DustTrak and confirm that their settings are correct. For example: log interval, time constant, and date/time. - Record some video, downlink, and examine. - Experimentally determine the maximum setpoints that the mass flow controller will meet given ISS vacuum and GN2 sources. Determine if any desired inlet velocities or diagnostic combinations are affected. - The registry value, DisableChecksumCheck, can be set to 1 to avoid the startup delay associated with calculating the checksum each time.

- Revisit the decision about whether the heater controller offset correction will be done automatically as part of the test sequence or manually using the HeaterCorrectOffset utility prior to the test sequence. Adjust the CorrectOffset registry value appropriately.

SAME-DOC-007 3 3.0 STARTING THE SOFTWARE 3.1 Ground Computer On the ground computer you’ll need to first log on. Then start TReK with SAME configuration files. Also start SAMEDisplay. More TBD. 3.2 SAME Flight Software The software that controls the system starts automa tically upon power on. Within 30 seconds of turning on 120V power to the system there should be telemetr y data received at the SAMEDisplay application. The GMT will be updating and startup messages will appear in the log window. The Run Mode will change from Startup to Unitialized.

SAME-DOC-007 4 4.0 TEST CHECKLIST This is a list of important things to do or confirm pr ior to, during, and after the running of a sample test. Placement of a highly visible printout of this lis t on console is recommended. Steps depend on whether sample heater offset correction is being done automatically or manually. Check the CorrectOffset registry value to find out (0=manual, >0=automatic). - Once per carousel open the gate valves and turn on the diagnostics for TBD minutes. Downlink the data and verify correctness. The purpose is to collect baseline measurements of the MSG work volume required by the science team. 4.1 With Automatic Heater Offset Correction - Power on the system, wait for telemetry reception. - Send the Initialize command. - If the desired sample is not engaged, engage it using the Self Test command. - Turn on the 12VDC Heater Power. - Note the sample resistance and compare to ground measured resistance. If they differ significantly, TBD. Determine the setpoint. - Look at test parameters and change as necessary. Use manual positioning option, but carousel and sample number must be correct. - Start the test. - When the test pauses check the following: o A “sample type is confirmed” message appears in the log. o The offset correction returned a value less than 50uV in the log. o The sample resistance is still good. Within TBD % of before.

o The desired diagnostics are powered and readings are nominal. o GN2 regulated pressure and vacuum pressure are good. Range is TBD. - If the offset correction returned a value greater than 50uV, abort the test and restart. If the offset is still greater than 50uV, change the CorrectOffset registry value to 0 (manual) and use the manual heater offset correction checklist instead. - Resume the test. - Watch the log for details about when the sample heater will start. When it does, be ready to send an Abort command. - Watch the sample resistance and compare to the desired setpoint and MaxRt. The software will too, and will abort heating if the resistance/temperature gets too high. But watch anyway and send the Abort command in the highly unlikely event of too high resistance/temperature. - After sample aging, during exhaust, watch the output of the diagnostics for unexpected results. - After test is complete, power on any P-Trak or DustTrak that was used and retrieve the latest logged test ids. Turn back off. - As desired, force a transfer of the current housekeeping and log files to the MLC. Their transfer during power down has a slight chance of failing. Doing it here ensures success. - Perform any other desired OS or system maintenance, such as directory listings or self tests. - Disengage the sample.

SAME-DOC-007 5 4.2 With Manual Heater Offset Correction - Power on the system, wait for telemetry reception. - If the desired sample is engaged, DO NOT send the Initialize command. - If the desired sample is not engaged, send Initialize, engage sample using the Self Test command, and send Shutdown command with Restart option to bring system back to uninitialized state. - Send the OSCommand command with parameter ‘/root/HeaterCorrectOffset_g’. If this command returns 0 in the log, then proceed, otherwise repeat until it does. (Look at the value returned, not the details message which always says the same thing.) See section 7.5 for details about the HeaterCorrectOffset utility. - Send the Initialize command. - Turn on the 12VDC Heater Power. - Note the sample resistance and compare to ground measured resistance. If they differ significantly, TBD. Determine the setpoint. - Look at test parameters and change as necessary. Use manual positioning option, but carousel and sample number must be correct. - Start the test. - When the test pauses check the following: o A “sample type is confirmed” message appears in the log. o The sample resistance is still good. Within TBD % of before. o The desired diagnostics are powered and readings are nominal. o GN2 regulated pressure and vacuum pressure are good. Range is TBD. - Resume the test.

- Watch the log for details about when the sample heater will start. When it does, be ready to send an Abort command. - Watch the sample resistance and compare to the desired setpoint and MaxRt. The software will too, and will abort heating if the resistance/temperature gets too high. But watch anyway and send the Abort command in the highly unlikely event of too high resistance/temperature. - After sample aging, during exhaust, watch the output of the diagnostics for unexpected results. - After test is complete, power on any P-Trak or DustTrak that was used and retrieve the latest logged test ids. Turn back off. - As desired, force a transfer of the current housekeeping and log files to the MLC. Their transfer during power down has a slight chance of failing. Doing it here ensures success. - Engage the next desired sample using the SelfTest command. Engaging the next sample here shortens the time for starting the next test. - Perform any other desired OS or system maintenance, such as directory listings or self tests. - Send the Shutdown command with Shutdown option and power off system, or proceed to next test.

SAME-DOC-007 6 5.0 RUNNING A TEST 5.1 Initialization Select the Initialize button on the System tab, sending the Initialize command, and wait until the Run Mode changes from Unitialized to Ready. 5.2 Setting parameters From the Testing tab, select Change… to change to the set of test parameters you want to look at. Create a new test by selecting the CreateNew button. Select Set anywhere in the window to change the parameter for the selected test. The Test Setup group box is the way to choose which di agnostics to use. Select the Pri. or Sec. radio button to see the difference in setup between primary and secondary aging. Heater Control Setpoint should be set after knowing the unheated resistance of a sample, a.k.a. R0. Nominal setpoints are a multiple, Rt/R0, of R0 depending on sample type: Sample Type Setpoint Multiplier, Rt/R0 DBP TBD Kapton 1.380 Lampwick 1.245 Silicone 1.327 Teflon 1.440 To find the R0 of a sample, engage the sample to th e inlet tube either by manual blocking or using the SelfTest command with EngageSample option (on Syst em tab). Then on the Smoke Generation tab turn on the 12 VDC Heater Enable (right click on the ‘ LED’ and select ‘Set On’). Sample Resistance will settle to a valid measurement within 4 seconds.

5.3 Registry File Concerns Assuming you’ve set the test parameters to a specif ic carousel number, sample number, heating setpoint and duration, you may think you are ready to go. Y ou may not be. There are a bunch of sample-related limit checks that may cause an error or warning prior to heating. There are also many timing constants that affect the system behavior. These can be cha nged by selecting Set Registry… on the System tab. See SAME-DOC-005, Software Interface Control Document for key names and descriptions. A system timing simulator, currently located in SAMEFluidMode l.xls, will be available on console to help see the effect of registry value changes. Testing with the engineering unit is also recommended. Alternately, registry values can be changed by editing the registry.txt file on the DACU. This file is located in the /config directory. Also in that dir ectory is registry.orig.txt which contains the original registry settings. Important: Changes to registry values will not take e ffect until you restart the software. Follow the steps for shutting down, below, but use the restart parameter option.

SAME-DOC-007 7 5.4 Running the Test From the Testing tab select Start… and enter the test number to run, if it hasn’t already been entered in the field, and select Send. After sample positioning and aging chamber setup has occurred the test will pause so you can examine the log for any warnings or errors. Then send the Resu me button. The test should proceed to finish. You can abort anytime by sending the Abort command. An abort causes all valves to be turned off as well as all diagnostics. 5.5 Shutdown It is recommended that the system be gracefully shut down using the Shutdown button on the System tab, then cut power about 2 minutes later. Current housek eeping and log files are transferred to the laptop during the first minute. Use the second minute to ensu re that the system did not restart, looking for the restart of low rate telemetry packets and updating GMT. If the system restarts, select Shutdown again or send the OS command with parameter, ‘/bin/shutdown –b’. 5.6 Self-Tests The flight software has a few operations available through the SelfTest command. These may be useful for other than self-test purposes, for instance to engage a sample to the inlet tube to check R0.

Parameters depend on the self test: Self Test Parameter Definition Disengage Carousel no parameters Increment Carousel no parameters, rotates carousel one position Engage Carousel no parameters Dynamic Dilutor Parameter1: setpoint in sccm Parameter2: duration in seconds ISS Detector no parameters Fill Chamber Parameter1>0: Fill rate is this parameter divided by 10 in LPM Parameter1=0: Fill rate is ChamberSelfTestFillRate registry value Parameter2 not used. Exhaust Chamber Parameter1>0: Exhaust rate is this parameter divided by 10 in LPM Parameter1=0: Fill rate is ChamberSelfTestExhaustRate registry value Parameter2>0: Percentage to exhaust. Parameter2=0: Exhaust entire chamber. Sample Heater Parameter1>0: Duration in seconds Parameter1=0: Get previous run’s data and save to file. Do not heat sample. (Useful for aborted heating sequences.) Parameter2: not used. Setpoint ratio, Rt/R0, is SampleHeatingSelfTestRatio registry value. STS Detector no parameters Watchdog Timer no parameters. System will reset in 2 minutes.

SAME-DOC-007 8 6.0 PROCESSING FILES 6.1 Transferring files from DACU to the MLC All files will be automatically transferred from th e DACU to C:\ftp on the MSG laptop. Housekeeping files (.hkp) are transferred on the hour and upon shut down (with either the shutdown or restart option). The Log file is also transferred upon shutdown. P- Trak, DustTrak, and heater files are transferred soon after they are created. P-Trak and DustTrak file s are not automatically created since their data is embedded in the housekeeping data. To explicitly retrie ve logged data select the Transfer Data button on the DustTrak and P-Trak tabs. This should be do ne no more frequently than once per minute because the filename is derived from the GMT, including the latest minute, but not the latest second. If you need the data immediately or a file doesn’t get downlinked for some reason you’ll have to do it manually using one of two methods described here: 6.1.1 Using SAMEDisplay and FTP Cmd command. You’ll need to identify what file you need and the dir ectory it is in. Files are stored in a directory named according to GMT year and day. For instance /data/2006_132/. The .log file will be named 2006_132_00.log in this example. Housekeeping files will be 2006_132_15.hkp, 2006_132_16.hkp, etc. according to the GMT.

With the flight software and SAMEDisplay running (does not need to be Initialized), select the FTP Cmd from the System tab. Type: LCD /data/2006_132, for example, to change local directory (on the DACU) and send the command. Then select FTP Cmd again a nd type: PUT 2006_132_16.hkp, for example, and send the command. Watch your letter case – it matters. 6.1.2 Using SAME processor command line to transfer files For this to work you’ll need a keyboard and mon itor connected to the GSE port on the SAME DACU. Also, verify that the switch on the SAME DACU is sw itched to Override position. This is obviously a ground use only method. From the command line on the GSE monitor (if the so ftware is running you can get another console window by typing <CTRL><ALT>n, where n is 1 or 2), na vigate using cd and ls to the directory with the file you want to transfer. Type: ftp 192.168.1.1 <Enter>. Type: anonymous<Enter> for name and just <Enter> for password. Then at ftp> prompt t ype: bin<Enter>, then t ype: put 2006_ 132_16.hkp, for example. File should end up in C:\SAME Data on laptop. After done transferring file(s), type: bye<Enter> on the DACU. You can also use the two above methods to transfer files to the DACU using GET and get instead of puts. 6.2 Converting Housekeeping file to engineering units Use SAMEFileConverter. More instructions TBD.

SAME-DOC-007 9 7.0 MISCELLANEOUS PROCEDURES AND INFORMATION 7.1 Obtaining a directory listing An example: - OSCommand(‘ls –l /data/2006_237 > /data/dir.txt’). - FTPCommand(‘LCD /data’). - FTPCommand(‘PUT dir.txt’). - Have MSG cadre downlink the file dir.txt. 7.2 Replacing the registry file Normally you would change individual entries usi ng the SetRegistry command. This method could be used to set the registry to a known state, perhaps a f ile under source control, using an uplinked file. And this is the only way I could get the copied-over registry.txt file to ‘take’. If the system is shut down nicely through the shutdown command then it appears to revert to the old registry file. - FTPCommand(‘LCD /config’). - FTPCommand(‘GET registry.new.txt’) - OSCommand(‘cp /config/registry.txt /config/registry.old.txt’) - OSCommand(‘cp /config/registry.new.txt /config/registry.txt’) - Do a hard shutdown: power off - Power on and the new settings should take effect. 7.3 Piston Calibration Piston calibration, a.k.a. piston characterization, is a process of adjusting some registry values so that piston rates and time marks are correct for current conditions.

This process should be performed whenever there is a change of hardware, especially the aging chamber and piston itself; a change of environment, such as the move to the ISS; a change of fluid source strength; or a change of hardware condition, perhaps after many tests have been run. 7.3.1 Inlet Velocity Actual inlet velocity is required to match desired inle t velocity to within +/- 0.5 cm/sec. Actual velocity is not a directly measured value. It is a function of piston bottom to top travel time, chamber volume, and inlet tube diameter. The equation is: t Vv *60*105.2= where, v = actual velocity (cm/sec) V = chamber volume (L) = 5.65 t = piston travel time (seconds) 2.105 = conversion beween LPM and cm/sec Increasing the registry value, FillLeakRateLPM, will in crease the actual velocity. To determine piston travel time, perform the following steps: - Run a test with the desired inlet velocity and no heating (setpoint set below R0 and/or heater duration set to zero and/or no sample engaged.) - Abort the test during or after the aging period. - Obtain the drive side pressure data during chamber fill and graph it.

SAME-DOC-007 10 - Pick the points where the piston begins moving, characterized by the start of increasing pressure, and where the piston stops moving, characterized by drastically decreasing pressure. - Subtract the start time from the stop time and calculate velocity. Adjust FillLeakRateLPM and repeat as necessary. 7.3.2 Sample Heating Start Time Ideally, the start of sample heating is calculated so that the end of sample heating occurs before the piston reaches the top of the chamber. Actually, even before that, so that most of the smoke in the inlet tube at the end of heating enters the chamber as well. And really, even before that, so that some clean air follows the ‘last’ of the smoke and more of the smoke enters the chamber. The amount of the latter clean air is determined by the BackEndCleanAirOffset registry value. Because there is no direct physical measurement of where the piston is in the middle of its stroke, the software must estimate when the stroke begins and how long the stroke will take. Then it can back off from there to determine sample heating stop and start times. The registry values, FillWaita.b, where a.b is 0.0 to 5.0 by 0.5, help compensate for timing inconsis tencies which are a function of fill rate in LPM. (These values were more drastically a function of f ill rate before the FillLeakRateLPM registry value was increased from 0.0.

See section 7.3.1.). Piston chamber fill movement begins by evacuating the the drive side of the piston at a rate of 3.0 LPM until the drive side pressure reaches 13.2 psia. These values have been determined to be reliable, but can be changed if necessary by altering the registry values, FillStartRateLPM and FillStartPressurePSIA. Then the software waits for a period determined by th e desired fill rate, a function of inlet velocity, and the FillWait registry values. For a fill rate of 3.0 the software waits for the value of FillWait3.0. For rates in between, the wait time is interpolated. After wai ting this time the software marks the start of piston movement, logging a message for the user. Sample heating and other start and stop times are based on this mark. To determine the best FillWait registry values, - Perform the following steps for each rate, R= 0.5 to 5.0 by 0.5, and then estimate FillWait0.0 interpolating by hand on a graph of the other values versus rate. - Fill the chamber using the SelfTest command and the rate. - Note when the drive side pressure reaches 13.2 psia. The software issues a “x seconds before piston moving mark” message to indicate this point. The aim of this procedure is to get the ‘x’ right. - Note when the piston reaches the top of the chamber. Visual confirmation is best, but examination of the drive side pressure also works.

The start of the drastic drop in pressure is the point at which the top is reached. Do not rely on the “Aging chamber is filled” log message. After offset correction is performed, all subsequent resistance me asurements will include the o ffset correction. Until the system is powered off, that is. At power up the offset correction is zero. Offset correction should be run for each sample while the sample is engaged with the inlet tube and sample heater contacts. Occasionally the offset correction circuitry produces a co rrection that is obviously too high. The result is that subsequent reports of resistance are lower than ac tual.

This can be detected at the time of the test pause by looking at the sample resistance and by lo oking for the log message indicating the value of the offset correction. It should be approximately 200uV or less. If the offset correction at the time of the test pause is too high, then the test must be aborted and restarted to give the offset correction circuitry a second chan ce. To avoid this time-consuming detour a utility separate from the flight software has been developed. It is HeaterCorrectOffset_g in the /root directory of the DACU. It can be run from the flight software by sending the OSCommand command with a parameter of ‘/root/HeaterCorrectOffset_g’. The HeaterCorrectOffset utility app lies 12VDC to the sample heater , waits a few seconds, and then requests an offset correction from the heater microcontro ller. If the returned off set is in range then the utility exits, otherwise it requests the offset correction ag ain for several times until it is in range. Either way, 12VDC is removed from the sample heater befo re the utility exists. As long as system power (not 12VDC) remains applied, the offset correction initiated by the utility will be used by the flight software. If the utility fails to correct the offset to within the desired range then it returns a -1 (which is reported in the flight software log as 65280), otherwise it returns a zero to indicate success.

There is one caveat to running the HeaterCorrectOffset utility. The flight software must be either not running, which will not occur during flight, or must be in the uninitialized state. Once the software is initialized the utility cannot gain serial access to the heater micr ocontroller. Thus the sequence gymnastics in section 4.0. Additionally, if the HeaterCorrectOffset utility is used, then offset correction prior to the test pause should be disabled. Otherwise an incorrect correction he re will negate the use of the utility. Setting the CorrectOffset registry value to zero will disable au tomatic offset correction during the test, allowing the value created by the HeaterCorrectOffset utility to be used.

SAME-DOC-007 14 8.0 KNOWN ISSUES - Aborting a test occasionally causes the software to restart. If this should happen you’ll need to reissue the Initialize command. - Try to avoid running a test sequence through the change of hour (i.e. 12:45-13:05). Transfer of the housekeeping file at the top of the hour takes a good bit of processor time and the processor is close to 100% capacity, possibly affecting diagnostic measurement retrieval. - It is recommended that the system be gracefully shut down using the Shutdown button on the System tab, then cut power about 2 minutes later. However, about 20% of the time the software will hang or restart before completely shutting down. If it restarts, issue the Shutdown command again or issue the OS command with parameter, ‘/bin/shutdown –b’. If it hangs (you may only know this if you have a monitor connected to the GSE port) a hard power off will have to suffice. The operating system will clean up any file ‘litter’ on the next power up. - Maximum inlet velocity with the FillLeakRateLPM registry value equal to 0.30 is 9.8 cm/sec. Above this the software does not correctly use the FillWait registry values to time chamber fill operations, including sample heating start time. 10.0 cm/sec can be achieved if FillLeakRateLPM is 0.25 LPM or less.

But timing is affected in other ways and ground testing or flight testing without sample heating is recommended. - Whenever the P-Trak is on, the DACU requests a measurement from it once per second. Occasionally the P-Trak does not respond with a measurement and the DACU substitutes a -999 value instead to mark this occurance. If the P-Trak is logging during this time, that missing data can be recovered by issuing the Transfer Data command to retrieve the logged data. It is recommended that this be done for each test, soon (within days) after the test is complete. - The P-Trak memory can hold approximately 60 20-minute tests. When all memory is used the unit does not respond with any serial measurements while logging. In other words, continuous - 999 readings is one indicator of full memory. It is suggested that memory be cleared after 50 tests to be safe. - Sample heater offset correction occasionally produces an incorrect correction factor. The result is that reported sample resistance is lower than actual. For more information see section 7.5. - Using ground support equipment there was insufficient fluid flow during chamber exhaust to maintain overpressure of the diagnostic duct, as required, when the STS detector and both DustTraks are in use. When the STS detector is used it is recommended that at most one DustTrak is used.

- If the heater gives an “Abort on MaxRt” error, the system must be power cycled before proceeding. Otherwise, as will be apparent, the resistance measurement will be in error. - When specifying inlet velocities below 2 cm/sec, the FillWait registry values may not be accurate. The registry value, BackEndCleanAirOffset, must be adjusted to ensure correct heater timing. For 1 cm/sec, a value of 170 seconds is good. But run a test with no heating to be sure. - During ground testing the connection between the DACU and the MSGSimulator occasionally drops out. Packet count numbers of the MSGSimulator no longer increment and change from green to blue. To reestablish the connection deactivate it and activate it again.

SAME-DOC-003 Rev A 1 1.0 INTRODUCTION The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) instrument is an experiment payload planned for the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) located on the International Space Station (ISS). Thr oughout this document the term “project” is used to refer to the SAME project in its role as payload developer. 1.1 Purpose The purpose of this Software Description Document is three-fold: (1) to describe the Software Management Plan (SMP) for the project (2) to identify what product specification and procedure documentation will be produced as part of the software effort for the project, and (3) to identify and describe the records that will be produced as part of the software effort. This document is inte nded to be used as a roadmap of the software development effort, describing some aspects of the road within the document itself and, as applicable, pointing to other software documents and records which will be completed as the project progresses. The basis for this document, including structure, are two Glenn Research Center (GRC) Manuals, GRC - P2.6.4 and GRC -M2.6.4. Refer to these documents for more detailed background information and terminology definitions. 1.2 Scope This Software Description Document establishes the project's management processes for the software to be developed by the project to satisfy its requirements.

It also contains requirements to be satisfied by the providers of all software purchased, contractually acquired, developed, or maintained for the support or execution of the project. And e xcept for software and hardware interfaces used to estimate capabilities and schedules for the availability of support resources, it does not apply to software applications that provide company-wide capabilities not specific to this project. The term "software" as used in this document includes code, documentation, associated data, and "firmware", which is software installed in a medium that cannot be dynamically changed. The project software is comprised of several software “packages”, each executing on a separate platform. Located within the MSG will be a microcontroller-based data acquisition and control unit (DACU) that is responsible for direct control of the experiment. Connected to this controlle r is the MSG Laptop Computer (MLC) which will contain software to provide a crew interface into the DACU. Ground support software will be developed to collect and analyze on -orbit data at the GRC Telescience Support Center (TS C). Test software may be dev eloped to assist in the development and testing of hardware subsystems. This document is applicable to all of these packages. Any s pecific exceptions will be identified in the appropriate section.

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 2 2.0 INSTRUMENT OVERVIEW The SAME instrument is designed to quantify the size and distribution of smoke particulate in low gravity so that this information is available for the future design of effective low gravity smoke det ectors. The instrument will also be used to evaluate the performance of two existing U.S. spacecraft smoke detectors and one commercial smoke detector. Measurements will be made for the smoke from several materials found in spacecraft considering the effects of sample temperature, air flow, smoke residence time and aging. The primary targets are materials that produce liquid smoke particulate but solid smoke producers will also be considered. Figure 1 SAME Instrument Assembly Inside MSG WV The instrument is installed and operated in the MSG Work Volume (WV) which provides a minimal level of containment (see Figure 1). A general description of the major subsystems follows below. See SAME-DOC-001, Concept Description Document, for more detail. • Sample Carousel Turning Module, Sample Carousel and Heater Wire Coil These components are used to select and heat a sample in order to generate smoke. • Camera A camera and light(s) are mounted to see the sample and production of smoke. • Aging Chamber The aging chamber has a piston and two gate valves for holding the smoke for a time before releasing it downstream.

The piston is moved by pressure and vacuum provided by MSG and controlled by SAME. • Thermal Precipitator Module This assembly collects samples of smoke on TEM grids for post-flight inspection. It has access to smoke before and after the aging chamber. Aging Chamber Data Acquisition and Control Unit (DACU) Power Distribution and Control Unit Thermal Precipitator Module Sample Carousel Smoke Inlet Duct ISS Smoke Detector STS Smoke Detector Carousel Mounting Brackets Camera Controller P-Trak Enclosure Dynamic Dilutor Commercial Diagnostics Enclosure Fluid Control Unit

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 3 • Smoke Diagnostics After the aging chamber, the smoke is passed to several diagnostics: the TSI P-Trak™ particle concentration counter, the TSI DustTrak™ , a residential-grade ionization detector, the ISS photoelectric smoke detector and the STS ionization smoke detector. • Fluids Control Unit Pressure and vacuum supplied by MSG is controlled for smoke aging chamber piston movement and for all other fluid flow to and from the diagnostic equipment. • System Diagnostics Besides the diagnostic instruments measuring smoke characteristics, there are pressure transducers, temperature gauges, and voltage and current sensors to monitor system performance. • External Interfaces External interfaces provided by MSG include power, video recording, temperature control, post - pyrolization venting, nitrogen and air supply/vacuum, an RS-422 interface for commanding and telemetry, ethernet for file transfer, and a laptop for crew access to the SAME experiment. A SAMS unit measures local µg and vibrations and forwards that data to the ground requiring no SAME or MSG processing. • Avionics Contained in the Data Acquisition Control Unit (DACU) box, the SAME avionics conduct automated experiments, controlling the other sub-systems to produce and analyze the smoke. Commands from the ground are processed.

Experiment data is saved to files on a local storage medium and forwarded to MSG for subsequent downlink. Housekeeping data is downlinked every second and supplied to MSG. Off - nominal conditions are reported to MSG and the ground. In addition, a means for the crew to access SAME data and control is provided.

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 4 3.0 AVIONICS OVERVIEW SAME avionics are located in the DACU within the MSG Work Volume (WV). Cables will stretch to the SAME diagnostic hardware for control and feedback, to J311 of the WV for command and data transfer, and to J404 of the WV for ethernet connection to the MSG laptop computer (MLC) for file transfer and crew display operation. There is also a cable for the camera. 3.1 Data Interfaces To interface to the MSG, and subsequently to ground systems, the DACU CPU will communicate primarily to the MSG Rack Controller, also known as the SPLC (Standard Payload Computer) using an RS-422 interface (see Figure 2). SAME will use this interface to receive uplink commands and send health and status (H&S) data and low rate telemetry (LRT) data. Figure 2 SAME to MSG Data Interfaces Payload commands are transmitted from the ground through the ISS Payload MDM and eventually to the SPLC via MIL-STD-1553. The SPLC abstracts this interface from the payload developer, relieving the burden of knowing the details about the 1553 bus and command validation. A packet containing SAME health and status is automatically transmitted in the reverse direction on the 1553 bus and is received on the ground. Also included in the payload health and status packet is the Experiment Control Word or ECW, a single dedicated memory word that represents the status of the payload.

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 5 File-based SAME science data such as experiment measurement data and instrument ancillary data will be transferred to the MLC using FTP utilizing a 10BaseT ethernet connection. Once these files are stored on the MLC, the MSG Operations Team at the Payload Operations Integration Center (POIC) will periodically initiate their downlink and forward them to the SAME Operations Team. Since SAME is not permitted to transmit data on the ISS LAN, the DACU will automatically switch the active network connection fro m the MLC to SAME and ISS using a custom designed ethernet switch when the FTP transfer is required. In its normal state, the MLC will be connected to ISS LAN. The camera looking at the SAME sample is hooked up via an NTSC cable to a feedthrough inside the WV which is then patched on the outside to a video recorder channel in the video drawer. 3.2 DACU Overview The DACU is the central point for SAME control. It is ultimately responsible for all experiment operations and interfacing with the environment external to SAME. It contains all of the logic necessary to autonomously operate experiments. A brief list of its major responsibilities is as follows: 1. Receive, validate and process commands from the MSG. 2. Periodically transmit SAME system status and select parameters to the MSG. 3. Transmit completed and requested data files to the MLC via FTP. 4.

Manage and store all science and system files on the local data storage medium. 5. Autonomously control the progress of preprogrammed tests. 6. Provide diagnostic information and manual control of all sensors and controls using the GSE port. 7. Control the MSG video recorder(s) capturing SAME images. 8. React to sensor(s) out of tolerance by notifying MSG and ground systems, and performing software inhibits or other actions as appropriate. 3.3 Crew Display Overview During long periods of LOS or failure of telemetry, it is beneficial to provide limited visibility into SAME operation. Payloads may utilize the MLC to present payload status to the crew and provide a mechanism to control the payload directly from it. Two options for providing the SAME Crew Display are possible. Option 1 is the preferred solution at this time because of a likely delay in an upgrade to provide a dedicated ethernet link between the MLC and an experiment. 3.3.1 Option 1 - Custom Win32 or Java Based Application All data transmitted to the SPLC via H&S and LRT is also transmitted to the MLC via the MSG 1553 bus, and is therefore available on the MLC. SAME may develop a custom Win32-based or Java-based application that displays a limited set of the SAME downlink data for the crew to see and provides commanding to the SAME instrument.

3.3.2 Option 2 - Embedded Web Pages A dedicated ethernet interface between the MLC and SAME may be leveraged to provide a web-based interface into the DACU using the MLC native web browser. The operating system running on the DACU is capable of running an embedded web-server such as Apache or NASA’s Tempest servers.
