An RS422 interface is used for communications with the SPLC. An ethernet interface is used for communications with MLC. An RS232 interface is available while not on orbit for development, maintenance, and debugging activities. 4.2.1 SPLC Communications 4.2.1.1 Serial Port Configuration [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-1-1] A single bi-directional RS422 channel between the DACU and the SPLC shall be used to communicate with the MSG systems.

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 7 4.2.1.2 Data Format [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-2-1] All data that the DACU transmits to and accepts from the SPLC shall conform to the ESTEC Data Link Format as specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC0001, MSG RC ASW Interface Control Document, section 3.5.1.1. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-2-2] All data that the DACU transmits to and accepts from the SPLC shall conform to the byte and bit order as specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, MSG RC ASW Interface Control Document, section 1.4.3. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-2-3] All data that the DACU transmits to and accepts from the SPLC shall conform to the word alignment as specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, MSG RC ASW Interface Control Document, section 2.3. 4.2.1.3 Health and Status Packet [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-3-1] Once per second, the DACU shall transmit to the SPLC a health and status packet containing information such as voltages, currents, and pressures necessary to verify safe and proper operation. Included in this information are the C&W flags which indicate nominal or off-nominal operation to the rack systems. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-3-2] The content of the health and status packet shall conform to the format specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, MSG RC ASW Interface Control Document. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-3-3] The Cycle Counter field in the health and status packet shall be incremented once per second up to the value 0xffff, then roll over to 0.

[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-3-4] The C&W flags fields in the health and status packet shall be asserted only upon the conditions listed in Section 6.2. 4.2.1.4 Low Rate Telemetry Packet [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-4-1] Once per second, the DACU shall transmit to the SPLC a low rate telemetry packet representing the current state of the instrument. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-4-2] The content of the low rate telemetry packet shall conform to the format specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, MSG RC ASW Interface Control Document. 4.2.1.5 Video Command Packet [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-5-1] The DACU shall have the ability to control MSG video drawer functions by sending video command packets to the SPLC. The controllable video drawer functions are determined by the requirements of the video drawer command group, Section 4.4.5. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-5-2] The content of video drawer packets issued by the DACU shall conform to the format specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, MSG RC ASW Interface Control Document. 4.2.1.6 Time of Day Packet [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-6-1] The DACU shall accept time of day packets from the SPLC when they adhere to the format specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, MSG RC ASW Interface Control Document.

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 8 4.2.1.7 Experiment Command Packet [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-7-1] The DACU shall accept experiment command packets from the SPLC when they adhere to the format specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, MSG RC ASW Interface Control Document. 4.2.2 MLC Communications Upon completion of a science run, all data files will be stored on DACU internal storage. A copy of these data files will automatically be forwarded to the MLC via FTP on a point-to-point cross-wired ethernet cable. The SAME Operations Team will submit a request to the MSG Team at MSFC to downlink the files on the M LC at the earliest possible time. The downlinked files will then be electronically forwarded to GRC. Because the connection is made directly to the MLC, no bandwidth restrictions are necessary to ensure ISS LAN resource availability. 4.2.2.1 FTP Usage [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-2-1-1] All data files stored on the DACU local storage shall be automatically forwarded to the MLC via FTP for backup and downlink. 4.2.2.2 Network Details [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-2-2-1] A dedicated standard 802.3 (10BaseT) ethernet connection from the MLC to the DACU shall be used to perform the FTP transfer. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-2-2-2] Communications with the FTP server shall be done utilizing a server IP address of 192.168.1.1, port 21.

[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-2-2-3] The DACU will automatically switch the ethernet source from MLC→ISS to MLC→SAME when communication to the MLC is required. When the transaction is completed, the original MLC→ISS connection will be restored. 4.2.2.3 SAME File Maintenance [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-2-3-1] The DACU shall provide the ability to remove SAME files from the FTP server as needed to ensure proper storage space utilization. 4.2.3 Remote Console Communications [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-3-1-1] The DACU shall provide a telnet console login session on an RS232 port. All administrative features and capabilities available via telnet shall be supported. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-3-1-2] The telnet console RS232 serial port settings shall be, 19200 baud, no parity, 8 data bits, and 1 stop bit.

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 9 4.3 Data Storage Requirements The data storage requirements reflect two main needs. First, that a record of all status, measurements and events is preserved beyond the flight of the instrument. And second, that individual values of status, measurements or events can be easily located in stored data. 4.3.1 Storage Media [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-1-1-1] The DACU shall store all files on a media that can preserve all generated files for extraction after payload down-mass. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-1-1-2] The storage media shall have a capacity of at least 520 megabytes. 4.3.2 File Conventions 4.3.2.1 Directory Structure Because the execution of ISS instrument experiments are highly scheduled, the date and time that procedures and ground commanding is performed is usually reliably recorded by NASA cadre and experiment ground operation teams. As such, finding the data files for a previously run experiment or for a particular logged event is facilitated by a data storage structure based on the date. Therefore, [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-2-1-1] All files created shall be organized into a hierarchical directory structure based on the date that files were created. 4.3.2.2 File Names [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-2-2-1] All files created shall have unique file names.

4.3.3 Stored Data 4.3.3.1 Housekeeping Data [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-1-1] Once per second data relating to the status of the instrument shall be stored to a file. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-1-2] Each second of housekeeping data stored to a file shall be time-tagged. 4.3.3.2 Messages [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-2-1] Messages generated by the instrument shall be stored to a file. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-2-2] Each message stored to a file shall be time-tagged. 4.3.3.3 Experiment Results [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-3-1] Experiment results shall be stored to a file [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-3-2] Experiment results stored to a file shall be time-tagged. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-3-3] DELETED.

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 10 4.4 Command Requirements Commands are the primary means of initiating SAME instrument operations. Commands to an instrument are typically formatted into an array of data and inserted into command packets and then transmitted from the ground operation station or from the crew display on the MSG MLC on-board the ISS. When command packets reach the DACU the command data within is extracted and interpreted and the appropriate software functions are executed. The command requirements below deal mainly with the functions required by the instrument and not with how those functions are implemented or with how the command data is formatte d. See SAME-DOC-005, Software Interface Control Document, for the latter information. 4.4.1 General Command Requirements [SAME-SW-REQ-4-4-1-1-1] DELETED [SAME-SW-REQ-4-4-1-1-2] DELETED Table 2 DELETED DELETED [SAME-SW-REQ-4-4-1-1-3] At the start of execution of a command the DACU shall generate and downlink a message that includes the name of the command and its parameters. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-4-1-1-4] At the successful completion of a command the DACU shall generate and downlink a message announcing the successful completion. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-4-1-1-5] The DACU shall perform out-of-bound checking on all command parameters and reject commands with out-of-bound parameters.

[SAME-SW-REQ-4-4-1-1-6] The bounds for command parameters shall be those specified in SAMEDOC-005, Software Interface Control Document. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-4-1-1-7] The DACU shall allow for suspension of bound checking on command parameters. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-4-1-1-8] The DACU shall indicate when a command is being executed with bound checking suspended. 4.4.2 System Command Group [SAME-SW-REQ-4-4-2-1-1] The DACU shall accept a set of commands to perform system level operations. SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 14 4.5 Experiment Sequencing Requirements 4.5.1 Miscellaneous Sequencing Requirements [SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-1-1-1] Residence time of smoke in the aging chamber shall be controllable from 0 to 100 (or greater) minutes per aging period. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-1-1-2] The DACU shall command the diagnostic instruments to sample the smoke once the diagnostic duct is filled from the aging chamber. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-1-1-3] The DACU shall control the timing of diagnostic measurements such that a steady state signal is achieved on all instruments. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-1-1-4] The DACU shall allow the option of multiple smoke samples from the aging chamber with separate aging times. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-1-1-5] The DACU shall purge the diagnostic duct between multiple smoke samples from the aging chamber. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-1-1-6] The DACU shall control the system to allow the P-Trak to sample air from the MSG work volume. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-1-1-7] The DACU shall control the system to allow the DustTrak to sample air from the MSG work volume. 4.5.2 Test Matrix Modifiable Parameters [SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-2-1-1] DELETED. 4.5.3 Test Definition [SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-3-1-1] DELETED. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-3-1-2] There shall be predefined tests with parameters as determined by the Principal Investigator.

[SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-3-1-3] Additional tests shall be possible to define with parameters determined by uplink commands. [SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-3-1-4] It shall be possible to confirm all parameters for a specific test.

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 15 5.0 SUBSYSTEM REQUIREMENTS 5.1 Sample Carousel 5.1.1 Sample Selection [SAME-SW-REQ-5-1-1-1-1] The DACU shall control a motor to rotate the sample carousel to a specified sample number. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-1-1-1-2] The DACU shall use four proximity sensors to confirm correct positioning of the correct sample carousel. 5.1.2 Sample Positioning [SAME-SW-REQ-5-1-2-1-1] The DACU shall mate the selected sample tube with the smoke generation duct and the sample contacts with heater wire coil contacts by controlling a linear actuator. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-1-2-1-2] The DACU shall confirm correct mating of a sample tube and sample contacts by monitoring the resistance between the two heater wire coil contacts. 5.2 Sample Heater (Heater Wire Coil) [SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-1] The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall control the sample surface temperature and duration of the heating. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-2] The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall achieve steady state temperature of the heater within 5 seconds. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-3] The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall set the temperature of the heater wire coil to any temperature between 50 and 500 degrees Celcius. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-4] The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall provide active temperature control of the heater.

[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-5] The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall control the heater temperature and duration so as not to ignite the sample. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-6] The DACU shall measure and store the sample temperature at least once per second. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-7] The DACU shall measure and store the gas plume temperature at least once per second. 5.3 Camera and Lighting 5.3.1 Lighting [SAME-SW-REQ-5-3-1-1-1] The DACU shall control power to any combination of the camera lights. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-3-1-1-2] DELETED.

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 16 5.3.2 Camera [SAME-SW-REQ-5-3-2-1-1] The DACU shall control the gain and gamma settings of the camera. 5.4 Aging Chamber [SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-1] The DACU shall control the aging chamber piston upward velocity to achieve 1 to 10 cm/s average flow velocity in the smoke generation duct. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-2] The DACU shall control the aging chamber piston upward movement by controlling a solenoid on the vacuum line, by sensing and controlling a mass flow controller on the vacuum line, and by sensing a pressure transducer monitoring the drive side pressure of the piston. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-3] The DACU shall control the aging chamber piston downward velocity in order to provide smoke at the rate required for the particular diagnostics in use. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-4] The DACU shall control the aging chamber piston downward movement by controlling a solenoid on the GN2 line, by sensing and controlling a mass flow controller on the GN2 line, and by sensing a pressure transducer monitoring the sample side pressure of the piston. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-5] The DACU shall control a mixing fan in the aging chamber to be on during a specified portion of the residence time.

5.5 Thermal Precipitator Module 5.5.1 Valve Control [SAME-SW-REQ-5-5-1-1-1] Using digital outputs the DACU shall control the valves of the thermal precipitator module so that at most only one valve is open at a time. 5.5.2 Heater Control [SAME-SW-REQ-5-5-2-1-1] Using a digital output the DACU shall control power to one thermal precipitator module heater at a time. 5.6 DustTrak 5.6.1 Control [SAME-SW-REQ-5-6-1-1-1] The DACU shall control the DustTrak via an RS-232 serial port. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-6-1-1-2] The DACU shall turn the DustTrak on and off by controlling the on/off keypad using custom electronics. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-6-1-1-3] The DACU shall control the DustTrak keypad using custom electronics. 5.6.2 Data Reception [SAME-SW-REQ-5-6-2-1-1] The DACU shall receive data from the DustTrak via an RS-232 serial port. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-6-2-1-2] The DACU shall sample DustTrak data at a minimum rate of 0.2 Hz.

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 17 5.7 P-Trak 5.7.1 Control [SAME-SW-REQ-5-7-1-1-1] The DACU shall control the P-Trak via an RS-232 serial port. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-7-1-1-2] The DACU shall turn the P-Trak on and off by controlling its momentary on/off switch via custom electronics. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-7-1-1-3] The DACU shall control the P-Trak keypad using custom electronics. 5.7.2 Data Reception [SAME-SW-REQ-5-7-2-1-1] The DACU shall receive data from the P-Trak via an RS-232 serial port. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-7-2-1-2] The DACU shall sample P-Trak data at a minimum rate of 0.2 Hz. 5.8 Ionization Detector (Residential Smoke Detector) [SAME-SW-REQ-5-8-1-1-1] The DACU shall record measurements from the ionization detector at a minimum rate of 0.2 Hz. 5.9 ISS Detector The ISS detector is an Allied Signal/HoneywellTM engineering model. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-9-1-1-1] The DACU shall control the ISS detector. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-9-1-1-2] The DACU shall sample the output of the ISS detector at a sampling rate of 1 Hz or greater. 5.10 STS Detector The STS detector is a Brunswick DefenseTM engineering model. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-10-1-1-1] The DACU shall control the STS detector. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-10-1-1-2] The DACU shall sample the output of the STS detector at a sampling rate of 1 Hz or greater.

5.11 Dilution Air [SAME-SW-REQ-5-11-1-1-1] The DACU shall control the dilution of smoke using analog input(s) and output(s) and discrete output(s) to a voltage sensitive orifice and measurement instrumentation.

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 18 5.12 Miscellaneous Diagnostic Measurements [SAME-SW-REQ-5-12-1-1-1] The DACU shall record the air flow speed in the smoke generation duct with a range of at least 0 to 15 cm/s using calibration coefficients as necessary. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-12-1-1-2] The DACU shall record the MFC settings and the pressure transducer data at the rate of at least 0.1 Hz to be used in the calculation of the air flow speed. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-12-1-1-3] The DACU shall record the air flow speed in the smoke generation duct. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-12-1-1-4] The DACU shall measure and store the ambient air pressure of the work volume at a rate of at least 0.1 Hz. [SAME-SW-REQ-5-12-1-1-5] The DACU shall measure and store the ambient air temperature of the work volume at a rate of at least 0.1 Hz.

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 19 6.0 OFF-NOMINAL AND CONTINGENCY REQUIREMENTS 6.1 Maintenance Mode Operation The software will contain provisions to allow experiment operations to continue in the event of the following: [SAME-SW-REQ-6-1-1-1-1] In the event of a loss of the ability to write to the data hard drive, the system shall continue to accept uplink commands and transmit status data to ensure safe operation. [SAME-SW-REQ-6-1-1-1-2] In the event of a loss of ethernet communication between the DACU and the MLC, operations shall continue. Data recorded on the flight avionics may be manually commanded for retransmission once communication is regained. 6.2 Caution and Warning Three discrete bits in the health and status packet are used to indicate to MSG the presence of a payload condition warranting a warning, caution, or advisory classification and reaction. See MSFC -RQMT-2888, MSG Investigation Interface Requirements Document, Section 3.11 for details of each level. The specific payload conditions that result in warning and caution levels are determined by the Payload Safety Review Panel (PSRP) during Phased Safety Reviews. Automatic safing will be performed if the warning or caution bit is set. The advisory bit can be used to reflect errors and off-nominal conditions seen only in the low rate telemetry data to the health and status data.

If, due to limited communication coverage or communication error, the health and status data is received while the low rate telemetry is not, then these off-nominal conditions will still be noted and time-tagged. 6.2.1 Warning There are no conditions that constitute a “Class 2 -Warning” condition and a subsequent set of the Warning bit in the Health and Status packet payload ECW. 6.2.2 Caution There are no conditions that constitute a “Class 3 - Caution” condition and a subsequent set of the Caution bit in the Health and Status packet payload ECW. 6.2.3 Advisory There are no conditions that constitute a “Class 4 - Advisory” condition and a subsequent set of the Advisory bit in the Health and Status packet payload ECW. 6.3 Automatic Safing [SAME-SW-REQ-6-3-1-1-1] In the event of a GN2 regulated pressure reading of over 21 psig, the DACU shall automatically shut off the main GN2 valve. [SAME-SW-REQ-6-3-1-1-2] In the event of a vacuum pressure reading of over 19 psia, the DACU shall automatically shut off the main vacuum valve.

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 20 7.0 CREW DISPLAY REQUIREMENTS 7.1 Graphic Standards The development and approval process for the project crew display follows the guidelines in SSP 58700-ANX5, U.S. Payload Operations Data File Management Plan, Annex 5: Payload Display Review , and in SSP 58700ANX6, U.S. Payload Operations Data File Management Plan, Annex 6: Payload Developers Review Guide . [SAME-SW-REQ-7-1-1-1-1] The crew display shall meet all applicable standards defined in SSP 50313, Display and Graphics Commonality Standard. 7.2 Interfaces 7.2.1 Host Computer [SAME-SW-REQ-7-2-1-1-1] The crew display shall be able to run on the MSG Laptop Computer with features and operating system as described in MSFC-RQMT-2888, Microgravity Science Glovebox Investigation Interface Requirements Document, Section 3.3.5. 7.2.2 MLC Server [SAME-SW-REQ-7-2-2-1-1] The crew display shall send commands from the MLC to the instrument using the MLC Server Socket Interface. [SAME-SW-REQ-7-2-2-1-2] The crew display on the MLC shall receive health and status data and lowrate telemetry from the instrument using the MLC Server Socket Interface. [SAME-SW-REQ-7-2-2-1-3] The crew display shall meet the MLC Server Socket Interface requirements documented in MSFC-RQMT-3098, Software Requirements Specification (SRS) for Microgravity Science Glovebox Laptop Computer Server Software, Section 4.6.

7.3 Features 7.3.1 Commanding [SAME-SW-REQ-7-3-1-1-1] The crew display shall include a subset of the full instrument command list. 7.3.2 Data Display [SAME-SW-REQ-7-3-2-1-1] The crew display shall display a subset of the full instrument health and status and/or low-rate telemetry data. 7.4 Enhanced Mode [SAME-SW-REQ-7-4-1-1-1] DELETED

Smoke Experiment aka Characterization of Smoke Particulate for Spacecraft Fire Detection Engineering Report Characterization of Ignitor Wire Candidates Submitted by: ZIN Technologies, Inc Len Miller April 2002

SMOKE Experiment Ignitor WIre Characterization Study April 2002 Purpose: The purpose of this report is to document the results of a study conducted in search of the ideal type of wire to be used for the hot wire ignitors for the Smoke Experiment. Objective: The objective of this study was to find a wire with a consistent, linear resistance versus temperature characteristic and with a “significant” slope. Scope: This study was conducted in the Phase A Laboratory (Bldg 77, Room 154A) on commercially available wire. The ignitor manufacturing technique and the pyrolization of samples is beyond the scope of this study. Procedure: Each type of wire was mounted on a test fixture. The test fixture was then placed into a ThermCraft laboratory oven. The oven was programmed to ramp up to a set point, hold the set point for fifteen minutes, and then ramp to the next set point until the final temperature of approximately 800 oC was attained. (See oven cycle graph in Appendix C.) Resistance readings were taken near the end of each “dwell” period. Several of the wire types were subjected to additional tests to examine the effects of the previous thermal cycle(s). The test fixture held approximately thirty-four inches (0.86 meters) of wire. A stainless steel sheathed type-k thermocouple (Omega Part No. KQSS-116U-24) was placed inside the oven in close proximity to the wire under test.

Leads of high temperature furnace wire (#18 AWG) were brought out of the oven to enable the test conductor to measure the resistance of the wire under test. The resistance of the leads and the terminations was characterized by subjection the fixture and leads to a thermal cycle with a copper bus bar shorting the terminals of the fixture. The fixture resistance was subtracted from the total resistance reading for each test point to determine the net resistance of the wire under test. The results were recorded in an Excel Workbook. Several different data plots were prepared and studied.

SMOKE Experiment Ignitor WIre Characterization Study April 2002 Summary and Conclusions: This study examined the characteristics of eight types of wire: anodized mild steel, pure iron, Alomega (similar to Alumel), -Stainless steel, pure platinum, platinum-rhodium, tungster-5%rhenium, and tungsten-26%rhenium. Traditional heating wires, Nichrome and Kanthal were also included for comparison. Pure platinum has close-to-ideal characteristics. However the cost of the material may be prohibitive. Alomega and stainless steel ran a close second. Mild steel, iron and tungsten-composites oxidized in the oven and their characteristics changed significantly from one thermal cycle to the next. Nichrome and Kanthal have too flat a slope to meet the objectives. Further testing will be conducted to determine the optimum wire type and wire diameter. Representative test samples will by pyrolized using various ignitor configurations. The quality and quantity of the smoke will be visually evaluated. Test Results: The tests were conducted in the Phase A Lab from February 6, 2002 through March 20 2002, by Len Miller and Nathan Funk of Zin Technologies, Inc. The individual results for each test were tabulated and plotted. For those wires subjected to more than one thermal cycle, the comparative results were plotted. Finally, an overall plot of the combined results was prepared.

The entire Excel Workbook, with tabulated test results and plots thereof, is included in Appendix A of this report. Photographs of the laboratory apparatus are in Appendix B and a graph of the thermal cycle is in Appendix C.

ABSTRACT Title of Document: SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION FLAMES Keenan Thomas Dotson, M.S., 2009 Directed By: Assistant Professor, Peter B. Sunderla nd, Department of Fire Protection Engineering Smoke points were measured in microgravity aboard t he International Space Station (ISS) as part of the Smoke Points in Coflow Experim ent (SPICE), and in normal gravity conditions. In microgravity conditions incr easing the coflow velocity or decreasing the burner diameter increased the smoke point flame length. A simplified prediction of centerline jet velocity did not yield residence-time-based criticalities or data collapse. Simulation of non-reacting flows sho wed that the simplified centerline velocity prediction was able to predict velocity de cay for only relatively weak coflows. An improved model may yield different resu lts. In normal earth gravity coflow velocity exhibited mixed effects. For burner diameters of 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm, smoke points increased with increases of coflow velocity. For an unconfined coflow burner with a burner diameter of 13.7 mm smo ke point length decreased with increasing coflow velocity for ethylene and propyle ne, while increasing for propane flames.

1 Chapter 1. Introduction Soot formation is an important but unresolved probl em in combustion science. In many circumstances soot production in flames is des ired. Nevertheless, once soot escapes the flame and becomes smoke, it is rarely i f ever wanted in a combustion system. Soot is estimated to be responsible for up to 52,000 premature deaths in the U.S. 1 and is believed to contribute to climate change an d glacial melting. 2 Radiation from soot in flames allows reading by candlelight, provides heat to campers, and cooks our food. On the other hand this radiation ca n represent a loss of efficiency and increased heat loads in engines. Also the spread of unwanted fires is in many cases is through the radiation heat transfer originating fro m soot particles. Smoking flames emit carbon monoxide, which is the major cause of death in fires. 3 1.1. Smoke Point The laminar smoke point is the condition (or lumino us flame length) where a laminar diffusion flame begins to emit soot. Smoke points a re the prevalentmethod used to determine fuel sooting propensity in diffusion flam es. The longer the luminous (visible) flame length at its smoke point, the lowe r the sooting propensity of the fuel. In normal gravity, laminar smoke points have been m easured for many gaseous and condensed fuels.

4,5,6,7,8,9 Laminar smoke points have been found to correlate with soot volume fractions 10 and radiative loss fractions 11 of turbulent diffusion flames. Yang et al. 12 found that gas turbine soot emissions correlate wi th a threshold sooting index (TSI) based on fuel molecular weight divided by the laminar smoke point. Smoke points have been shown to correlate with the smoke release from turbulent buoyant 4 -6, 7 -9

2 flames, 13 and have been applied to developing general soot m odels for computation combustion simulations 14 and heat release measurements. 15 Smoke points for gaseous fuels are determined from a jet flame apparatus. A surrounding coflow of excess oxidant (over-ventilat ed conditions) is typically necessary for buoyant flames to reduce flame flicke ring. It is also most common to confine the coflow and jet within a quartz chimney to reduce disturbances from exterior flows. Shorter smoke point flame lengths a re indicative of a higher sooting propensity. A flame that has a lower inclination to form soot will exhibit a smoke free flame for longer flame lengths; that is longer flam e residence times are required to create the necessary amount of soot to reach the smoke point condition. 1.2. Soot Formation, Growth, and Oxidation General consensus has that the soot formation proce ss begins with the formation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). From these precursors fine soot particles nucleate. These particles grow by addition of PAHs or through surface reactions. The Hydrogen Abstraction by Carbon (Acetylene) Addition (HACA) mechanism is one of the most often cited for soot growth mechanisms.

I n addition, coagulation, in which small particles coalesce into larger particles and agglomeration, where multiple particles combine into larger pearl-necklace-like s tructures, also contribute to morphology. Soot oxidation occurs from participatio n from species such as O 2, O, and OH present near and downstream of the flame she et. OH-based oxidation is the most dominant soot oxidation mechanism, occurring f rom slightly rich to lean

3 conditions within the flame. O 2-based oxidation becomes more important as the flame becomes leaner and the super-equilibrium levels of OH decline.16 Both soot formation and soot oxidation are temperature dependent. Detailed measurements have provided greater insight into sooting phenomena. In premixed ethylene flames, Harris and Weiner 17,18 determined that soot reaches a final particle size due to a decrease in reactivity of th e particle that stops surface growth, and the dominate growth mechanism is by acetylene. In diffusion flames Kent et al. 19,20 have shown that soot particles are formed primaril y on the fuel side of the flame reaction zone. The number of particles decrea ses by coagulation away from the peak formation zone (a few millimeters inside the r eaction zone on the fuel side), while particle size and soot volume fraction increa se by the addition of hydrocarbon species. Soot typically convects towards the fuel s ide of the flame after it has formed from buoyancy. The soot path ultimately follows on the local streamlines. Thermophoretic forces modify these paths slightly t owards cooler regions within the flame. Santoro et al. 21,22 discovered a unique feature of coflow diffusion fl ames. The annular region near the base of the flame is a loca tion of intense nucleation and agglomeration of soot.

This formation region is the cause of the soot 'wings' seen in diffusion flames near their smoke points. Gomez et al. 23 found that soot formation begins at a temperature around 1350 K in diffusion flames and that dilution does not change this temperature but rather shifts the locat ion at which this temperature

4 occurs. Sunderland and Faeth 24 determined soot nucleation to become significant a t 1250 K. Kent and Wagner 25 found that smoke burnout in the oxidative region o f the flame ceases when the tip of a buoyant diffusion fl ame cools to approximately 1300 K. This is the direct cause of the smoke poin t flame. Urban et al. 26 found that the luminous tip of a nonbuoyant (microgravity) fla me reaches 1000 K at its smoke point. In buoyant flames this decrease in temperatu re is attributed primarily to heat conduction, and in nonbuoyant flames this can be si gnificantly enhanced by radiative quenching. 16 Radiative quenching is believed to also cause the visible tip opening in nonbuoyant smoke points of flames of relatively long residence times.26 In diffusion flames, oxygen and fuel meet at a narr ow reaction zone, the flame sheet. Kinetics does not determine the location or tempera ture of this zone, but rather stoichiometry does. Diffusion limits the flow of th e reactants to this narrow flame sheet and, for strong flames, is much slower than t he kinetic reaction rate. Furthermore the soot formation/oxidation times are believed to be greater than the time necessary for diffusion of reactants. 27 If chemical kinetics is practically instantaneous, then residence time becomes the dete rmining factor for soot formation and oxidation.

It has also been suggested that the ratio of soot formation and soot oxidation times also determines when the smoke poin t will occur. Lautenberger et al. 27 describe this process for buoyant laminar flames. “Increasing the flame height increases the residence time and allows more time f or the flame to produce soot. Once formed, this soot requires additional time to oxidize in the upper parts of the

5 flame if it is to be entirely consumed below the fl ame tip. As soot travels through the flame (in a Lagrangian sense), it radiates away energy and cools the flame gases.” Also corroborating what was mentioned previously ab out a limiting temperature at which soot oxidation ceases, typically at the smoke point flame height, the radiative heat loss from the flame by soot radiation is about 30% of the total heat release rate of the flame. 28 The cooled flame gases can no longer oxidize the s oot and one could consider the soot formation/oxidation time to appro ach the diffusion time. 27 Smoke is then released from the tip of this flame and it has just surpassed its characteristic smoke point because the required time for soot oxidation is now less than the time the soot is capable of being oxidized post flame sheet. Important review articles on soot formation mechani sms are available from Frenklach 29 , Mansurov 30 , and Glassman. 31 Richter and Howard 32 in a particularly detailed fashion reviewed the formation of PAHs and their growth to soot. Soot oxidation is well covered by Stanmore et al. 33 1.3. Fuel and Diluent Effects For diffusion flames, work by Schalla and McDonald 34 showed that fuel sooting propensity decreases with hydrocarbon family in the following order: aromatics > alkynes > alkenes> alkanes.

According to Glassman 31 , increasing the molecular weight of the fuel increases the soot formation rat e by increasing the radical concentration and the Arrhenius pre-exponential factor for the overall rate coefficient. In premixed flames, the number of carbon-carbon (C- C) bonds determines the critical

6 sooting equivalence ratio in a predictable fashion. However, the number of C-C bonds is only an indirect measure of the pyrolysis rate of the fuel. In diffusion flames H radicals are important to the fuel pyrolysis process, facilitating the initial pyrolysis of the virgin fuel as well as the subsequent attack on fuel intermediates. H radicals facilitate abstraction reactions much faster than hydrocarbon radicals do. Despite this importance of H radicals, Schug et al. 4 have shown that the initial overall carbon-hydrogen (C/H) atom ratio of the fuel does not determine the sooting propensity. Nevertheless the degree of mole cular unsaturation correlates with higher sooting propensity, perhaps likely due to th e greater ease these molecules can form acetylenes and PAHs. In over-ventilated coflow diffusion flames, additio n of inert to the fuel stream typically reduces sooting propensity. Longer smoke points result. However the addition of inert can also alter the flame temperat ure. This occurs by the inert acting as a heat sink, this effect depending on the heat c apacity of the inert. 4,35 The peak flame temperatures will be reduced, which for a dif fusion flame reduces soot formation, increasing the smoke point. Additionally , the temperature field of the flame can be altered through transport effects.

Ine rt species with high thermal diffusivities have their volumetric dilution effect s countered by a thermal effect of extending the high temperature range where soot for mation is possible. 36 The temperature of the pyrolysis zone determines the so ot propensity and correlates well

7 the fuel mass flow rate at the smoke height. Shock tube experiments have shown that the soot formation rate peaks around 1900 – 2300 K.31 1.4. Buoyancy Effects Soot is transported in flames primarily by convecti on, modified slightly by thermophoresis. The primary difference between a bu oyant and nonbuoyant jet flames is that, in general, a buoyant flame, the fl ow is accelerating, while for a nonbuoyant jet the flow is decelerating. This is of course neglecting volumetric expansion from combustion related heating. In gener al, for a buoyant flame the flow streamlines move towards the flame axis, while for the nonbuoyant flame the flow streamlines are drawn outwards from the flame axis. 16 Therefore in a buoyant flame, once soot is nucleated in the soot production regio n near the flame sheet, it is drawn into the fuel rich core, allowing continued growth. In a nonbuoyant flame as the flow is drawn outwards, the soot moves in a more direct path to the flame sheet and oxidative region downstream. 16 It had been predicted that smoke points would not o ccur in nonbuoyant gas-jet flames. 37 This was based on the assumption that residence ti me would be independent of flow rate in microgravity flames. As flame lengt h and mass flow rate are directly proportional, an increase in velocity would lead to proportional increase in length and residence time would remain unchanged.

In normal gr avity flames the residence time scales with the square root of the flow rate. Subsequent work 38 observed smoke points of nonbuoyant flames aboard a parabolic aircraft an d used numerical predictions to

8 show that residence time increases with flame lengt h for nonbuoyant flames without coflow. Urban et al. 39 reported smoke points of microgravity flames obser ved on a space shuttle. However, microgravity smoke point me asurements are difficult in parabolic aircraft owing to g-jitter and in drop facilities owing to limited test times. 1.5. Velocity Field Effects By varying the burner diameter, coflow velocity, an d fuel dilution, flame shape and residence times in the soot formation and soot oxid ation regions can be changed. Reductions in the burner (fuel jet exit) diameter i ncrease the mean fuel jet velocity, reducing overall flame residence time, assuming tha t flame length only depends on the mass flow rate of fuel. There has not been subs tantial research into the burner diameter effect on smoke points. The work of Kent a nd Wagner 25 showed that reducing burner diameter (increasing fuel jet veloc ity) shifts the centerline sootvolume-fraction profile downstream, without modifyi ng peak values. Therefore it should be expected that the smoke point luminous fl ame length should increase from the soot profile shifting downstream, directly leng thening the flame or reducing the region of the flame where soot formation is possibl e.

Increasing fuel dilution, in addition to modifying soot propensity by volumetric and thermal effects, increases the fuel jet velocity at a particular mass flow rate of hydrocarbon fuel. An increase in coflow velocity will generally decre ase entrainment towards the flame axis. The coflow velocity can modify the residence time by countering flow deceleration in nonbuoyant flames, and accelerating flow in both nonbuoyant and

9 buoyant flames. Nonbuoyant flames are substantiall y more likely to have their velocity fields modified by these previously mentio ned factors as their flow is not subject to buoyancy related acceleration, which can tend to dominate the flow field.16 Schalla and McDonald 34 were the first to investigate the effects of coflo w velocity on the smoke point of laminar diffusion flames. Their work showed that increasing coflow velocity increased the fuel mass flow rate a t the smoke point up to a point, after which the effect ceases. A modified plot of t heir results is shown in Figure 1.1. Berry-Yelverton and Roberts 40 showed that the smoke point of ethylene increased with decreasing initial fuel to air velocity ratio, and therefore with increasing coflow velocity, as shown in Figure 1.2. These tests were over a range of fuel/air velocity ratios, 0.6 - 1.4. The results of Schalla and McDon ald were also over an initial fuel to Figure 1.1. A recent 2.5 s drop tower study by Jeon et al. 41 found that for small coflow velocities the soot volume fraction increases with coflow velo city for nonbuoyant flames. The study was of ethylene flames with a 7 mm burner. Th is was attributed to an increase in flame temperatures as luminosity increased in th e annular regions of the flame. 22 Chapter 3. Experimental Procedure All of the tests performed required determining when the s moke point condition was reached. The smoke point is a transition between two different flame behaviors, nonsmoking and smoking. There are several indicators of t he smoke point. A nonsmoking flame does not have any obvious smoke product ion, and it is helpful to view the flame against a white or black background to determ ine this. Generally a white background it best for observing smoke production visual ly. A non-smoking flame has a relatively sharp luminous boundary at its lumin ous flame tip. This is somewhat dependent on overall soot concentrations within the fl ame. The tip is usually closed, though soot ‘wings’ are also typically present. These horn-like structures at the luminous flame tip are produced in an annular region c ontaining the majority of the flame sheet. The luminous flame tip is also bright, an d orange or yellow in color. A sooting flame usually opens up at its tip and is usu ally not sharply defined. The tip also darkens and becomes redder due to the cooling of t he soot. 3.1. 64 Chapter 5. Conclusions Smoke points of microgravity and normal gravity gas-jet diffusion flames were observed. Microgravity conditions emphasized small burn ers and effects of coflow velocity. These flames allow extensive control of resid ence time, which may be important in smoke point phenomena. An increase in co flow velocity increases the smoke point length. A decrease in burner diameter incre ases the smoke point length. These two effects can be explained qualitatively by considering residence times; increased fuel and/or coflow velocities yield increased smoke point lengths. The effect of coflow velocity could also be explained by in creased O 2 transport if soot oxidation downstream of the flame sheet is transport lim ited. The fuel sooting propensities in these flames are as fol lows: propane < ethylene < 50% propylene < 75% propylene < propylene, however ethy lene is less sooty than propane for the 0.76 mm burner. To the first order, luminous length at the smoke point is proportional to fuel mass flow rate, consisten t with past theory and experiments. A second-order effect is that this length increases for low ua,o / u f,o velocity ratios. Flames of this nature approximate the behavior of a jet flame in still air. Smoke points of normal gravity gas-jet diffusion flames w ere also observed.

For the smaller burner tests in a confined coflow environment, sm oke point length increased with an increase in coflow velocity or a decrease in no zzle diameter. For a very large burner in an unconfined coflow, the smoke point length decreased with increasing

65 coflow velocity for propylene and ethylene, but increase d for propane. This, and results of a previous study showing domains where the s moke point is invariant to changes in coflow velocity, indicate that the relatio nship of smoke point to coflow velocity and nozzle diameter is more complicated than initially expected. It has been hypothesized that the different responses may be due to different soot oxidation regimes, transport-limited, kinetics-limited, and residen ce-time-limited. Simplified analysis of the residence time and soot forma tion time to soot oxidation time ratio of the SPICE microgravity flames failed to yi eld substantial collapse of the smoke point data or a residence time related criticalit y. This may be due to the simplified nature of the analysis, such as neglecting combustion related volumetric expansion. COMSOL® simulations have shown that the simplified Schlichting-based analysis does not adequately predict the centerline v elocity decay of air jets with initial air to fuel velocity ratios larger than around 0.2 – 0.5. However there is evidence that the analysis would more adequately pred ict the centerline velocity decay of jets with an initial uniform flow. This current study has not proven a particular smoke poi nt mechanism.

It has shown that the smoke point depends on choice of coflow velo city and burner diameter; these factors cannot be assumed away as negligible. The cofl ow jet flame geometry is perhaps not tractable enough to lend itself to fundamen tal analysis of sooting phenomena. Given that a smoke point depends on a la rge number of inputs, more rigorous controls would be necessary to isolate particu lar factors. It is hoped;

66 however, given the results shown and the hypotheses p resented, a more defined experimental procedure could be developed to directly i nfluence and measure residence times, formation rates, and oxidation rates as they relate to the smoke point and sooting phenomena.

Smoke points were found for ethylene, propane, propylene, and mixtures of 50 and 75% propylene by volume in nitrogen. Burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76 and 1.6 mm and coflow velocities varied from 5.4 – 65 cm/s. These flames afford good control over residence time via variations in dilution, burner diameter , and coflow velocity. Increasing coflow velocity decreases luminous flame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. Introduction Soot formation is an important unresolved problem in combustion science. Soot is estimated to be responsible for up to 50,000 prem ature deaths in the U.S. [1] a nd is believed to contribute to climate change and glacial melting [2]. Radiation from soot in flames allows reading by candlelight but also contributes to he at loads in engines and the spread of unwanted fires. Smoking flames emit carbon monoxide, which is the major cause of death in fires [3]. The smoke point is the condition (or length) where a flame begi ns to emit soot. Smoke points indicate the sooting propensity of a fuel in diffusion flames. In normal gravity, laminar smoke points have been measured for many gaseous a nd condensed fuels [4–9]. Laminar smoke points have been found to correl ate with soot volume frac tions [10] and radiative loss factions [11] of turbulent diffusion flames. Yang et al. [12] found that gas turbine soot em issions correlate very well with a threshold sooting i ndex (TSI) based on fuel molecula r weight divided by the laminar smoke point.

Smoke points have been shown to co rrelate with the smoke release from turbulent buoyant flames [13] and have been applied to developing general soot models for computational combustion simulations [14] and heat release measurements [15]. In a 1988 paper [16], Glassman predicted that smoke points would not occur in nonbuoyant gasjet flames. He based this on the assumption that residence time scales with the square root of fuel flow rate in normal gravity but is independent of flow rate in microgravity flames. Subsequent work [17] observed smoke points of nonbuoyant fl ames aboard a parabolic aircraft and used numerical predictions to show that residence time increases with flame length for nonbuoyant flames without co-flow. Urban et al. [18] reported smoke points of microgravity flames observed on a space shuttle. Microgravity smoke point meas urements are difficult in parabolic aircraft

2 owing to g-jitter and in drop facilities owing to limited test times. Attributing smoke point behavior to total resi dence time helps with qualitative explanations of smoke point behavior but to date has not yielded successful quant itative correlations [8]. This may be because smoke points arise from a comp etition between the times available for soot formation and soot oxidation. De lichatsios and co-workers suggest ed that smoke point length is proportional to soot formation time [19–20]. Quantitative correlations may also be possible from an examination of radiative losses, which have been observed to be 20 – 30% for normal-gravity smoke point flames and to increase with adiabatic flame temperature [5]. Soot is transported in flames by convection and thermophoresis. By varying the burner diameter, coflow velocity, and fuel dilution, flame shape and residence times in the soot formation and soot oxidation regions can be changed. A decrease in coflow velocity will generally increase entrainment of flow towards the flame axis. Kent and Wagner [21] found that smoke burn out in the oxidat ive region of the flame ceases when the tip of a buoyant diffusion flame cools to approximately 1300 K. Urban et al. [22] found that the tip of a nonbuoyant (microgravity) fl ame reaches 1000 K at its smoke point.

In buoyant flames this decrease in temperature is attr ibuted primarily to he at conduction, while in nonbuoyant flames it is attributed largely to ra diative quenching [23]. The radiative quenching effect causes a visible tip openi ng in nonbuoyant smoke points of flames of relatively long residence time [22]. A recent 2.5 s drop tower study by Jeon et al. [24] found that for small coflow velocities the soot volume fraction increases with coflow velocit y. This was attributed to an increase in temperature. Lin and Faeth [7,25] studied the effects of coflow velocity on weakly-buoyant flames near the smoke point. They observed flam es in normal gravity, but at low pressures to reduce the effects of gravity. They found that increasing the coflow velocity reduced soot volume fractions and increased the smoke point le ngth. This was attributed to decreased flame residence time and modified soot pathlines. Refs. [7 and 24] both showed that luminous flame lengths decrease with increasi ng coflow velocity. Their bur ner diameters, 7 and 10 mm, respectively, were much larger than those considered here. Faeth and co-workers [25–27] applied the fl ame shape analyses of Spalding [28] and Mahalingam et al.

Experimental The Smoke Points in Coflow Experiment (SPI CE) module was brought to the International Space Station (ISS) in 2008. It was operated in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) by various crew members in 2009. Smoke points were at tempted for all fuels for fuel jet diameters of 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm. The conditions for which smoke points were found are summarized in Table 1. In some cases (e.g., te sts involving ethylene) the fuel supply was depleted before desired smoke points could be found, as the supply was limited to two 75 cc bottles of each fuel at gage pressures of 760 – 1440 kPa, depending on the fuel. The SPICE module contains a rectangular duct th at has an approximately 76 mm square cross section with rounded corners. A DC fan supplie s coflowing air from the glovebox contents. The air passes through a honeycomb and screen to reduce swirl and then enters the duct. The air and combustion products leave the duct through a pe rforated copper plate followed by a copper screen.

The screen is 50 mm upstream of th e burner discharge and the plate is 120 mm downstream. Fan voltage is varied to control the coflow velocity, which is measured with a hotwire anemometer between the inlet honeycomb a nd screen. This anemometer was calibrated in normal gravity using a hot-wire anemometer 36 mm downstream of the duct entrance. Fuel flow rate was adjusted manually and controlled with a mass flow meter. The flames were ignited with a hot-wire ignitor. Video was recorded with an analog color video camera and downlinked in real time. Still images were recorded with a 12 bit Nikon™ D100 single-lens reflex color digital still camera (with 3008 × 2000 pixels) with a 60 mm lens. Most of the tests were conducted by setting the coflow velocity, igniting the flame, and adjusting the fuel flow rate. Approximate smoke points were identified in the video by the flight crew and simultaneously by the ground support crew in Cleveland. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after each two such burns the MSG contents were flushed with ISS cabin air. After the tests the video record was analyzed to identify smoke point conditions. The associated coflow and fuel flow rates were obtained from digital data r ecorded in the video.

The smoke point lengths, LSP, were obtained from the vi deo record and are the measured distance from the burner tip to the tip of the luminous flame on the flame axis. The luminous flame tips were not sharply defined in most images, but rather involved a transition from bright yellow to black across an axial distance of 2 – 5 mm. Flame hei ght was thus measured to the point where the centerline grayscale intensity changed most rapidly between these yellow and black regions. This helped reduce the sensitivity of measured flame height to camera exposure settings. Smoke points were obtained for five fuels, as summarized in Table 1. Smoke points were

Results and Discussion Some smoke points, propane and ethylene in part icular, were identified by the onset of gradual (rather than sharp) dimming and reddening of the luminous flame tip in the downstream direction. Rounding of the tip al so was associated with th e smoke point. For conditions sufficiently above the smoke point, quenched soot could be seen leaving the flame. The brightest flames did not always display significant redden ing or darkening near their tips, except well above the smoke point. This occurred for the pu re propylene and propylene mixtures, and the smoke point was identified by the rapid transition to an open-tipped, soot emitting flame. The flames generally reached steady conditions within 5 s of ignition or a change in flow rate of fuel or air. Flames of propylene and propylene mixtures were generally more luminous than those of methane, ethylene, and propane, attribut ed to their higher propensity to form soot. The smoke point transition was more abrupt in th e propylene-based fuels than for propane or ethylene.

Periodic flame motion was observed in some flames, especially those with high coflow, long length, and low fuel velocity, and is attributed to non-uniform coflow. This effect was small and did not prevent clear measurement of flame length. Figure 1 shows images for representative flames near their smoke points. Two sequences are shown, and in both the smoke point occurs betw een the third and fourth flames. In the top sequence, coflow velocity decreases from left to right at constant fuel flow rate. This increases luminous flame length and reduces the smoke poi nt leading to soot emission. The luminous length decreases in the fourth image owing to incomplete combustion. In the bottom sequence fuel flow rate is increased at constant coflow velocity, increasing flame length as expected. As seen in Fig. 1, luminous length is more sensitive to changes in fuel flow rate than to changes in coflow velocity. Table 1.

Conclusions Smoke points of microgravity gas-jet diffusion flames were observed. Conditions emphasized small burners and effects of coflow velocity. These flames allow extensive control of residence time, which is important in smoke point phenomena. The major conclusions are as follows. 1. An increase in coflow velocity increases the smoke point length. 2. A decrease in burner diameter increases the smoke point length. 3. These two effects can be explained qualitatively by considering residence times; increased fuel and/or coflow velocities yield increased smoke point lengths.

INTRODUCTION • Three investigations will be performed: SPICE, SLICE, and BASS. • These investigations will be performed inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG). • SPICE is based on the Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) hardware which flew on STS-87 in 1997. • SPICE hardware is already on-orbit. It has successfully completed all of its objectives with the collection of 200 data points in the first half of 2009. Spare gas onboard will now be used to collect additional data. New fuel is being flown on ULF5 to support the SLICE and BASS experiments. • SPICE hardware will also be used to perform SLICE and BASS. • SPICE burns different fuels to investigate the point at which they begin to smoke. • SLICE burns different fuels to investigate the structure of flames when lifted from the fuel nozzle. • BASS burns different materials to investigate how they burn in microgravity.

The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find the laminar smoke-point properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the largest laminar jet diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for two fuel types under different nozzle diameter / co-flow velocity configurations. SPICE will stabilize an enclosed laminar flame, measure the overall flame shape to validate the theoretical and numerical predictions, measure the flame stabilization heights, and measure the temperature field to verify flame structure predictions. SPICE Science Overview 4

Target Setting: The target setting is just above the setting that produces a distinct edge (only a small portion of the tip will emit smoke). The smoke will probably emerge from the center of the tip but may emerge at the tip edges (horns) for the larger nozzle. The pictures show the onset of smoke points for various fuels on the KC-135. The size of the flame when it emits smoke is a fuel property. The expected size sequence will be Propylene, Ethylene, Propane and Methane (probably no smoke point). The diluted propylene smoke points will be longer than pure propylene. SPICE Smoke Point Determination Cue Card Background: The smoke point is the flame length, above which, soot particles are no longer consumed in the flame and instead emerge through the flame tip and glow as they cool. The glowing soot causes a change from a sharp edge to a gradual transition between the bright flame and black background. SLICE Science Background • The goal of the SLICE investigation is to investigate the structure of lifting and lifted flames; whereby the flame detaches from the nozzle and stabilizes at a downstream position. • The results of the SLICE experiment will be used to minimize risk and maximize the scientific return of the CLD (Coflow Laminar Diffusion) Flame experiment, which is one of the four ACME (Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments) investigations that are currently in development for conduct within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). 6 The lifted nature of the flames can be discerned from the outward flare of the flame base in the example images below (which are not at the same scale) and the distance from the nozzle tip (which is not visible). BASS Science Background • The BASS investigation tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (ie. pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature). • To test this hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials requires extended microgravity time – longer than available in drop towers or parabolic aircraft. If this hypothesis is true, it implies serious safety concerns over the utility and margin of safety provided NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 (upward flammability test used to evaluate materials intended for use in the habitable environments of US spacecraft). Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible). • There are important differences in the suppression of fires in space compared to on Earth. On Earth it is understood that best results are generally obtained when the extinguisher “attacks” the base of the flame, which is both the stabilization point and the point of fresh air entrainment. For a fire burning in microgravity, the best point of application of suppressant may not be immediately apparent, especially for a partially obstructed flame or a wake-stabilized flame.

Depending on the geometry of the flame and the characteristics of the extinguisher (distance from flame, dispersion angle) it is possible that the suppressant stream will be ineffective or might actually make the flame worse through the entrainment of oxygen. 7

Earth Applications • SPICE The smoke-point phenomena is a classical metric in the understanding of the heat release and spread rate of fires. It is commonly used in fire modeling on Earth and to understand the soot growth and emission by flames. The dominant characteristics of many flames of practical interest are nonbuoyant. SPICE seeks to extend our understanding by looking at the interaction of ambient flow with the smoke point, enabling us to better predict heat release from non-buoyant flames in practical combustors (e.g. jet engines and furnaces). • SLICE The twin purposes for the SLICE research are increased efficiency and reduced pollutant emission in practical combustion devices. More explicitly, the experiment is being conducted to advance combustion modeling capability, which “allows system designers to improve efficiency and reduce harmful pollutants in ways never before possible” (as stated by an external reviewer of the SLICE experiment). In other words, the SLICE research is being conducted to advance energy technology and improve our global environment. • BASS It is highly desirable to develop a new and/or improved Earth-based test method for material flammability. The data obtained in this experiment will begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity 9

ii Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) Abstract The laminar smoke point is the condition (and the l uminous flame length) where a flame begins to emit soot. Smoke points indicate the sooting propensity of a fuel in diffusion flames. In normal gravity, laminar smoke points have been measured fo r many gaseous and condensed fuels. Laminar smoke points have been found to correlate with soot volume fractions and radiative loss fractions of turbulent diffusion flames. SPICE pro ject measured laminar smoke points in non) buoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in co)flowing air aboard the International Space Station. Fifty)two smoke points were found for ethylene, pro pane, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen mixtures. Burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm and co)flow velocities varied from 5.4 – 65 cm/s. These flames afford extensive control over residence time via variations in dilution, burner diameter, and co)flow velocity. Increasing c o)flow velocity decreases luminous flame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. Smaller burners have longer smoke points for co)flo wing flames. These trends can be explained qualitatively by considering total residence time e ffects.

The luminous flame lengths generally correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoic hiometric mixture fraction, although they increase slightly as air velocity decreases. The me asured smoke point lengths were found to correlate with burner diameter to the –0.91 power t imes coflow velocity to the 0.41 power. The measurements allow estimates of pseudo threshold so ot indices (TSI) for microgravity diffusion flames, indicating an unusually high sooting propensity for propane in microgravity. A model of residence times in coflowing flames is developed, a nd although residence time helps explain many of the observations, it does not correlate the measured smoke points. The measurements yielded estimates of sooting propensities of the present fuels in microgravity diffusion flames. Acknowledgments The authors acknowledge G.M. 1 INTRODUCTION SPICE project, from it was rewarded in 1997 to it was conducted onboard ISS in 2009, covered more than a decade time span. During these years, the project experienced a few cycles of active and inactive status. A brief project history is given below. SPICE project was awarded on December 3, 1997 by the Microgravity Science and Application Division of NASA Headquarters to Professor Gerard M. Faeth of the University of Michigan for his proposal titled as Laminar Smoke Point Properties of Nonbuoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames in response to NASA’s 1996 Solicitation for Glovebox Investigations issued in late 1996. The original proposal of Professor Faeth was meant to be a supplement to the Laminar Soot Processes Experiment which was a combustion project under NASA Grant No. NAG3-1245, conducted onboard STS-73 and STS-94 in 1997. In the awarding letter, the experiment was planned to be carried out onboard STS-107, for which the launch date was then scheduled in May 2000. From December 1997 to the end of 1999 was the first phase of the project. In this period, the experiment was planned to be conducted in the Middle Deck Glove Box of a Space Shuttle and the SPICE hardware was fabricated and assembled in GRC. Various project reviews necessary for the flight project, were completed.

In addition, significant efforts on science side were made to explore proper camera settings for different flame conditions by conducting reduced gravity experiment in parabolic flight on board the KC-135 aircraft. From the end of 1999 to March 2002, the project was inactive. The second phase of the project was from March 2002 to January 2005. In this period, SPICE was a part of MRDOC contract to ZIN Inc., for a potential UF-1 Flight. Since the target facility of SPICE was switched from Space Shuttle’s Middle Deck Glove Box to the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), ZIN’s major effort was to retro-fit hardware for use with MSG in International Space Station (ISS), which included: designed and assembled Power/Video Unit to support MSG video interfaces, designed and fabricated a new mechanical camera supports, redesigned fuel bottle assemblies and developed new cabling. Project was cancelled again at the end of 2004. ZIN developed storage plan for hardware which was presented to NASA in December, 2004. The SPICE apparatus was put in storage in January 2005 and all the documents were archived waiting for future flight opportunities. At that time, the LSP project and the re-flight LSP-2 were completed, thus the objectives of SPICE were later changed to a standalone investigation of smoke point of jet diffusion flames with coexistence of air flows.

One important event soon after the SPICE became inactive again was the sudden death of Professor Faeth of the University of Michigan, the PI of the project. It was not until March 2006 that the SPICE was resurrected in May, 2006 as part of the Small Payloads Projects Task under MRDOC that Dr. David Urban, the Co-I of the project, succeeded Professor Faeth as the PI of the project. In addition, Professor Peter Sunderland of University of Maryland, former Ph.D. student of Prof. Faeth was recruited as a Co-I of the project. An updated Science Requirement Document was edited. The test matrix was finalized. Additional tests in camera were conducted. Minor hardware modifications were made and a number of project reviews were conducted. The SPICE hardware was shipped to KSC on June 18, 2008 and later lifted up to ISS by ULF-2 in October 2008. SPICE experiments were finally conducted in ISS MSG from February through June of 2009. What Follows is the science significance and justification of the SPICE project. Soot formation in hydrocarbon-fueled flames is an important unresolved problem in combustion science. Soot is estimated to be responsible for up to 52,000 premature deaths annually in the U.S. 1 and is believed to contribute to climate change and glacial melting.

2 Radiation from soot in flames is beneficial in many applications but also contributes to unwanted heat loads in engines and the spread of fires. Carbon monoxide emitted by smoking flames is the major cause of death in fires. 3 Knowledge of Soot formation is needed for developing computational combustion.

2 The differences between soot processes in buoyant and nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames can be seen by comparing their soot production regions as plotted in Fig. 1. Soot formation in diffusion flames generally is limited to fuel-equivalence ratios, φ, in the range 1-2, which are marked on the plots. Unlike gases, which both convect and diffuse, soot mainly convects with the flow velocity so that it moves along the streamline. For buoyant flames, the dividing streamline generally is inside the soot formation region so that most of the soot initially forms near the flame sheet, where φ, =1, and then moves radially inward toward cooler regions having higher fuel concentrations. The soot formation process for nonbuoyant flames is completely different: most of the soot initially forms near the cool core of the flame, where φ is close to 2, and is drawn directly toward the flame sheet. Results from an MSL-1 combustion project, the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP), revealed that the smoke height phenomenon in microgravity can be substantially different form that seen in normal gravity. The removal of buoyancy induced acceleration can cause the smoke point phenomenon to be dominated by radiative heat losses for conditions of low overall flame velocity. Under these conditions the flame extinguishes at the flame tip allowing soot to be emitted.

In spite of this effect, it is still possible to have flames that either emit soot along all stream lines or do not emit soot anywhere, for conditions where radiation losses do not dominate. Figure 1. Soot path lines through buoyant and non-buoyant flames The information of smoke-point properties and flame shapes is needed to improve our understanding of heat and mass transfer mechanisms for different flame conditions. Unfortunately, while the laminar smoke-point properties of buoyant jet diffusion flames at normal gravity are well known, corresponding information for nonbuoyant flames is limited and questionable. Thus the insights of soot generation and oxidation processes under microgravity conditions are critical to devise better fire safety strategy in spacecraft needed for long term space travels and other space exploration activities. In addition, the improved understanding of soot processes in laminar flames will help us, by analogy, to gain better understanding of soot processes in practical turbulent flames. The objectives of the SPICE experiments is to find the laminar smoke-point properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames for several fuels under different nozzle diameter/co-flow velocity configurations. Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify models of the

3 flame shapes under co-flow conditions. In particular, the experiments are planned to be conducted under the following conditions: six types of fuels: methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, 75% propylene mixed with 25% nitrogen in moles, and 50% propylene mixed with 50% nitrogen in moles; three nozzles: 0.4, 0.8 and 1.6 mm ID and two air velocities: 100% and 50% of the maximum air flow velocity (near 50cm/s). The operation procedures are as such that the air velocity is set first, then start the fuel flow and ignite the flame. Fuel flow rate is adjusted until the smoke point is reached. Thus, for each combination of a fuel and a nozzle size, two smoke point fuel flow rates are obtained. One is under 100% air velocity and the other is under 50% air velocity. Then in the case of 50% air velocity, the fuel flow rate is reduced to 50% of the smoke point fuel flow rate to get a flame length with that fuel flow rate. SPICE EXPERIMENT SETUP A. For this reason, the information of air velocity distribution before igniting of the flame is needed. The air velocity was measured with an anemometer at different locations in the flow duct at different fan speed.

The top window and the front window were replaced by two windows with holes on them to accommodate anemometer prob. Figure 13 shows various hole locations through which air velocities were measured. Some expressions used in describing a spatial location are explained as follows. A “Station” refers to a plane perpendicular to the flow direction. The value of a “Station” indicates the distance between the nozzle tip and the plane. There are only two Stations in use: 13 mm and 56 mm, defining two planes 13 mm and 56 mm downstream of the nozzle tip. “Height Off Floor” refers to the distance above the floor of the flow duct. The Floor of the flow duct is the lower wall of the flow duct, perpendicular to the front window. The three positions in Height Off Floor in use are 19 mm, 36 mm, and 57 mm define three planes in parallel with the flow duct floor. The 36 mm one is in the middle of the flow duct so that it includes the nozzle. The third direction is expressed in terms of “Centerline”, “20 mm to the Inside” and “20 mm to the Outside,” which define three planes in parallel with the front window of the flow duct. There are totally 18 intersections of these three sets of planes. Air velocities were measured at these 18 locations at 6 different fan dial settings.

Note that for the safety concern, even at 0 fan dial setting, there is a minimum DC voltage applied to the fan to maintain a low velocity air flow which prevents fuel gas from accumulating in the flow duct.

17 DISCUSSION Although it is convenient to classified all flames, laminar vs. turbulent and diffusion vs. premixed, into two categories based on their soot emission conditions, i.e., soot emitting flames and non-soot emitting flames, the conditions delineating the two or the conditions of onset of soot emission are difficult to define. Up to date, these conditions have been documented solely based on experimental observations. Many efforts have been made to develop a universal method of defining the onset of soot emission, i.e., smoke point, conditions, in terms of primary parameters of the flame. But none of these efforts has been quite successful yet. The primary parameters of the flame mentioned here refer to parameters used to set the flame, not those generated by the flame. The primary parameters of jet diffusion flames include fuel type, fuel and oxidizer supply rates, ambient temperature and pressure, and configuration of the device where the flame takes place, such as nozzle diameter and dimensions of the combustion chamber. The flame temperature, gas velocity and species distributions as well as flame shapes and derived parameters such as heat generation and heat loss, are the parameters generated by the flame which is not considered as primary parameters.

If a method that relates smoke point to those primary parameters were found, we would be able to predict whether a flame emits soot or not based on the planned flame conditions. In the course of pursuing such a universal method, a number of surmises of the mechanism of soot emission have been proposed to associate smoke point with certain flame generated parameters. Those surmises served as a middle step in hoping to help further development of the aforementioned method. The first surmise, and least controversial, is that smoke points occur when soot temperature drops below a critical temperature prior to soot burnout. This temperature is about 1300 K in normal gravity 8,9 and 1000 K in microgravity.10,11 The second is that smoke point occurs when radiative loss fraction reaches 0.2 – 0.4 for normal-gravity flames 12-16 or 0.4 – 0.6 for microgravity flames.17 Since the radiative fraction of heat loss increases with fuel flow rate, smoke point will occur as the fuel flow rate is higher than Figure 19. 18 certain value. This is consistent with experimental observations. The third surmise is that the smoke point correlates to the ratio of luminous length divided by stoichiometric length. This ratio increases with flow rate. Once it reaches about 2, smoke point occurs.15,18,19 The last surmise suggests that smoke point correlates with the centerline flame residence time. This is the most complex 8-11,17,18,2024 surmise because flame residence time affects the soot processes in twofold. An increase in residence time can lead to soot emissions by increasing the time available for soot formation. Because this generally also increases the time available for soot oxidation, it has been proposed that smoke points are associated with conditions where the time available for soot formation exceeds that for soot oxidation to certain extent.21 This is difficult to prove because to evaluate the flame residence time requires the velocity distribution alone the centerline and the flame length, both of which are resulted flame parameters, not readily available from primary parameters of the experiment. In addition, the soot formation time and oxidation time are conceptually defined. Practically, these times are not measurable and they might be overlapped, i.e., for the same soot aggregate, adding and oxidizing carbon particles may happen simultaneously.

Because of these difficulties and ambiguities, the fame residence time theory cannot be proved or disproved rigorously. However, these obstacles do not prevent us from checking the residence time theory against the observed smoke point data with the help of some approximated velocity distribution and flame length information. More detailed discussion of this effort can be found in the publications resulted from the SPICE project listed in Appendices B through F. The results showed that although residence time is helpful in understanding the present smoke points, it does not yield quantitative correlations. CLOSING REMARKS Smoke points of 55 microgravity gas-jet diffusion flames in coflowing air were measured in earth orbit. The conditions emphasized small burners and the effects of coflow velocity. These flames allow extensive control over residence time, which is important in smoke point phenomena. The major conclusions are as follows: 1. An increase in coflow velocity increases the smoke point length. 2. A decrease in burner diameter increases the smoke point length. 3. These two effects can be explained qualitatively by considering residence times; increased fuel and/or coflow velocities yield increased smoke point lengths. 4.

The sooting propensities of the present fuel mixtures in microgravity increase according to ethylene < propane < 50% propylene < 75% propylene < propylene. This is the same as in normal gravity except for the exchanged positions of ethylene and propane. 5. Consistent with past theory and experiments, luminous length at the smoke point is proportional to fuel mass flow rate. However there is a slight increase in luminous length as ua / u f decreases. 6. Although residence time is helpful in understanding the present smoke points, it does not yield quantitative correlations of smoke points. 7.
