Introduction The purpose of this report is to provide a description of the experimental hardware and operations of used in the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments ( ACME) project that is sufficient for informed interpretation of the experimental results. In contrast, it is not the intent of this document to review the project management, engineering development, design process, etc. although such aspects may be briefly addressed. The ACME suite of experiments are being carried out on the International Space Station ( ISS) in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). ACME features investigations with gaseous fuels, such as methane and ethylene. In addition to the fuel state , the current ACME experiments use laminar, non -premixed (i.e., diffusion) flames for their studies. To simplify analysis, these flames are furthermore either axisymmetric or spherically symmetric, depending upon the experiment. Currently, ACME includes six independent experiments of which the first five were selected for testing in spaceflight by NASA while the sixth was selected by the Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS) and the National Science Foundation (NSF). The CIR facility was launched in 2008 and with the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) was used for a series of liquid-fueled experiments from 2009 to 2017.

The facility was reconfigured and set up for ACME testing by the ISS crew in September and October 2017, where over 2 5 astronauts from Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan, Russia and the United States have thus far supported the project’s research. As of this writing, over one thousand ACME flames have been ignited on the ISS, where that began in Nov. 2017. It is expected that the planned ACME testing will be completed in 2021, when the CIR operations should subsequently shift to the Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) project. The discussion of the CIR hardware herein is limited, but the research facility is described in various documents, such as those listed below. ACME Engineering Implementation 19 May 2022 6 ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter. As depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1 and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm). Most burners will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux transducers. The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring of the pressure differential across the outlet surface. The igniter will have a crew -exchangeable tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper -motor drive will allow for precise positioning. Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner, porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment. Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm, and the fabricated gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm.

However, only the larger gas -jet burner was used during the spaceflight tests. The burners are addressed in detail in section 3.C. Unfortunately, the spherical burners have not always yielded spherically symmetric flames, presumably as a result of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local flame quenching. Two types of igniter tips have been used during ACME testing. Most tests have been conducted using a loop igniter tip like those which had been successfully used in the droplet combustion experiments which preceded ACME research in the CIR. However, some tests were conducted with a coil igniter tip, where that included the second round testing for both the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) and Structure and Respons e of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s -Flame) experiments, with the exception of the latter’s first day testing. The CFI-G investigation will also use the coil igniter tip. For more information about the igniter tips, see section 3.D. The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner.

The maximum fuel flow is 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), wherea s much higher flows, e.g., 10 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), are possible for the oxidizer and nitrogen lines. The crew can exchange the mass flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow accuracy. The gas delivery system enables on -orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer (but not both simultaneously), coflow,

Gases can also be delivered premixed to the space station where that is necessary in some circumstances, such as the blending of different fuel gases. CIR’s standard bottle sizes are 1, 2.25, and 3.8 liters but ACME will sometimes use smaller bottles as a haz ard control to limit the deficient reactant (e.g., fuel) that can be released into the combustion chamber. Thus far, ACME tests were not conducted with carbon dioxide as a diluent. Furthermore, the fuel diluted with helium was premixed prior to launch rather than on orbit. Ultimately, oxidizer flows of up to 20 slpm (on a nitrogen basis) were possible, while the nitrogen flow was limited to a maximum of 5 slpm. ACME has not used gas bottles smaller than 1 liter as indicated above; the bottle fill pressure was instead limited as an additional hazard control. ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are alread y in use on orbit. All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber.

Collectively, the imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot volume fraction; and operational support. However, it is unlik ely that all functions would be exercised at any one time as will become apparent in the subsequent discussion. Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a high -definition digital camera mounted outside of the chamber and a standard analog camera mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning mirror). Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development. The analog camera signal will be downlinked in near real time to support the experiment operations. Light - emitting diodes within the ch amber can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both support the operations and provide reference images. The 12-bit digital camera records at up to 30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus. The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging. Color imaging can also be carried out with a blue -green BG7 Schott glass filte r, which balances the color planes to avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green.

The natural flame color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23 -24]. Alternately, CH* imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430 -nm bandpass filter with a 10 -nm full width at half -maximum transmission (FWHM). A 450 -nm bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract interfering broadband soot emission. However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so such subtraction effectively requires a separate test with each filter and of c ourse reproducible flame conditions. The video from the analog operations (i.e., ops) camera , also referred to as the internal camera, is not archived in space. The video is instead recorded on the ground in the operations center. Its gain was sometimes adjusted for improved imaging of dim flames, e.g., approaching extinction. The sensitivity of the color digital camera , often referenced as the ACME DataCam (i.e., Data Camera), to the dim microgravity flames was such that it was often used with long exposure times and thus low framing rates, for example on the order of 1 frame per second. Both soot pyrometry and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) are possible, where ACME is equipped with a crew-replaceable array of 5 silicon carbide (SiC) fibers. During set up, the crew can manually orient the array so that it is orthogonal to either ACME’s color digital camera or the HiBMs camera with the LCTF. An alternate fiber array including a platinum wire will be used for inflight characterization, which in combination with preflight calibration will enable determination of the soot volume fraction [24]. In contrast to the preceding paragraph , ACME did not use a HiBMs camera for pyrometry, but instead relied on use of ACME’s color DataCam for such temperature measurements . The measured test conditions include the chamber pressure and temperature, the three gas flow rates, and the electrical potential of the electrode mesh.

Acceleration me asurements are provided by the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) [18], which is the primary instrument for such measurements on ISS and previously served that role for the space shuttle. The flame behavior is observed optically with a variety o f instruments. For most ACME experiments, including E -FIELD Flames, the radiant emission is measured with 6 thermopile detectors with a spectral range of nominally 0.2 -11 microns. Five radiometers are in a crew - exchangeable linear array that is mounted p arallel to the chamber axis. The other detector is downstream and off axis from the burner. Chemiluminescent emission is measured with a set of three Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) modules. Their spectral range is 230-700 nm, i.e. in the visible and near ultraviolet, but two are equipped with narrow bandpass filters for measurement of OH* and CH* emissions, respectively. The third PMT is equipped with a neutral density filter to prevent saturation, although the gain values for all three PMTs are independently and readily adjustable. Like many of the components, the array of PMT modules can be removed from the chamber insert by the crew. In addition to their scientific value, PMT measurements are used operationally to detect ignition and automatically deact ivate and retract the igniter.

The radiometer or PMT measurements can similarly be used to detect extinction and automatically end the gas flow and test. Imaging measurements of the flames complement the optical sensors described above. Color imaging is provided by an analog color camera within the chamber and a high -definition (1360 x 1024), 12-bit color camera mounted outside the chamber on CIR’s optical bench. The latter is equipped with a motorized lens with independent control of the zoom, iris, an d focus. It has a filter barrel with a fused silica window (for color imaging), a blue -green BG7 Schott glass filter, and bandpass filters for imaging CH* and HCHO (formaldehyde) chemiluminescence. The digital color camera was characterized prior to launch for color-ratio pyrometry and measurement of the soot volume fraction, via the techniques of [19, 20]. A 14-micron fiber array can be seen at the top of Figure 4(b). However, the fibers interfere with the electric field preventing the use of Thin Filament Pyrometry in the E-FIELD Flames experiment.

Spherical Burners The spherical burners have thus far been used for the CFI -G, Flame Design, and s -Flame experiments. In contrast to initial plans, spaceflight burners were only fabricated with a 6.35-mm porous sphere. It was initially expected that flames which were more spherical might be generated with larger diameter porous spheres, but 2.2-s drop testing indicated that 6.35-mm diameter spheres were as good or better than the larger sizes in creating spherical flames. Multiple copies of the spherical burner were launched to the ISS because of concerns that they might be damaged and/or might prove to yield flames which aren’t sufficiently spherically symmetric. The porous spheres were fabricated from sintering 316 stainless steel with 10-micron media grade, for which the porosity is approximately 41% and the density is 4.6 g/cm3. More specifically, each sphere was formed by sintering together sintered disks, where the supply tube should extend to the sphere’s center. Neglecting the interior of the supply tube, there is presumably no cavity within the porous sphere.

Each sphere was furthermore sinter-bonded to its stainless-steel supply tube. As a side effect, the tubing lost its temper and became very pliable because of the high temperature required for the bonding . Therefore, a close -fitting support tube, with an outer diameter of 1.8 mm, was added to the design. It doesn’t quite extend to the porous sphere as can be seen in Figure 46. The gap between the support tube and the burner is often obvious in flame imaging because the supply tube is more reflective than the support tube. Each burner was equipped with an extremely fine, sheathed, type-K thermocouple which was embedded as much as ~1 mm into the porous sphere. The thermocouple hole was 0.76 to 1.0 mm deep (and 0.25-0.30 mm in diameter) where the thermocouple was meant to be inserted fully, i.e., until reaching the hole’s bottom, but that may not be its exact position. The junction is of course not at the extreme end of the sheathed thermocouple, but it is very fine and presumably close. If the porous sphere is imagined as a globe with the supply tube as the south pole, the thermocouple is inserted in the lower hemisphere, between the equator and pole as seen in Figure 46.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 3 1. Overview The Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which the tests were conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Peter B. Sunderland of the Department of Fire Protection Engineering at the University of Maryland. The two Co-Investigators (Co-Is) are Profs. Richard L. Axelbaum and Forman A. Williams who are respectively from the Washington University of St. Louis and the University of California, San Diego (UCSD). Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NA SA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME including CFI-G and the rest of the ACME investigations. In ACME’s preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team include d Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam who are also with CWRU. The ISS operations for CFI-G were conducted from March to Oct. 2021 in two sequential rounds of testing. The two rounds occurred during Increments 64 -65 and 65 -66 and respectively featured normal and inverse flames.

The inverse flame tests were conducted with the chamber filled with a mixture of nitrogen and gaseous fuel while an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed from the burner. As a result, the inverse flames were effectively inside out, e.g., where the soot formed outside rather than inside of the flames. Although it was in the second round, the final day of CFI -G testing was carried out in the normal flame configuration, with gaseous fuel (with or without nitrogen) flowing into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere. This was an added test day carried out under conditions in which low-temperature combustion occurred during the first round of testing. CFI-G was a late addition to ACME, where the experiment was jointly selected for spaceflight by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS) rather than NASA. The selection was notably announced after the core ACME hardware had launched to the ISS and just weeks before ACME’s on-orbit operations began. It is effectively an extension of ACME’s Flame Design experiment for which the PI and Co-I are respectively Axelbaum and Sunderland. And it is likewise a follow-on to the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI), led by Williams, in which liquid droplets were burned rather than gaseous fuel.

Although CFI-G wasn’t selected for spaceflight by NASA, its ISS operations and the development of its unique hardware, software, and procedure were carried out by the same teams of personnel as the other ACME experiments, primarily from ZIN Technologies, Inc.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 4 2. Science Overview A. Background This background is the Project Summary from the experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on Combustion and Thermal Transport Processes Research on the International Space Station to Benefit Life on Earth. Overview: Cool diffusion flames were discovered in 2012 aboard the ISS. This spawned a rapidly growing research field, but only a small number of measurements at limited conditions are available. Consequently, cool flame kinetics m echanisms cannot be adequately tested or advanced. This could be impeding the development of cleaner and more efficient internal combustion engines. It is proposed here to observe cool diffusion flames supported by porous spherical burners fed with propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. Normal and inverse flames will be considered for a broad range of dilution conditions and pressures. The ISS is the ideal platform for observing cool diffusion flames because they typically require 20 s to establish and they could burn indefinitely. Tests will be performed using the ACME insert in the CIR. Minimal hardware development will be required because the spherical porous burners and gas delivery system will be those used by the Flame Design flight experiment, w hile the diagnostics will be those used by the CFI flight experiment.

The objectives are to observe diverse cool diffusion flames aboard the ISS, to simulate the tests with an advanced CFD model, and to identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism th at accurately models these conditions. Intellectual Merit: Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool flame chem istry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose understanding has large economic consequences. The proposed experiments will take advantage of many state -of-the-art diagnostics that are already available on the ISS. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. An advanced CFD model will simulate the flames and will aid the testing and development of cool flame kinetics models. Observing cool flames burning as steady spherical diffusion flames will yield valuable insight into cool flame chemical kinetics. The measurements proposed cannot be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities. Broader Impacts: The research will be disseminated widely to the combustion research community and to industry.

Rationale for Microgravity This is the ‘Justification for Testing Aboard the ISS’ section (3.1) of the experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on Combustion a nd Thermal Transport Processes Research on the International Space Station to Benefit Life on Earth . The included equation is formatted differently in this copy. Previous ground -based microgravity experiments have demonstrated the scientific value of spherical, burner -supported diffusion flames. These one -dimensional flames offer a simple, fundamental configuration to improve the understanding of diffusion flame behavior and to explore such effects as transport, kinetics, soot formation, and radiation , which can be more pronounced under microgravity conditions (Atreya et al. 1992; Law et al. 2001; Lecoustre et al. 2012).

Spherically-symmetric flames are not generally practical in normal gravity. This can be explained by considering the Richardson num ber, which is the ratio of the buoyancy force to the inertial force, Ri = g (ΔT L) / (T u2) , (1) where g is the acceleration of gravity, T is temperature, L is the characteristic length scale, and u is the characteristic velocity. Taking as representative values L = 50 mm, u = 5 cm/s, ΔT = 2000 K, and T = 300 K, Ri = 1300 in normal gravity. Ri can be reduced with a judicious choice of fuels and inert; Law et al. (2001) have shown that nearly spherical flames can be created in normal gravity using low pressure hydrogen inverse flames. However for typical spherical diffusion flames the only way to obtain Ri << 1 is to reduce g by four orders of magnitude. This requires a microgravity environment. Available microgravity drop tower facilities do not offer sufficient time to observe quasi -steady spherical diffusion flames, let alone their radiative extinction followed by cool diffusion flames. Experiments performed in the 5 s drop facility confirm that typical spherical diffusion flames continue growing during 5 s (see Fig. 2). Observations of cool flames in the FLEX, FLEX -2, and CFI droplet experiments involved or will involve burn times of up to 60 s. Analytical work supports these observations of slo w flame development.

Radial velocities in spherical diffusion flames scale with 1 / r2, where r is radius. Thus, at only a few burner diameters distance from the sphere, diffusion is the dominant transport mechanism. The characteristic diffusion time is r2/D, where D is mass diffusivity. For r = 25 mm and D = 20 mm2/s, this diffusion time is 30 s. Decreasing the flame size can reduce this time, but will not permit the observation of radiative extinction followed by cool diffusion flames. Our analytical and numerical calculations indicate that approximately 30 s of jitter-free (less than 10-5 g) microgravity is needed to approach quasi-steady state for these flames. The ISS is the only microgravity platform that can provide this environment.

Hardware Shortcomings CFI-G’s two primary challenges were in initiating cool flames and discerning their presence. Based on the findings of the earlier studies with droplet combustion, non-premixed cool flames can be directly ignited by limiting the ignition energy or can occur after the self -extinguishment of (normal) hot flames. Tests intended to directly ignite cool flames sometimes unintentionally resulted in hot flames. Meanwhile, evidence of cool flames was first discovered in review of the data a few days after the testing. During that testing, it wasn’t known that the cool flames were present after hot flame extinction and the tests were terminated, which unknowingly and sadly shortened the duration of the cool flame combustion. In later testing with the long/near thermocouple, two of the tests exhibited repeated hot flame quenching and reignition, which resulting from intervening low -temperature combustion.

It appears that the closest thermocouple, approximately 1 cm from the burner surface, was a factor in the reignition. The exposed type-B thermocouple includes platinum, a catalyst for the oxidation of hydrocarbons. The catalysis contributed to the rapid reignition limiting the duration of the lowtemperature combustion in these tests. A challenge for cool flame detection was concern about potential damage to the CFI intensified camera by exposing it to bright light, especially from the energized igniter, while the intensifier gain was set high. There were also issues with the Image Processing and Storage Units (IPSUs) which affected CFI-G operations. All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC) in Clevel and, Ohio. A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are normally conducted in a period of 10 hours of less. Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per two weeks. Summary of Preliminary Results Abstract for Spherical Gas-Fueled Cool Diffusion Flames : An improved understanding of cool diffusion flames could lead to improved engines. CDFs are investigated here using a spherical porous burner with gaseous fuels in the microgravity environment of the International Space Station. Normal and inverse flames burning ethane, propane, and n-butane were explored with various fuel and oxygen concentrations, pressures, and flow rates. The diagnostics included an intensified video camera, radiometers, and thermocouples. Spherical CDFs burning gases were observed for the first time. However, these CDFs were not readily produced and were only obtained for normal n-butane flames at 2 bar with an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39. The hot flames that spawned the CDFs were 2.6 times as large. An analytical model is presented that combines previous models for steady droplet burning and the partial -burning regime for CDFs. The results identify the importance of burner temperature on the behavior of these CDFs. They also indicate that the observed CDFs reside in rich regions near a mixture fraction of 0.53. Abstract for Cool Diffusion Flames in a Stably Stratified Stagnation Flow: Cool diffusion flames have been a growing research topic since their discovery in 2012.

Until now their study has been hindered by the high cost of the experimental systems used to observe them. A method is presented here for observing CDFs inexpensively using a pool of liquid n-heptane and parallel plates heated so as to produce a stably stratified stagnation flow. The flames were imaged with a color camera and measurements included gas phase temperatures, fuel evaporation rates, and formaldehyde emissions. These are the first observations of CDFs burning near the surface of fuel pools. The measured peak temperatures were between 705 – 760 K, whic h corresponds to an increase in gas temperature of 70 K. Autoignition first occurred at 550 K. Cantera autoignition simulations for homogeneous mixtures with the CRECK mechanism predicted a cool flame temperature of 885 K, which is significantly higher than observed. Publications: • M. Introduction Tests for the Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI -G) experiment are conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. As explained in the research proposal: Cool diffusion flames were disco vered during droplet experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS) in 2012, and this initiated a rapidly growing field of combustion research. Droplet experiments necessarily involve unsteady burning rates, so cool diffusion flames have never been observed as steady spherical flames. A natural progression toward understanding cool diffusion flames is to observe quasi-steady spherical flames on porous burners, and this is the topic of this proposal. The flames to be studied are rich in the physics and chemistry of combustion and thermal transport processes.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 29 Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose understanding has large economic consequences. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. The tests, performed with gaseous fuel and a porous spherical burner, cannot be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities. CFI-G had the following experimental hypotheses and experimental objective when it was proposed in 2017: Hypotheses The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames.

Experimental Objective A. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. where Zst and Tad are respectively the stochiometric mixture fraction and adiabatic flame temperature. However, it was later determined that the CIR facility could not support testing with pentane because of the fuel’s low vapor pressure so the test matrix was revised to instead include testing with ethane in addition to the propane and n-butane. The additional research objectives are as follows, where CFD stands for Computational Fluid Dynamics. B. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations. C. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements. D. Disseminate the results as widely as possible. The experiment is carried out using the same spherical burner configuration as ACME’s Flame Design and s -Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames) experiments. Introduction Tests for the Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI -G) experiment are conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CI R) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. As explained in the research proposal: Cool diffusion flames were discovered during droplet experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS) in 2012, and this initiated a rapidly growing field of combustion research. Droplet experiments necessarily involve unsteady burning rates, so cool diffusion flames have never been observed as steady spherical flames. A natural progression toward understanding cool diffusion flames is to observe quasi-steady spherical flames on porous burners, and this is the topic of this proposal. The flames to be studied are rich in the physics and chemistry of combustion and thermal transport processes.

Introduction The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. In this experiment, an electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts is established between the bur ner and a flat, circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner . The motion of the charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are strongly affected by a strong electric field. The resulting ion -driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting behavior of the flame. Measurements are made of electric-field strength, the ion current passing through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, soot, and stability. Conducting the tests in microgravity allows for great simplifications in the analysis of ion-driven convection and flame interaction, enabling new understanding and the development of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth. An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions produced as a result of the combustion reactions. The induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the soot and stability limits, and direct the heat transfer.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 2 experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how the electric field can be used to manipulate the ions and control non-premixed flames for practical benefit. For example, electric fields ca n enable stable burner operation at fuel -lean conditions with reduced pollutant emission, i.e., where the flame is not reliably sustained without the electric field. As another example, the role of electric fields on soot formation can be dramatic. It ap pears that the ion driven wind alters the local convection and strongly influences the residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame. The experiment contributes to our critical understanding of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields. More specifically, E-FIELD Flames has the following experimental objectives: A. Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi -ion current as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of inert (nitrogen) in the fuel. B. Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. C.

Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel (methane and ethy lene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. D. Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize the combustion behavior of near -limit lifted flames and use the associated i on-driven wind to stabilize or reattach these flames. The effect of the electric field on the flame is studied through tests conducted with a range of flame and electric field conditions. The fuel, fuel jet velocity, air flow, electric -field voltage and polarity are the primary parameters of the E-FIELD Flames experiment. Tests are conducted with methane and ethylene, including nitrogen dilutions of each, which provide a broad range of sootproducing conditions, i.e., from soot -free to highly sooting. T hey are conducted with both a simple gas-jet burner and the coflow burner that was also used for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment. Tests with the coflow burner is conducted with and without a coflow of air, where the results of the latter are compared with those from the gas-jet burner to assess the effect of air entrainment on the flame.

The coflow burner also provides a different electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane). In a typical test, the mesh electrode is energized at increasing potentials (relative to the burner), where the flame’s response (e.g., ion current, luminosity, shape) to the resulting field strength is measured. The field strength is changed in repeated steps or is instead smoothly ramped. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi -steady flames in microgravit y. Microgravity f lame flicker is then the result of electric body forces alone . Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum - dominated flames, which are important for most practical combust ion, can be studied at low

Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoy ant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. Chemi-ion species, electronica lly excited chemiluminescent species are are very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol E-FIELD Flames and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests.

The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it may alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. For example, the mesh voltage can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or soot limit. This was not done during Increments 5 5-56, where the console commanding during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed in the analog ops video that the flame had extinguished. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing. III. Results A. Similarly, bottles were launched with ethylen e concentrations of 30%, 50%, and 100%, again with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis) . But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations. In all cases, the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis). Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data E-FIELD Flames tests sometimes automatically abort (due to the controlling software script), where that is typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter. The first test of the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been sufficiently primed. Ignition is sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the automatic flame detectio n are such that detection threshold is reached because of the igniter glow rather than a flame. As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite. This is typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module. The OH* chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible spectrum. However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to false ignition detection. The key measurement for the E-FIELD Flames experiments is the ion current as a function of applied voltage, i.e., the voltage-current or V-I curve. This curve provides information on the flames ability to produce chemi -ions based on its saturation ion current, and it provides a measure of combustion performance in that ion production is a function of carbon influx into the flame and the vigorousness of the combustion process. More compact, higher temperature flames produce more chemi -ions than do larger more diffuse reaction zones of lower overall temperature for the same fuel flow. The first effect (i.e., the relationship between carbon influx and peak ion current) can be seen in Figure 2, where the flow of 15 cm/s methane produces slightly above 2 microamps of ion current at the peak (1.5 kV/cm) and the flow of 19 cm/s methane has a peak of 2.75 microamps. Introduction The Electric -Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E -FIELD Flames) experimen t wa s conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. In this experiment, an electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts was established between the burner and a flat, circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner . The motion of the charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are strongly affected by a strong electric field. The resulting ion -driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting behavior of the flame. Measurements we re made of electric -field strength, the ion current passing through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, soot, and stability. Conducting the tests in microgravity allow ed for great simplifications in the analysis of ion -driven convection and flame interaction , enabling new understanding and the development of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 2 An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions produced as a result of the combustion reactions. The induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the soot and stability limits, and direct the heat transfer. The purpose of the E -FIELD Flames experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how the electric field can be used to manipulate the ions and control non-premixed flames for practical benefit. For example, electric fi elds can enable stable burner operation at fuel -lean conditions with reduced pollutant emission, i.e., where the flame is not reliably sustained without the electric field. As another example, the role of electric fields on soot formation can be dramatic. It appears that the ion driven wind alters the local convection and strongly influences the residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame. The experiment contributes to our critical understanding of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields. More specifically, E-FIELD Flames has the following experimental objectives: A. Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi -ion current as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of iner t (nitrogen) in the fuel. B.

Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. C. Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (n itrogen) added to the fuel stream. D. Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize the combustion behavior of near -limit lifted flames and use the associated ion -driven wind to stabilize or reattach these flames. The effect of the electric field on the flame is studied through tests conducted with a range of flame and electric field conditions. The fuel, fuel jet velocity, air flow, elect ric-field voltage and polarity were the primary parameters of the E-FIELD Flames experiment. Tests were conducted with methane and ethylene, including nitrogen dilutions of each, which provide a broad range of soot-producing conditions, i.e., from soot-free to highly sooting. They were carried out with both a simple gas-jet burner and the coflow burner that was also used for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment.

Tests with the coflow burner were conducted with and without a coflow of air, where the results of the latter are compared with those from the gas -jet burner to assess the effect of air entrainment on the flame. The coflow burner also provided a different electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane). In a typical test, the mesh electrode was en ergized at increasing potentials (relative to the burner), where the flame’s response (e.g., ion current, luminosity, shape) to the resulting field strength was measured. The field strength was changed in repeated steps or was instead smoothly ramped. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal -gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flame s, which is a buoyancy -

ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 3 driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Therefore, the flicker in the E -FIELD Flames was a result of electric body forces alone . Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, wh ich are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normalgravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, c hemi-ion species, electronically excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry.

With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol E-FIELD Flames and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include t he gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it may alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. For example, the mesh voltage can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or soot limit. This was not done during Increments 5 5-56 or 57 -58, where the console commanding during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed in the analog ops video that the flame had extinguished.

Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight A total of 219 flames were ignited for the E -FIELD Flames expe riment, with 142 and 77 respectively ignited during Increments 55 -56 and 57-58. Note that the investigation’s testing was completed during Increment 57, so no flames were ignited during Increment 58. The first and second rounds of testing respectively occurred in March-May 2018 and September-November 2018 . The two rounds of tests resulted in 120 and 99 ignited flames conducted with coflow and gas-jet burners, respectively. The coflow burner was developed for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Fla me (CLD Flame) experiment, where CLD Flames’ second round occurred between the two rounds of the E -FIELD Flames experiment. The ‘interruption’ in the E-FIELD Flames testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. E-FIELD Flames does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are independently conducted with two different gas eous fuels, methan e and ethylene. Both are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.

Methane (CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds. Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting because of its carbon double bond. For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed with nitrogen over a broad range of dilutions. For limited cases, the fuel and nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch. ACME bottles were launched with methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis). Similarly, bottles were launched with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 50%, and 100%, again with a balan ce of nitrogen (on a volume basis) . But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations. In all cases, the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis). No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected for E-FIELD Flames; all of the ISS results were electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently planned ACME experiments. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data E-FIELD Flame s tests sometimes automatically a borted (due to the controlling software script), where that was typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter. As a result, there was little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt. The aborts normally occur red because of com munication issues with IPSU-1. These are infrequent, but there are some days when tests aborted repeatedly. Tests are of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite. The first test of the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been sufficiently primed.

Ignition was sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of the igniter glow rather than a flame. As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite. This is typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (P MT) module. The OH* chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible spectrum. However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to false ignition detection. Status of Data Analysis Data from the tests making up the E-FIELD Flames experiment includes video recordings from the operations camera for general flame behavior, high resolution images from the ACME data camera at various exposures and frame rates as dictated by the flame luminosity, intensified camera images, and non-imaging data at 125 Hz. The non-imaging data file is processed using Matlab scripts (modified from those developed by CLD Flame researchers) to separately show trends of ion current and flame luminosity as a function of the applied field, and the flame parameters (fuel, flowrate, burner type). The PMT data is also extracted to evaluate flame luminosity oscillations. Image data is processed using the OMA software (also developed and used by CLD Flame researchers). The overall data volume is large with a storage limit of 127 ,000 MB per test day. All of the data has been downloaded to the hard drive with a backup system at UC Irvine. A t this stage, the data has been sorted into appropriate segments so that comparisons can be made between burner geometries (jet versus coflow from the prior round of testing), fuel type and dilution (methane versu s ethylene; no dilution, modest dilution, high dilution) and fuel flow velocity.

The fuel flow velocity and dilution conditions were sometimes selected to hold total carbon flux into the flame constant. At this stage, the analysis remains comparative and qualitative, to show the major differences in behavior in microgravity and normal-gravity (1-g) flames, and to show particularly how buoyancy modifies the electrical response of the flames. E. Preliminary Research Findings Distinctly different results were seen in E-FIELD Flames’ second round tests with the gasjet burner when compared with the first round tests with the coflow burner. For example, the ion current response to the electric field strength with an upward ion driven wind in microgravity is a clear parabolic trend (which is similar to the trend observed in 1-g flames with the coflow burner as presented in the prior report). The parabolic behavior is evident even with the strong oscillations observed during the rise. This rising trend is not observed with the coflow burner. The behavior of the soot and its charge state are complicated since in the regions of high field strength, particularly near the fuel tube where the field lines converge, soot can emit or collect free charges. Hence, the soot transport is driven directly by the field and by the ion-driven wind (and thermophoresis) which means it can travel differentially to the bulk flow.

These various transport elements can push the soot through the flame to burnout, hold it in stasis in the flame for additional growth, or drive it to the burner where it accumulates. More work is needed to sort through these elements. This report shows the initial results of the E -FIELD Flames experiment using the gas -jet burner in the International Space Station (ISS). The positive field allows the soot to concentrate and compresses the flame into a high current density thermal source. The flames demonstrate an unpredicted oscillation before extinguishing with increasing field strength. This oscillating phenomenon was not observed during the tests with the coflow burner from the first round , with the exception of a case that introduced the airflow at 30 cm/s which increased the surface reaction while the flame tended to balance between electric field effects, ions, and c harged soot. The negative field allows the flame to maintain its spherical characteristic in microgravity.

The yellow soot appears fo r both of the electric field directions within the flame around the tip and disappears with increasing field strength after reaching the current peak. Overview The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames ( E-FIELD Flames ) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which tests are conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack ( CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Derek Dunn -Rankin of the University of California, Irvine ( UC Irvine). Dr. Yu -Chien (Alice) Chien , also of UC Irvine, served as the Project Scientist at the university. Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is NASA’s Project Scientist (PS) for ACME including E-FIELD Flames and the rest of the ACME investigations. The experiment had two Co-Investigators, the first of which was Prof. Felix Weinberg of London’s Imperial College. Prof.

Weinberg was a pioneer in researching the effects of electrical fields on flames in microgravity, but unfortunately died in 2012 (see http://www.imperial.ac.uk/news/117808/tribute-felixweinberg/) before the hardware was built and the tests were conducted on the ISS. The second Co - Investigator was Dr. Sunny Karnani who did his doctoral research in preparation of the spaceflight experiment and afterward worked for ClearSign Combustion Corp. , which markets Electrodynamic Combustion Control (https://www.clearsign.com/technology/electrodynamic-combustion-control/). Science Overview A.

Background With minor editing, t his background is the Executive Summary from the experiment’s Science Requirements Document (SRD) of March 2010. This project utilizes electric fields in microgravity combustion science to establish a fundamental understanding of chemi -ionization and ion -driven convection in flames. It also uses this understanding to demonstrate electrical manipulation of sooting behavior and stability limits in the absence of buoyancy. This work is based on prior foundation studies that included simulating zero-g combustion of small gas jet diffusion flames in an earth-gravity laboratory, and the electric field control of flame electrodynamics. The current SRD proposes to use the extended -duration microgravity environment to further develop an understanding of electric fie lds in combustion processes and their potential applications.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 4 The research centers on the fact that electrical forces, acting on charge carriers created through chemi-ionization, can provide for measurement and manipulation of flames in microgravity environments. For example, using the drag exercised on flame ions, electric fields have demonstrated observable influences on flame shape, sooting behavior, burning velocity, extinction, and stability. The source of these influences almost certainly resides in ion wind effects. In microgravity, where there are no density -driven buoyant effects to contend with, ion winds represent an important (and perhaps the only) body force that can be applied to manipulate combustion systems. This project includes both academic study of electric field effects and aspects for practical utilization of electrical control of combustion processes.

The prior laboratory experiments have shown that electrical properties of flames can be used to produce enhanced combustion performance by: (a) manipulating flame ions in order to change flame chemistry – this is generally considered a minor influence because flame ion concentration is typically small, but it may be critical at near -limit conditions; (b) creating a neutral wind (ion driven convection) locally at the flame front – this process can provide a local actuator for flame convection control; (c) using electric fields to affect soot formation and transport – ions and soot are closely linked because there are shared chemical pathways and because soot particles are charged by the flame ions; and (d) using electrical properties to characterize flames – e.g., there is a relationship between flame temperature, the carbon content of a fuel, and the ion current it can produce at saturation. In 1-g, the above -mentioned processes are confounded by complex buoyancy interac tions that cannot be unraveled.

Hence, to evaluate them in detail, we propose the following experimental objectives for an extended microgravity environment: (A) determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel flow rate and the amount of inert (nitrogen) in the fuel; (B) compare the time response of the flame’s chemiluminescence and ion current to rapid cha nges in electric fields; (C) determine sooting behavior in relation to the electric field influences; and (D) manipulate the limit behavior of lifted flames using electric fields. The experimental approach includes a simple gas jet diffusion flame and a c o-flow burner. The basic variations in the tests are in the burner type, the fuel type (nomina lly nonsooting and sooting), and in the level of inert dilution of the fuel to vary the flame strength. The co-flow or environment gas will have a nominal molar composition of 21% O2 and 79% N2. The experimental concept is to ground the burner to the test chamber and to install an electrically active planar mesh electrode downstream of the burner mouth. The potential of the mesh electrode can be either positive or negative, with a steady voltage or with a time varying potential (including a rapid step change) to examine the flame’s steady state response and time response.

The data to be recorded include the applied voltage, the ion current, the flame broadband lumin osity, the CH* luminosity, flame images of OH* and visible light showing the flame shape as a function of electric potential and flame shape changes during transients in the electric field. In addition, a desired measurement of temperature in and near the flame will monitor the thermal field as a function of the electric field conditions. The data from these measurements will allow a chemical and physical understanding of flame ion production and information showing the potential to use these ions to electrically control the flame both via modification of the local chemistry near extinction limits and through changes in the local convection using the ion driven wind. For example, a lifted diffusion flame near its blowoff condition is sensitive to mixing at the flame anchor point. Therefore, electric fields acting

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 5 on near-limit flames can exert a large influence because they can affect the local mixing behavior. The role of electric fields on soot formation will be dramatic under conditions where the ion driven wind has a large influence on flow residence time (or on ion residence time, if chemical ef fects are found important) in sooting flames. Generally, the convective flows driven by electric fields acting on flame ions and those driven by buoyancy have been found to be of the same order of magnitude in earth gravity. In addition, raising the temperature often increases the ion production rate and the response to an electric field, but increasing temperature also increases the buoyancy effect, making it difficult, on earth, to separate ion wind effects from those due to buoyancy. In the zero -g environment, it will be possible to eliminate the buoyancy confusion and develop sufficient understanding to predict the response of flames to electric fields under all conditions. Extended run times are crucial for all of the studies because the timescales of flame property changes (which includes chemi -ionization) are dominated by convection (length scale/velocity) and past studies have shown that soot studies require high quality zero gravity timescales longer than is available in aircraft and drop towers.

In addition, exploring instabilities and extinction behavior in near -limit flames requires experiments lasting tens of seconds. Overall, the goal o f this zero -gravity study is to understand chemi -ionization behavior and the resulting ion driven winds suffic iently well so that electrical properties of flames can be used to characterize (by monitoring ion current) and control them (via direct chemical or local convective influences). Electric field effects on flames have been documented for decades (even centuries), but flames in 1-g all include buoyancy influences that affect ion generation behavior. For flames near transitions and limits, buoyant influences always confound any understanding of the role of ion driven winds in using electric fields to characterize and manipulate flames. The proposed study removes this confounding influence and allows definitive measurement and analysis of the electric field effects on jet diffusion and co-flow flames. B. Rationale for Microgravity This is the ‘Justification for Extended-Duration Microgravity’ section of the experiment’s SRD from March 2010. See the SRD itself for the references, etc. as they are not included in this report. As described in the Background and Overview (Section 1.1), electric field effects and buoyancy effects have been found to be of the same order of magnitude.

In addition, in some cases, raising the flame temperature will increase the O atom concentration, thereby increasing the ion production rate and increasing the response to an electric field . At the same time, increasing temperature increases the buoyancy effect, making it difficult to separate ion wind effects from buoyancy. In the zero-g environment, it will be possible to eliminate the buoyancy confusion and develop sufficient understandin g to predict the response of flames to electric fields under all conditions. For electrically driven flames, microgravity is also necessary to create conditions that produce symmetric flames suitable for Abel inversion and steady-state analysis. While in general natural convection can enhance symmetry relative to non -buoyant flames, a flame at 1 -g in an electric wind experiences buoyancy as a disruptive influence on symmetry. Even when buoyancy effects can be minimized, we have found that there are periodic disturbances that disrupt the ideal symmetry. Highly symmetric conditions of extended microgravity are also useful for numerically simulating these various effects by our electrokinetic model or more comprehensively by others.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 6 Finally, in order to fully evaluate the potential for control, it is important to examine the effects separately. An example of the importance of microgravity for the electric field effects studies is shown in Figure 2.6. This figure compares the capillary flame used for 1-g experiments (which has some similarities to the jet -flame companion study) when it i s oriented vertically to when it is oriented horizontally relative to gravity. These flames behave differently in shape, size, and ion production demonstrating the substantial in fluence played by buoyancy even in the relatively small capillary flames. Grav ity effects in the co -flow flames have been described in the SRD for the CLD Flame experiment, and the same influences will be important when we apply electric fields. Only in ex tended microgravity will it be possible to separate the ion driven wind effects from buoyant wind effects. Figure 2.6. Effect of orientation on combustion of 1.8 mm jet diffusion flames in 1-g. Extended run times are crucial for all of the studies beca use the timescales involved extend beyond drop tower capabilities and the microgravity quality required for symmetry and stability exceeds aircraft microgravity.

The electric -field flame interaction tests carried out in the NASA Glenn 2.2 Second Drop Tower tests by Yuan and Hegde [55] showed that the flame did not appear to re ach steady state during the 2.2 sec. drop. Furthermore, their results showed substantial differences in flame shape between cases where the electric field was activated half-way through the drop and at the beginning of the drop, again suggesting that stead y state was not achieved. Although, we varied the range of tests performed at the Drop Tower, our research group encountered similar obstacles. Drop times were insufficient to achieve a steady flame after voltage changes in one direction. Additionally, we were unable to capture the removal of soot from the ignition event and the subsequent response of the flame to the electric field. Furthermore, testing has shown path dependence in the response time of the flame when subjected to step voltages of varying polarities. Properly mapping the steady-state ion current as a function of applied voltage requires that the flame stabilize at each applied voltage. Generally speaking, the timescale of flame property changes (which includes chemi-ionization) is dominated by convection (length scale/velocity), which is on the order of 0.1 second.

In order to ensure quasisteady conditions of the VI characteristics for a single flame configuration with some fidelity (e.g., 50 steps of 200 V each, with 2 seconds between steps for settling after the change), requires more than 100 seconds of continuous high quality microgravity. Each condition and voltage cannot be

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 7 run individually (i.e., with separate drop tests) because the 2 second settling time requires that the flame begin at a settled initial condition before taking another relatively small voltage step. If we tried to step to the initial condition, allow settling, take the base measurement, then step the voltage and again wait the required settling time, we would exceed 5 seconds for each test in nearly all cases. To run a return voltage sweep to examine hysteresis might take a further 100 seconds. Furthermore, these times are based on 1-g results which under low ion wind conditions are likely to be faster than occ urs in microgravity since their the convective timescales can be substantially smaller (under low electric field forcing conditions, for example). Understanding the electric field effects on soot is another area that requires high quality zero gravity timescales longer than is available in drop towers. A variety of zero gravity diffusion flame experience has shown that quasi-steady soot formation requires many seconds [22, 56, 57]. The long du ration is necessary since we are exploring the relative importance of residence time modification of these processes in these flames.

In addition, as mentioned above, instabilities and extinction behavior in near -limit flames generally have a stochastic ch aracter so that relatively long observation times are needed to quantify electric field effects. For example, lifted flames in electric fields can exhibit an oscillatory behavior where they alternately approach and recede from the burner exit until they finally reattach. Tens of seconds for this process is not unusual. Extended microgravity conditions will clarify the role of electric fields (via ion winds) on stability limits of flames. C. Science Objectives The proposed objectives text presented here is the ‘Experimental Objectives’ section of the experiment’s SRD from March 2010. Although the objectives were not formally changed, the slow response time of the high-voltage power supplies (recommended in the ISRD) limited the ability to accomplish objective B. To make up in part for this shortfall, the investigation was permitted to test with two different burner types (specifically gas-jet and coflow burners) , where th e use of multiple burner types was disallowed for ACME experiments to limit their scope.

Note that the hardware shortcoming was identified during the hardware development (and thus prior to spaceflight operations) , but the project management decided to accept the shortcoming and proceed with the existing design to avoid the cost and schedule ramifications of a redesign. The ultimate objective of this experiment is to develop an understanding of the mechanisms of chemi-ionization in flames and to describe the interplay between convective flows driven by those flame ions and their generation rate. With this information it will then be possible to detect and control flame behavior electrically. In 1-g, laminar diffusion flames are often controlled to a large extent by natural convection, and particularly by the rate at which natural convection brings fresh oxidizer to the reaction zone. Hence, the vigor with which combustion proceeds depends on local convection. As described in Section 1, an electric field acting on flame ions produces a body force and convection (analogous to buoyancy) which affects the combustion process. The change in the combustion process can in turn affect the ion production rate, which is responsible for the body force. This coupled interaction is very difficult to measure, study, and understand in 1-g because buoyant forces (of approximately equal magnitude) interfere.

In microgravity, there is no such complication and the body force in the flame is associated entirely with the ion-driven wind. 1-g experiments have demonstrated clearly that electrically driven convection can be used to modify the local flow field in a manner that changes combustion behavior. For example, it can stabilize lifted flames or force them to reattach. Electric fields have been seen to change soot formation,

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 8 though whether solely by residence time ef fects or their combination with chemical alterations has not been confirmed. In addition, ions can attach to soot particles providing them with enhanced mobility that can be manipulated. Furthermore, the electrical properties of flames provide a measure of their charact er. For example, non -premixed flames exhibit different relationships between ion production and ion wind forces than do premixed flames. The hydrocarbon fuel, and in particular, the carbon/hydrogen ratio, also affects these interactions. The goal of this p roject is to clarify and quantify this range of electrical effects and to then demonstrate the electrical manipulation of flame stability and soot in flames using the information obtained. To accomplish this scientific goal, there are four fundamental experimental objectives, in priority order, using a jet diffusion flame burner and a co-flow diffusion flame burner. The jet flame is the more critical configuration because it has a large 1 -g data foundation and it can be more easily modeled as an ion and thermal source. In microgravity, however, it will be primarily driven by ion wind convection (no buoyant contribution and at its low fuel flow rates, the injection momentum dies rapidly with distance from the injector) which may limit its operating range.

The co-flow flame allows a forced convection component to provide a wider range of flow conditions (fuel dilution and exit velocity) and a reproducible lifted flame for stability and soot behavior studies: A) Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of inert (nitrogen) in the fuel. For the above determination, a low -sooting and highly sooting fuel are included, and the inert weakens the flame sufficiently to permit near-limit conditions at moderate flow velocities, where the effects of electric fields will be most acute. As shown in Figure 1.10, the resulting voltage - current (VI) curve (also known as the voltage current characteristic - VCC) from these experiments will identify the voltage and current at which the ion current first saturates, the voltage at which the current begins to increase beyond saturation, indicating a change in combustion behavior, and the voltage at which the flame extinguishes. These data can be analyzed further to provide the ion production per carbon atom of fuel flux which describes the flame character (i.e., diffusion to partially premixed), and the ion wind strength for each condition.

In addition to the ir direct interpretative value for calculating ion-driven winds and body forces, these data can also be used in electrokinetic simulations to compute ion mobility values consistent with measured ion currents and to help validate the numerical simulations o f oth er researchers that include ion species and electrical effects in their flame calculations. B) Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (met hane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. These data provide the dynamic system behavior of the flame. This information comprises the time response of the flame (i.e., its surface area and luminosity) as compared to the time response of the ion current. These timescales can temporally separate the direct chemical effects of electric fields from ion diffusion and ion wind convective forcing. In addition, the system response is required to eventually build flame mo dels suitable for active electrical control, assuming linear behavior over small ranges.

C) Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 9 The interaction between soot and electric fields is very com plex because it combines the direct influence of electric fields on the chemis try, the ion wind effects on residence time and mixing, and the electric forces on the charged soot particles themselves. The zero -gravity environment, using the combination of the jet diffusion flame and the co -flow flame provides a wide range of conditions where these different influences can be allowed to dominate individually. For example, the forced convection environment of the co-flow burner will minimize the influence of the axial ion-driven wind, which helps to distinguish the direct electrical eff ects on ion chemistry in soot formation. In addition to demonstrating the direct control of soot behavior by electric fields, separating the influences can help distinguish between neutral molecule addition mechanisms of soot formation and those that presu me the importance of ionic species. For example, changing the strength and polarity of the electric field can change the availability of ion precursors, and electric convection can manipulate reactants’ time/temperature history. In addition, charges will accumulate onto soot, and the electric field can then act directly on the soot particles to change their residence time and path through the flame.

D) Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize the combustion behavior of near -limit lifted flames and use the associated ion -driven wind to stabilize or reattach these flames. Because the chemi-ion current per unit flame area can be used as an indicator of flame strength, its measure (both average and fluctuating properties) with low electric field voltage can be used to detect flames approaching their limit condition. By adjusting the electric field , 1 -g studies indicate that an ion driven wind can be used to reduce the liftoff height and stabilize the flame. This is an example of open loop electrical flame sensing, analysis, and control.
