The E-FIELD Flames experiment is being conducted in 2018 within the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) [15], which was launched in 2008 and us ed from 2009 to 2017 for a series of droplet combustion experiments [16]. The CIR facility is similar in size to a vending machine as can be seen in Figure 1.

It includes a 100-liter combustion chamber capable of operation at pressures of up to 300 kPa. The chamber features a ring of 8 sapphire windows and is equipped with a set of reconfigurable imaging systems. The CIR was designed with gas delivery, venting, thermal control, electrical power, data handling, image processing and storage, and vibration isolation to enable combustion research with gaseous, liquid, and solid fuels.

In this study, a high-voltage electric field is generated between the burner and a copper electrode mesh located above (i.e., downstream of) the burner outlet, as can be seen in Figure 4(b). The circular mesh is energized at up to 10,000 volts w ith either polarity, where the bur ner serves as the electrical return and the flow of flame -produced ions completes the circuit. The ion current between the burner and electrode mesh is measured from the voltage drop across a known resistor and application of Ohm’s Law. With and without the copper ring, the electrode mesh is 8.9 and 8.4 cm in diameter, respectively. The square copper weave has 7.1 wires/cm, a wire diameter of 0.43 mm, and a 48% open area. The mesh permits gas to pass through while also acting as an electrical element. The electrode mesh is mounted 37 mm above the coflow burner tip and is centered on and orthogonal to the chamber axis. The ACME chamber insert can also

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 14 accommodate an alternate electrode position of 52 mm above the coflow burner tip, but the closer position is being used to produce the highest field strengths. ACME’s non -imaging measurements are recorded at 125 Hz. The measured test conditions include the chamber pressure and temperature, the three gas flow rates, and th e electrical potential of the elec trode mesh. Acceleration measurements are provided by the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) [18], which is the primary instrument for such measurements on ISS and previously served that role for the space shuttle. The flame behavior is observe d optically with a variety of instruments. For most ACME experiments, including E -FIELD Flames, the radiant emission is measured with 6 thermopile detectors with a spectral range of nominally 0.2 -11 microns. Five radiome ters are in a crew - exchangeable linear array that is mounted parallel to the chamber axis. The other detector is downstream and off axis from the burner. Chemiluminescent emission is measured with a set of three Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) modules. Their spectral range is 230-700 nm, i.e. in the visible and near ultraviolet, but two are equipped with narrow bandpass filters for measurement of OH* and CH* emissions, respectively.

The third PMT is equipped with a neutral density filter to prevent saturation, although the gain values for all three PMTs are independently and readily adjustable. Like many of the components, the array of PMT modules can be removed from the chamber insert by the crew. In addition to their scientific value, PMT measurements are used operationally to detect igni tion and automatically deactivate and retract the igniter. The radiometer or PMT measurements can similarly be used to detect extinction and automatically end the gas flow and test. Overview of Experiment Test Operations The narrative description of the operations is from the ‘Methods / Experimental’ section of the following conference paper: Y.-C. Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Dunn-Rankin, “Electric Field Effects on Flames in Microgravity on the International Space Station,” 2018 Spring Technical Meeting of the Central States Section of The Combustion Institute, Minneapolis, MN, 20-22 May 2018. See the paper itself for the references, etc. as they are not included in this report. As a minor note, the size of some figures was adjusted in this report, but none were cropped. The CIR experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. Thus far, ACME’s activity has included the majority of the crew members, regardless of their nationalities. Most often the astronauts and cosmonauts exchange gas bottles, mass flow controllers, and igniter tips. In the latter case, the igniter tip exchange can occur after failure or proactively before failure when the crew already has changes to make changes in the interior of the insert. While these activities may seem mundane, the crew play a critical role in setting up the hardware for each experiment. As an extreme example, there were crew activities on 8 separate days in Sept.-Oct.

2017 to configure the CIR and ACME hardware for the first ACME experiment, namely the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment. In contrast, only two crew days were required to reconfigure the hardware for the first E-FIELD Flames tests because of the initial use of the same coflow burner. Planning is critical because crew activity is scheduled three weeks in advance, for which detailed procedures must be prepared and uplinked to the ISS. All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio. Typically, four to six people staff four consoles during the testing. The CIR hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer (DMO) consoles, and the ACME hardware is controlled from the Payload Developer (PD) console. Two shifts of personnel are scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because they typically last 14 hours with the many pre- and post-testing activities. Given that the tests are remotely commanded, the operations are carried out in the day and e vening in Cleveland, e.g., from 7 AM to 9 PM. A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are normally conducted in a period of 10 hours of less. Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per two weeks. On intervening weekdays, the image data is downlinked a nd the crew often swap one or both gas bottles.

Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2 -shift day for the RO and DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors and that data is not missing. Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew activity. As a result, the CIR consoles are normally actively staffed on four weekdays per week. A team of four carry out the detailed planning for the CIR and ACME console s taff, and the daily operational plans typically exceed 50 pages on days including testing. The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in near real time but doesn’t allow for commanding. In the case of E -FIELD Flames, arrangements were made so that the analog video is streamed to a secure computer at UC Irvine to allow the research team to participate in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s planned parameters. That team does not see t he telemetry during the testing, but is in communication via phone and e -mail with their NASA research partners at the GRC ISS Pa yload Operations Center (GIPOC). While there are many preparatory steps, the tests are ultimately conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files. In advance of the test day, the

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 20 UC Irvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in th e voltage sweep script and specifies other parameters that are configured outside of the script, such as camera settings. It i s also possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are changed in response to the analog video downlink or telemetry. For example, the electric field potential can be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations, the low rate results from several unavoidable factors. After a test is conducted, the 125-Hz nonimaging data is downlinked for immediate review by the science team. A small sample of images are often downlinked to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for those images are typically selected based on non-imaging data to provide extreme examples. The review helps to verify parameters or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the voltage range after determining where the ion current saturates for t he given flame conditions. After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber atmosphere after which the chamber is vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed.

Midway through a day’s E -FIELD Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minutes through a filter cartridge filled with molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a portion of the combustion products, e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products. The tests are only conducted when b oth Ku and S band communication is available through NASA’s Tracking and Data Relay Satellite (TDRS) System. Depending on the various orbits, there are periodic communication outages with a loss of signal (LOS) that can be a short handover (from one satellite to another) or can last as long as 30 minutes. A variety of constraints limit the number of tests that can be performed, both overall and on a daily basis. The next combustion experiments in the CIR will feature solid fuels and focus on flame spread and material flammability. That follow -on plan limits the duration of ACME operations, where each ACME experiment is allotted four months for testing. Although it requires additional crew time, these allotments are split into two rounds so that the investigators have a break from testing for careful review of the early results so that they can maximize the scientific outcome of their second round. This paper reports on early results from the first round of E-FIELD Flames.

While nitrogen is available fr om the space station, the combustion testing is limited by the available gas bottles that were and are launched to support the tests. For E -FIELD Flames and most of ACME’s experiments, the test matrices used to plan those gas resources were established in 2010. At that time, NASA limited the scope of the ACME tests matrices with the intent of focused experiments with limited obj ectives rather than comprehensive experiments. As such, the general target was 50 tests per experiment. For most ACME experimen ts, the limiting gas constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used to fill the chamber. This resource constraint is exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair of redundant safety timers to limit the fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers can be set for the oxidizer flow in the case of inverse flame testing). The timers can only be reset by venting the combustion chamber. Therefore, the timer limit combined with other constraints effectively corresponds to the day’s maximum flow time for the fuel (or more generally, the limiting reactant). For E -FIELD Flames, the safety timers are set to the maximum value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the 10 tests typically completed per day.
Another constraint is the available time in a day, where the console personnel and ISS resources, such as the video downlink, are planned for a limited numbe r of hours. When necessary for the

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 21 research, NASA does have continuous 24 -hour/day operations for some non -CIR experiments. But as discussed, the ACME tests are typically two minutes or less in duration, so the testing is almost always limited to the planned durations. Data limits are yet another constraint, where the on -orbit hardware can store a limited amount of data. More importantly, 127,000 MB is the most that can be reasonably managed in a two - shift transfer and downlink day. Therefore, tests da ys are limited to this amount of data, where image data from select cameras is often archived at reduced rates to mitigate this challenge. Nonetheless, the limit sometimes forces decisions to abandon recorded images. This detailed description of operations and hardware provides the context under which the ACME experiments are conducted. Their complexity makes the flame conditions seem trivial in comparison. It is a simple coflow flame, with just a small jet of fuel surrounded by a weak coflow of ‘air’ which also fills the chamber, but where tests are also conducted with no coflow. A test includes starting the gas flows to prime the system, energizing the igniter to initiate a flame, retracting the igniter, and allowing the flame to steady slightly before energizing the electric field to its initial value.

The flame is again allowed to steady before beginning a voltage sweep over a specified range with steps or smooth ramps of specified voltage changes and durations. The sweep can be in one direction or can include cycles of sweeps. After each test, a duplicate field sweep is made to ensure that there are no current leaks, i.e., other than the ion current through the flame. The first phase tests in E -FIELD Flames em ploy the coflow burner geometry shown in Figure 4, with the fuel tube extending slightly above the burner surface. The results shown in this paper are for tests conducted with 100% methane in a chamber atmosphere and coflow (when used) of synthetic ‘air’ (i.e., 21/79 oxygen/nitrogen by volume) at a nominal pressure of 100 kPa. The mesh is held at a negative potential relative to the burner in these tests. The sweeps shown in this paper extend to at least -7 kV, where the voltage is increased in small steps (e.g., of 100 V) lasting 1-2 seconds. The details of the voltage changes can be seen in the resulting plots.

Summary of Preliminary Results The following text is the abstract from a 2019 conference paper on early results from the first round of testing: Y.-C., Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, D., U. Hegde, U. and D. Dunn -Rankin, “Ion Current and Flame Changes with Electric Fields in Microgravity,” 11th U.S. National Combustion Meeting 2019, Pasadena, CA, 24-27 March 2019. This work presents changes in reaction zone shape and location, as well as ion currents obtained after applying an electric field onto a diffusion flame with fuel dilution in the International Space Station (ISS). As one of the projects of Advanced Combust ion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME), the E-FIELD Flames experiments were initiated in March and completed in November of 2018 with a series of flame studies on the coflow burner and the jet burner within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). The coflow burner, presented in this paper, consists of a small central fuel jet and a concentric outer ring flowing with synthetic air. The research examines fundamental hydrocarbon flame behaviors driven by the chemi -ion response during the combustion process.

The experiment is conducted by applying high voltage onto a copper mesh situated 37 mm above the burner tip, where measurements include images and ion currents over a range of electric field strengths and time histories depending on the region of interest (e. g., near the saturation transition). This paper specially investigates the flame behavior while flowing different methane/nitrogen mixture compositions. Among other effects, the results show that the electric field can stabilize the microgravity diffusion flame at very high dilution conditions, especially when there is no coflowing air. The preliminary results are discussed in greater detail in sections based on the burner configuration (coflow burner and jet burner), fuel (methane and ethylene), and dilution levels tested. First presented are the results from the methane flames with the coflow burner and then with the jet burner. Then, the ethylene flame results are presented. Before providing the results, it is important to clarify the terminology of polarity and field direction adopted for this system. Field direction and polarities The electric field is established between the two electrodes, burner and mesh, which are connected separatel y with positive and negative polarity, as the test requires.

Because this research has no gravi tationally relevant direction, any orientation can serve as the spatial reference coordinate. The vast majority of research in electric field related combustio n study is conducted at earth gravity, where the buoyancy is one of the key properties considere d and repeatedly discussed. In microgravity, a facing upright burner is equivalent to one facing upside down (or even sideways) scientifically because the buoy ancy/gravitation force is zero. To maintain the concept where the nominal field strength coinci des with the direction of an ion driven wind that results from positive ions flowing from high to low potential, the positive field direction aligns with the fluid flow direction (where the jet flows) from burner to mesh, as positive ions repel from the burner (Enominal= -V/d); a negative electric field is the opposite direction from mesh to burner, and the positive ions move toward the burner, as indicated in Figure 7.

Surprises and New Discoveries We expect many more discoveries to arise as we sort through the detailed data sets, but the initial surprises and discoveries include: (1) The behavior of the V-I curve is distinctly different in microgravity as compared to 1-g flames, where in microgravity there is not a distinctive saturation ion current plateau but rather the flames exhibit a distinct peak ion current that corresponds to the most compact flame. Th ese results show that buoyancy driven flows are an important influence on 1-g flames even when an electric field is applied. (2) When soot is present in a flame, electric fields create a wide range of unpredictable behaviors that include elimination of the soot through what appears to be enhanced mixing for combustion, showers of luminous particles that are likely to be incandescent soot agglomerates, and unstable dancing flames. Sooting is far more significant in flames in microgravity than is seen in similar conditions with 1-g flames. (3) There are clear correlations between flame luminosity, combustion intensity, and ion current.

The results suggest that the most robust burning also produces the highest ion current, even though the flame is most compact. (4) The very weak low fuel concentration flames were stabilized at ignition with very small electric fields, where without the fields the flames would quickly quench . This stabilizing feature of electric fields for weak zero gravity flames was a surprise, and it suggests that electric fields may be a good tool for approximating buoyancy body forces at partial gravity. (5) Jet flames under the influence of the electric field were unstable at high field strengths, and these flames experienced corona and then arc discharges due to the large field concentration near the jet burner tip. The flame behavior was dramatic but difficult to characterize, suggesting a spatially- and time-varying field/flame interaction.

F. Additional Objectives Achieved As we became more familiar with the conditions that provided the most impactful data, we reconstructed some test cases to provide more comprehensive matching of fundamental conditions. For example, it is known that flames of similar character (i.e., tempe rature and intensity) have saturation ion currents that scale with the input carbon to the flame. Thi s is because the dominant chemical pathway to the key ion species includes HCO+. Hence, to examine this feature of flames under electric field influence, we ran additional conditions with matching input carbon content.

Matching carbon content with higher or lower flow rate s: In addition to the core objectives achieved, experiments were run to match the carbon content of flames as a test for the role of fuel carbon in the ion-current peak production. Classical theory shows that ion current scales with carbon content for premixed flames, and some 1-g data shows similar trends for diffusion flames, but no one had determined if the concept held for zero-g flames. Flame response hysteresis: We also obtained data for flames where the electric field was ramped up and down to determ ine any effects of hysteresis in the ion current or flame response. This was an additional objective achieved. G. Impacts, Benefits, and Products The impact of this work is, as the original objectives identified, the delivery of a uni que data set of chemi-ion behavior in flames under sufficiently stable and symmetric conditions that models and theories can be evaluated against the results. As an example, the very distinctive shape of the V-I curve in microgravity, when matched in mode ls, will give a very good indication that the feedback between ion driven wind and changes in flame shape and burning behavior that then further change the ion current is captured accurately. These results have already garnered the interest of other groups working on electric field effects on flames.

The use of electric field effects on flames can be as sensor (variations of ion current as associated with combustion behavior) or actuator (ion -driven wind changes the flame shape and characteristics). Thi s work, as was origin ally planned, provides quantitative evaluation of the sensing and response potential of electric fields in combustion. The applications can include the control of flames.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 40 Follow-On Experiments We hope to have a third round of testi ng so that we can concentrate on flames in the coflow burner configuration that we found to be the more useful and symmetric than those with the jet burner. It is likely that the more uniform electric field is responsible for this observation. As noted above, useful results regarding the flame response time were obtained despite the slow response time of the power supply time through tests with fast upward voltage steps in some configurations. The step response is not as comprehensive as we would like, however, to confirm the links between the ion driven wind as actuator and sensor. For objective D, we obtained very interesting information about flame stabilization and destabilization using electric fields but not in the manner we expected. Rather the destabilizing influence of the field producing fluctuations in the flame was more pronounced a phenomenon than we had seen when buoyancy was also part of the body force involved. We did not get to limit flames except that w e showed clearly how in microgravity a flame can be stabilized with a small field rather than simply expanding and extinguishing. So that is some information again at the limit. We can discover more by concentrating on very low field strengths.

The outcomes of the first two rounds justify further testing because the results were so successful. The success showed how perfectly the E -FIELD Flames experiment fits the capabilities and limitations of the CIR. It is a configuration that can use the imaging c apabilities at their current performance effectively. The experiments manipulate flames between quasi-steady behaviors in microgravity rather than passively observing non -steady flames evolving. The first rounds of testing spanned the experimental configuration space in terms of gases, flow rates, field ranges, and burner types. These spanning experiments mapped the phenomena but did not allow a deep dive into the conditions that showed the most dramatic changes of flame character with changes in electric field strength. In addition, excessive amounts of soot made unraveling some of the gas phase ion chemistry more complicated in the pure fuel cases, so we can now concentrate on moderate sooting cases. In general, t he bonus tests let us go back to the known "b est case" situations and resolve the processes ( e.g., flame shape, luminosity, soot formation and disappearance, ion current). That is the matrix we proposed. It is not within the scope of the current work, but we continue to advocate for a Schlieren imaging capability in zero-g combustion systems.

The ability to image hot gas flows would benefit a range of experiments and would be particularly useful for the flames in electric field situations because alternative methods for determining flows would not be possible in the high field environments. It may be that the 5-second drop facility is appropriate for many of these companion tests.

Introduction The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. In this experiment, an electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts is established between the burner and a flat, circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner . The motion of the charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are strongly affected by a strong electric field. The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting behavior of the flame. Measurements are made of electric-field strength, the ion current passing through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, tempe rature, soot, and stability. Conducting the tests in microgravity allows for great simplifications in the analysis of ion-driven convection and flame interaction, enabling new understanding and the development of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 44 An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions produced as a result of the combustion reactions. The induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the soot and stability limits, and d irect the heat transfer. The purpose of the E -FIELD Flames experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and lea rn how the electric field can be used to manipulate the ions and control non-premixed flames for practical benefit. For example, electric fields can enable stable burner operation at fuel -lean conditions with reduced pollutant emission, i.e., where the fl ame is not reliably sustained without the electric field. As another example, the role of electric fields on soot fo rmation can be dramatic. It appears that the ion driven wind alters the local convection and strongly influences the residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame. The experiment contributes to our critical understanding of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields. More specifically, E-FIELD Flames has the following experimental objectives: A. Determine the relatio nship between electric field voltage and chemi -ion current as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rat e and the amount of inert (nitrogen) in the fuel. B.

Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. C. Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. D. Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize the combustion behavior of near -limit lifted flames and use the associated ion -driven wind to stabilize or reattach these flames. The effect of the electric field on the flame is studied through tests conducted with a range of flame and electric field conditions. The fuel, fuel jet velocity, air flow, electric -field voltage and polarity are the primary parameters of the E-FIELD Flames experiment. Tests are conducted with methane and ethylene, including nitrogen dilutions of each, which provide a broad range of sootproducing conditions, i.e., from soot -free to highly sooting. They are conducted wi th both a simple gas-jet burner and the coflow burner that was also used for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment.

Tests with the coflow burner is conducted with and without a coflow of air, where the results of the latter are compared with those from the gas-jet burner to assess the effect of air entrainment on the flame. The coflow burner also provides a different electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane). In a typical test, the mesh electrode is energized at increasing potentials (relative to the burner), where the flame’s response (e.g., ion current, luminosity, shape) to the resulting field strength is measured. The field strength is changed in repeated steps or is instead smoothly ramped. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e.,

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 45 gravity-driven) instability, is elimi nated yielding quasi -steady flames in microgravity . Microgravity flame flicker is then the result of electric body forces alone . Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum - dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much s tronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new unde rstanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustio n application. Chemi-ion species, electronically excited chemiluminescent species are very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. II. Methods/Research Operations A.

Discussion of Method/Protocol E-FIELD Flames and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include t he gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it may alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where c hanges are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. For example, the mesh voltage can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or soot limit. This was not done durin g Increments 55-56, where the console commanding during a test was typically limited to halti ng the test when it was observed in the analog ops video that the flame had extinguished. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undoc k from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight A total of 142 flames were ignited for the E -FIELD Flames experiment during Increments 55 and 56. The first round of testing occurred from March to May 2018, which was followed by a second round, which began in September 2018 and was still underway at the beginning of Increment 57. The first round of tests resulted in 120 ignited flames conducted with the same coflow burner used by the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, where CLD Flame’s second round occurred between the two rounds of the E-FIELD Flames experiment. The ‘interruption’ in the E -FIELD Flames testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. E-FIELD Flames does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene. Both are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood. Methane (CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds. Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting because of its carbon double bond.

For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed with nitrogen over a broad range of dilutions. For limited cases, the fuel and nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch. ACME bottles were launched with methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis). Similarly, bottles were launched with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 50%, and 100%, again with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis). But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations. In all cases, the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis). There a re no samples (e.g., of soot) collected for E -FIELD Flames, where all of the ISS results are electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently planned ACME experiments. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data E-FIELD Flames tests sometimes automatically abort (due to the controlling software script), where that is typically prior to gas fl ow and the activation of the igniter. As a result, there is little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt. The aborts normally occur because of communication issues with IPSU-1. These are infrequent, but there are some days when tests abort repeatedly. Tests are of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite.

The first test of the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been sufficiently primed. Ignition is sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of the igniter glow rather than a flame. As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite. This is typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* chemiluminescence with a P hotomultiplier Tube (PMT) module. The OH* chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible spectrum. However, the combination of ig niter settings and PMT gains can lead to false ignition detection. The key measurement for the E-FIELD Flames experiments is the ion current as a function of applied voltage, i.e., the voltage-current or V-I curve. This curve provides information on the flam es ability to produce chemi -ions based on its saturation ion current, and it provides a measure of combustion performance in that ion production is a function of carbon i nflux into the flame and the vigorousness of the combustion process. Introduction The Electric -Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E -FIELD Flames) experimen t wa s conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. In this experiment, an electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts was established between the burner and a flat, circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner . The motion of the charged ions, which are naturally prod uced within the flame, are strongly affected by a strong electric field. The resulting ion -driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting behavior of the flame. Measurements we re made of electric -field strength, the ion current passing through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, soot, and stability. Conducting the tests in microgravity allow ed for great simplifications in the

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 59 analysis of ion -driven convection and flame interaction , enabling new understanding and the development of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth. An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions produced as a result of the combustion reactions. The induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the soot and stability limits, and direct the h eat transfer. The purpose of the E -FIELD Flames experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how the electric field can be used to manipulate the ions and control non-premixed flames for practical benefit. For example , electric fields can enable stable burner operation at fuel -lean conditions with reduced pollutant emission, i.e., where the flame is not reliably sustained without the electric field. As another example, the role of electric fields on soot formation can be dramatic. It appears that the ion driven wind alters the local convection and strongly influences the residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame . The experiment contributes to our critical understanding of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields. More specifically, E-FIELD Flames has the following experimental objectives: A.

Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi -ion current as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the a mount of inert (nitrogen) in the fuel. B. Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. C. Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amoun t of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. D. Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize the combustion behavior o f near -limit lifted flames and use the associated ion -driven wind to stabilize or reattach these flames. The effect of the electric field on the flame is studied through tests conducted with a range of flame and electric field conditions. The fuel, fuel jet velocity, air flow, elect ric-field voltage and polarity were the primary parameters of the E-FIELD Flames experiment.

Tests were conducted with methane and ethylene, including nitrogen dilutions of each, which provide a broad range of soot-producing conditions, i.e., from soot-free to highly sooting. They were carried out with both a simple gas-jet burner and the coflow burner that was also used for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment. Tests with the coflow burner were conducted with and without a coflow of air, where the results of the la tter are compared with those from the gas -jet burner to assess the effect of air entrainment on the flame. The coflow burner also provided a different electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane). In a typical test, the mesh electrode was energized at increasing potentials (relative to the burner), where the flame’s response (e.g., ion current, luminosity, shape) to the resulting field strength wa s measured. The field strength was changed in repeated steps or was instead smoothly ramped.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 60 Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal -gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flame s, which is a buoyancy - driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Therefore, the flicker in the E -FIELD Flames was a result of electric body forces alone . Length scales are incre ased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronge r sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normalgravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but ma ny microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi -ion species, electronically excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry.

With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of com bustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the c ombustion application. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol E-FIELD Flames and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it may alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mo de, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. For example, the mesh voltage can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or soot limit. This was not done during Increments 55 -56 or 57 -58, where the console commanding during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed in the analog ops video that the flame had extinguished.

Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spac ecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight A total of 219 flames were ignited for the E -FIELD Flames experiment, with 142 and 77 respectively ignited d uring Increments 55 -56 and 57 -58. Note that the investigation’s testing was completed during Increment 57, so no flames were ignited during Increment 58. The first and second rounds of testing respectively occurred in March-May 2018 and September-November 2018. The two rounds of tests resulted in 120 and 99 ignited flames conducted with coflow an d gas-jet burners, respectively. The coflow burner was developed for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, where CLD Flames’ second round o ccurred between the two rounds of the E -FIELD Flames experiment. The ‘interruption’ in the E -FIELD Flames testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. E-FIELD Flames does not have living sub jects like a life science experiment, but the tests are independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene. Both are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.

Methane (CH4) is the primary component o f natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds. Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting because of its carbon double bond. For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed with nitrogen over a broad range of dilutions. For limited cases, the fuel and nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch. ACME bottles were launched with methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis). S imilarly, bottles were launched with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 50%, and 100%, again with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis). But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations. In all cases, the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis). No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected for E -FIELD Flames; all of the ISS results were electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently planned ACME experiments. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data E-FIELD Flame s tests sometimes automatically abort ed (due to the controlling software script), where that was typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter. As a result, there was little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt. The aborts normally occur red because of communication issues with IPSU-1. These are infrequent, but there are some days when tests aborted repeatedly. Tests are of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite. The first test of the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been sufficiently primed.

Ignition was sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the automatic flame detection are such th at detection threshold is reached because of the igniter glow rather than a flame. As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite. This is typically avoided by d etecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module. The OH* chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible spectrum. However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to false ignition detection. ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and synthetic air (i.e., 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen, on a volume basis) have unfortunately not always performed adequately. The fuel and especially nitrogen flows sometimes oscillate. Furthermore, the MFC used for the ‘air’ coflow behaves as if it is sticking in a few pla ces, where the flow rate won’t linearly ramp when commanded (as required for the CLD Flame experiment) . It t ends to stick in some places and then abruptly overshoot where that has sometimes been seen to extinguish the flame.

As a result, mass flow contro llers are tested - without flames - after they are first installed. Adjustments are often then made to (1) the settings that control when the valves open and (2) the Proportional -Integral-Derivative (PID) settings. In contrast, 219 flames were ignited in the experiment , so nearly three times as many flames were ignited than required. It should be understood that a complete set of image data is not available for all tests.

As discussed in section III.B, the IPSU-1 was not working at the beginning of the second round of testing, preventing use of both the HiBMs camera and the CIR’s collimated illumination package. Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice some image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted. This is intentionally done in order to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing within the project constraints. Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware. But neglecting that limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels graduall y become ‘hot’ over time. While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, they are a degradation of the image quality. It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there is not obvious indication of this and it has thus far not been e valuated with available measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS).

Status of Data Analysis Data from the tests making up the E -FIELD Flames experiment includes video recordings from the operations camera for general flame behavior, high resolution images from the ACME data camera at various exposures and frame rates as dictated by the flame luminosity, intensified camera images, and non-imaging data at 125 Hz. The non-imaging data file is processed using Matlab scripts (modified from those developed by CLD Flame researchers) to separately show trends of ion current and flame luminosity as a function of the applied field, and the flame parameters (fuel, flowrate, burner type). The PMT data is also extracted to evaluate flame luminosity oscillations. Image data is processed using the OMA software (also developed and used by CLD Flame researchers). The overall data volume is lar ge with a storage limit of 127,000 MB p er test day. All of the data has been downloaded to the hard drive with a backup system at UC Irvine. At this stage, the data has been sorted into appropriate segments so that comparisons can be made between burner geometries (jet versus coflow from the prior round of testing), fuel type and dilution (methane versus ethylene; no dilution, modest dilution, high dilution) and fuel flow velocity.

The fuel flow velocity and dilution conditions were sometimes selected to hold total carbon flux into the flame constant. At this stage, the analysis remains comparative and qualitative, to show the major differences in behavior in microgravity and normal -gravity (1-g) flames, and to show particularly how buoyancy modifies the electrical response of the flames. E. Preliminary Research Findings Distinctly different results were seen in E-FIELD Flames’ second round tests with the gasjet burner when compared with the first round tests with the coflow burner. For example, the ion current response to the electric field s trength with an upward ion driven wind in microgravity is a clear parabolic trend (which is similar to the trend observed in 1-g flames with the coflow burner as presented in the prior report). The parabolic behavior is evident even with the strong oscill ations observed during the rise. This rising trend is not observed with the coflow burner. The behavior of the soot and its charge state are complicated since in the regions of high field strength, particularly near the fuel tube where the field lines converge, soot can emit or collect free charges. Hence, the soot transport is driven directly by the field and by the ion-driven wind (and thermophoresis) which means it can travel differentially to the bulk flow.

These various transport elements can push the soot through the flame to burnout, hold it in stasis in the flame for additional growth, or drive it to the burner where it accumulates. More work is needed to sort through these elements. This report shows the initial results of the E -FIELD Flames experiment using the gas -jet burner in the International Space Station (ISS). The p ositive field allows the soot to concentrate and compresses the flame into a high current density thermal source. The flames demonstrate an unpredicted oscillation before extinguishing with increasing field strength. This oscillating phenomenon was not observed during the tests with the coflow burner from the first round , with the exception of a case that introduced the airflow at 30 cm/s which increased the surface reaction while the flame tended to balance between electric field effects, ions, and charg ed soot. The negative field allow s the flame to maintain its spherical characteristic in microgravity.

The yellow soot appears for both of the electric field directions within the flame around the tip and disappears with increasing field strength after reaching the current peak. E-FIELD Flames studies how electric fields at different voltages influence flames.

An electric field can strongly influence the motion of the ions produced by a combustion reaction. The resulting ion -driven wind impacts flame stability and soot production and reduces pollutant emissions. The results will lead to a better understanding of more efficient and less polluting combustion technology for use on Earth. Week 03: March 9-15 On GMT 073, we performed the firs t ACME E -FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames) test points. This first day was very successful with ten flames ignited for studying the effects of an electric field on laminar diffusion flames. Preliminary results show that the high-voltage electric field created forces similar to buoyancy, which dramatically affected the flame’s shape, intensity, and soot production. The ability to control flames with an electric field may have practical applications on Earth. For example, an electric field could be used to stabilize a flame in fuel-lean conditions, which would lead to reduced pollutant emissions compared to a typical combustor. E-FIELD Flames round 1 featuring the coflow burner Week of March 12, 2018 Crew begins first week of new ACME operations The Advanced Combustion Microgravity Experiment ( ACME) investigation is a set of studies of gaseous flames to be conducted in the Combustion Integration Rack (CIR), one of which being Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames). In E-FIELD Flames, an electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts is established between the burner and a mesh electrode. The motion of the charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are strongly affected by a high-voltage electric field. The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting behavior of the flame. Measurements are made of electric-field strength, the ion current passing through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, soot, and stability. Conducting the tests in microgravity enables new understanding and the development of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth. This week marks the first week of E-FIELD flames operations with a very successful first set of ten flames ignited for studying the effects of an electric field on laminar diffusion flames. Preliminary results show that the high-voltage electric field created forces similar to buoyancy.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 97 Appendix J. Summary of the ISS data collection The E-FIELD Flames data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where this is true for the other current ACME experiments. To be clear, there is no collection of soot or other physical samples that are subsequently transported to the ground. The E-FIELD Flames image data includes images from the ACME DataCam, the CFI intensified camera (used with the CH* filter), and the High -Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera (equipped with a red filter corresponding to the opposing CIR illumination p ackage). The DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI and HiBMs cameras are in a Tagged Image File (tif) format. In contrast, the analog video was recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). The data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available publicly through NASA’s Physical Science Informatics System (PSI).

Unlocking Mysteries in Microgravity:
NASA Glenn Provides the Keys With the Fluids and Combustion Facility What Is Microgravity?
 Gravity is a force that governs motion throughout the universe. It holds us to the ground and keeps the Earth in orbit around the Sun. Microgravity describes the environment in orbital space flight, which has very weak gravitational effects (one-millionth of what is felt on Earth) and which is sometimes referred to as a state of “weightlessness.” The condition of microgravity occurs when an object is in “free fall.” In free fall, an object falls faster and faster, accelerating with exactly the speed of attraction caused by gravity. Objects travelling around the Earth in a state of continuous free fall, or orbit, are essentially weightless even though their mass remains the same.
 Conducting research in a microgravity environment gives researchers a unique opportunity to study the true nature of processes and materials without having to consider the effects of Earth’s gravity. Thus, physics theories can be tested at levels of accuracy that are impossible on Earth. Microgravity experiments uncover the mystery of how gravity affects processes such as combustion science and fluid physics.

This knowledge can then help to improve the way we do things on Earth.
Astronaut Michael Fincke, Expedition 18 commander, works on the Combustion Integrated Rack in the Destiny Laboratory of the International Space Station.

Powering the Future 2 NASA Facts A World-Class Orbiting Laboratory The term “microgravity” will become more commonplace when the International Space Station (ISS) is fully operational. The ISS will be the largest orbiting space structure and the largest international scientific and technological endeavor in history. Sixteen countries, including the United States, are participating in this record-breaking project. The ISS is a permanent laboratory in space where studies can be performed without the effects of gravity.
 The space station provides researchers with all the laboratory space and equipment and electrical power needed for safe, long-term research by human beings in space. The ISS enables larger and longer experiments than were possible on the typical 2-week space shuttle mission. This gives scientists time for more detailed observation in the microgravity environment.
 The knowledge gained from ISS microgravity experiments is benefiting research on Earth in many fields. Our understanding of theories relevant to everything from hightemperature superconductivity to weather prediction will be advanced. New insights into areas such as human health and disease prevention and treatment will be achieved. In addition, scientists are using the microgravity environment to uncover other, more subtle forces and interactions in fluids and materials.

By essentially taking gravitational effects out of the equation, researchers are able to study as primary characteristics what would have been secondary behaviors on Earth.
 Simple investigations of fluid interfaces and combustion processes can be addressed in small, contained experiments, such as the shuttle Glovebox experiments. However, more complex and challenging investigations require dedicated facilities to contain fluids and products of combustion in a controlled and safe environment.
The ISS Fluids and Combustion Facility The United States Laboratory Module on the ISS contains the Fluids and Combustion Facility (FCF), designed and built at NASA Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, Ohio. The FCF was developed to accommodate the unique challenges of working with fluids and combustion processes in microgravity, as well as to provide services and capabilities comparable to those found in traditional Earthbased laboratories.
 Glenn was an ideal choice for this project because of their reputation for award-winning research, particularly in the areas of fluids and combustion, as well as their longstanding experience in developing experiment hardware and world-class test facilities. Glenn engineers and scientists have been involved in designing, producing, and managing space-based hardware and facilities since the 1960s.

As pioneers in rocket research, they had tested high-energy propellants even before the United States officially entered into the space business. Glenn Research Center advanced the propulsion technology that helped make space travel possible.
 The Center’s unique Zero Gravity Research Facility and other drop towers and laboratories were the source of foundational work in microgravity research. NASA’s Zero Gravity Trainer aircraft occasionally operates out of NASA Glenn in support of Glenn’s ground-based microgravity research. Some flights include astronauts participating in crew training so they can have low-gravity experience with experiment hardware and materials prior to shuttle missions. In all, these facilities give Glenn a unique ability to develop and test microgravity experiments.
 Glenn Research Center is NASA’s center of excellence for fluid physics and combustion science and has been responsible for 153 experiments on 47 shuttle flights. In addition to providing the FCF, they are a major contributor to the investigations onboard the FCF, in gloveboxes, and in other ISS facilities.

A forerunner of the FCF, the Glenndeveloped Combustion Module–1 (CM–1), which flew onboard the Shuttle Columbia, STS–83, in April 1997, laid the groundwork for the combustion portion of the new FCF with several hardware innovations.
 The FCF is ushering in a new era of fluids and combustion research. It is a modular, multi-user, permanent microgravity science laboratory that is making it possible for researchers on the ground, with the assistance of the astronauts in space, to schedule and perform studies of how fluids and flames behave in the absence of gravity at a cost that is not out of this world.
 The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) was delivered by the Space Shuttle Endeavour in November 2008 during mission STS–126. The Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) was delivered by Space Shuttle Discovery in August 2009 during mission STS–128. The two racks provide the basic physical and functional framework required to perform combustion science, fluid physics, and associated science Glenn researchers working on Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) during development.

 The end result is true facility operations with all of the capabilities that serious researchers expect on the ground without the effects of gravity. Combustion Science Combustion, or burning, is a process in which a substance reacts with oxygen to give off heat and light. Combustion meets almost 85 percent of the U.S. energy needs. While it does a good job of powering how we live on Earth, combustion is a major contributor to air pollution. The cost of combustion energy is about $450 billion each year in the United States. In any area of the economy where a huge amount of money is spent, even the smallest improvements in efficiency can mean savings of very large amounts of money. A mere 1 percent increase in fuel efficiency, like improving your gas mileage from 25 miles per gallon to 25.25 miles per gallon, would translate into a savings to America of nearly 100 million barrels of oil a year (roughly $5.5 million per day at today’s cost). Although today combustion is vital to transportation, materials processing, hazardous waste disposal, and many other areas, there is still only limited understanding of many of its fundamental characteristics.

There are over 2500 fatalities and tens of billions of dollars in property damage each year in accidental fires. Combustion research in microgravity can lead to advances in fire prevention, detection, and fighting. In addition, combustion research in microgravity can lead to more efficient use of energy, reduced pollution, and improved processes for making high-technology materials. Glenn Research Center’s experience with jet engines provides a solid background in combustion and Glenn scientists have already begun to study combustion in space. A simple example of microgravity’s effect in combustion is the behavior of flames in space. On Earth, hot air rises around a candle flame, which causes the flame to flicker and take on an elongated shape. In microgravity, however, no such distortion takes place. The flame, without the effects of gravity, has a steady, spherical shape. The FCF allows researchers to study aspects of combustion, such as flame behavior, that are impossible to observe on the ground. Their research will lead to a better understanding of whole processes, such as soot production, which will aid development of improvements in fire fighting and pollution reduction. Fluid Physics Of the four states of matter—solid, liquid, gas, and plasma—three are fluid, meaning they flow in response to an applied force.

An understanding of fluid physics is not only vital to advancing aircraft and spacecraft applications, such as airflow and propellant management, but is also essential to understanding the human body, aspects of everyday life, and many industrial processes. In microgravity, fluid positioning and flow characteristics can be studied from a new perspective. Scientists at NASA Glenn Research Center have played an important role in fluid physics research since the 1940s. With orbiting spacecraft, microgravity fluid physics became an important research area in which NASA Glenn has always played a leading role. Glenn is currently focusing its research on the enabling technology for space exploration (water and fuel flow, life support systems, temperature control, etc.) as well as on using the space environment (reduced gravity) to provide insight into phenomena that are important for Earth-based applications. One spinoff of the special nonintrusive instruments and techniques developed to perform the fluid experiments is a dynamic light scattering (DLS) probe and Hruby lens holder that make early detection of cataracts and other eye diagnoses easier. Glenn researchers have also experimented with the behavior of colloidal suspensions. A colloid is a system of fine particles suspended in a fluid.

Italian salad dressing provides a simple illustration of the effects of microgravity on the behavior of colloidal suspensions. In space you would need to shake the dressing only once, rather than between uses, which is needed on Earth. Paint, ink, milk, and orange juice are also common examples. Though these products are routinely produced and used, scientists know little about the underlying structure of colloidal systems because they are difficult to study in ground-based laboratories. Understanding their structures may allow scientists to manipulate the physical properties of colloids for the creation of new materials and products or to improve the manufacturing of known products. Operation of experiments via remote control is coordinated through the Telescience Support Center (TSC) at Glenn. Telescience is the systematic monitoring, command, and control of an experiment from a remote location and has already been implemented successfully by NASA on the shuttle/Spacelab and the Russian Mir Space Station. In concert with the work performed by the astronauts in space and the Cleveland-based operations team, the FCF principle investigator’s (PI’s) experiment can remotely monitor and control from the PI’s home site through Glenn’s TSC. The concept of telescience offers several advantages. Typically, the development of an experiment takes years and involves a varied group of scientists, engineers, and support personnel. Only a few of these people need to be on the operations team that travels to a NASA center to support actual mission operations.

A major benefit of remote operations is that the entire team that developed and built the experiment can be connected to the operations team to support data analysis, command decisions, anomaly resolution, and other real-time considerations. Also, some facilities that are not physically located at NASA centers can be included (e.g., colleges, universities, and industrial labs). Additional benefits are reductions in travel requirements and increases in the amount of science data acquired.
The Sky Is Not the Limit!
 With over 10 years of continuous occupation, the ISS was assembled by over 100 launches of Russian vehicles, the American space shuttles as well as European and Japanese vehicles. Over 150 spacewalks have been conducted in support of space station assembly totaling more than 944 hours. It has been visited by over 200 individuals, coming from 8 different countries. The newest star in the night sky continues to grow brightly, demonstrating to the world that its nations can work together in peace.
 Researchers at NASA Glenn, world leaders in microgravity science, continuously define scientific requirements and develop hardware for microgravity space experiments that will eventually have an impact on many areas of life here on Earth.

Microgravity research aboard the ISS’s FCF, developed by NASA Glenn, is helping to improve industrial processes, increase fundamental knowledge, advance our health care technologies, and make space exploration easier and safer. NASA Glenn has delivered and conducted 18 investigations on ISS with many more in the pipeline. This research is helping create new ideas for tomorrow’s products, today.
 Microgravity research on the ISS is showing life on Earth to us in ways we have never seen before. The sky is not the limit at NASA Glenn Research Center.

Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) Operational Requirements and Protocols Operational Requirements: Droplets must be deployed free floating without any residual momentum in the center of the field of view of the CIR diagnostics. Diagnostics must be capable of recording the radiant emissions of both hot and cool flames. CIR must store be able to store digital imagery data from a full day of test point (approx. 8 burns) for later downlink. Operational Protocols: Following setup and initialization of the CIR rack and MDCA, the chamber is filled with the appropriate atmosphere for the day’s test points. Conditions vary in pressure (0.5 atm to 5.0 atm) and oxygen concentration (10 to 30%). A settling time of approximately 2 minutes elapses prior to initiating the test in order to ensure that the temperature and pressure of the chamber gases have stabilized. This settling time is followed by the dispensing of a predetermined amount of fuel (based on the target droplet size) onto a support fiber. When sufficient fuel has been dispensed the dispensing needles are retracted and a dwell period of at least 10 seconds is allowed for the droplet internal fluid motion induced by deployment to subside.

This is then be followed by initiating power to an igniter pair for a selectable amount of time ranging from 1 second to 5 seconds after which the igniter will be retracted from the field of view. A near real-time download of the color camera video is required in order to verify successful droplet deployment, ignition, and overall progress of the experiment. Pressure and temperature data of the chamber environment is also required in near real time.
